Cardiac fibroma.description: A rare benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen. It usually arises within the ventricular myocardium, particularly the left ventricle, and may be found incidentally.

Cardiac hemangioma.description: A benign vascular tumor of the heart that can occur in any cardiac chamber or myocardial wall. It may remain asymptomatic or cause arrhythmia, obstruction, embolism, or pericardial effusion depending on size and location.

Cardiac myxoma.description: The most common benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising in the left atrium but occasionally occurring in the left ventricle. Symptoms may result from obstruction, embolization, or constitutional inflammation.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue, usually located in the subendocardial, subepicardial, or myocardial tissue. Many cardiac lipomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally.

Cardiac sarcoma.description: A rare malignant primary cardiac tumor, including undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, angiosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and myxofibrosarcoma. These tumors more often produce progressive symptoms because of invasion or obstruction.

Splenic infarction, potentially associat.normalized_text: Splenic infarction, potentially associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Splenic infarction, potentially associat.description: Splenic infarction is ischemic necrosis of part of the spleen caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow. In children, it can rarely complicate infections, including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, through inflammation or thrombosis.

Splenic abscess.description: A splenic abscess is a localized infection within the spleen, usually bacterial or fungal, that can produce fever, inflammation, and focal left upper abdominal pain. Imaging may show focal hypoechoic or complex splenic lesions.

Hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease.description: Hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease is disseminated Bartonella henselae infection that may cause fever and multiple inflammatory microabscess-like lesions in the spleen and/or liver, often in otherwise healthy children.

Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei i.normalized_text: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection) with hepatic and splenic abscesses
Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei i.description: A potentially severe tropical infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness, pneumonia, bacteremia, and characteristic multiple abscesses in the liver and spleen.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing one or more collections of pus in the liver, commonly caused by enteric gram-negative organisms, streptococci, or anaerobes. It causes fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and upper abdominal or diaphragmatic pain.

Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.description: An extraintestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica infection, usually acquired in endemic regions including parts of Southeast Asia. It commonly causes fever and liver abscess, sometimes with preceding or concurrent diarrhea.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection acquired through sandfly bites in endemic regions. It typically causes prolonged fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, and abnormal liver tests rather than an acute neutrophilic illness.

OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic at.normalized_text: OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic at.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, classically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spastic paraplegia, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or parkinsonism.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SP.description: A complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG7 variants. It produces progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic atrophy, visual impairment, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause gradually worsening spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and neurogenic bladder dysfunction; optic neuritis or optic atrophy may occur.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that predominantly affects the optic nerves and spinal cord, typically causing optic neuritis and myelitis. Most patients have aquaporin-4 antibodies, although seronegative disease occurs.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive ATP7B-related disorder causing impaired biliary copper excretion, with copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. It can cause hepatic disease, coagulopathy, neuroimaging abnormalities, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medications, which may produce cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, and impaired hepatic synthetic function.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and may present with jaundice, abnormal liver tests, and progression to chronic liver dysfunction.

Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.normalized_text: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) or other inherited cholestatic liver disease
Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.description: A group of inherited disorders of bile formation and transport that can cause persistent cholestasis, severe itching, jaundice, and progressive liver disease during childhood or adolescence.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An idiosyncratic systemic hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine, usually occurring within days to weeks of starting treatment, causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and inflammatory-marker elevation. It is not necessarily associated with dose or thiopurine methyltransferase activity.

Serum sickness-like reaction due to azat.normalized_text: Serum sickness-like reaction due to azathioprine
Serum sickness-like reaction due to azat.description: A medication-related immune reaction characterized by fever, rash, and joint pain, often developing one to two weeks after exposure to a new drug. Unlike classic serum sickness, complement consumption and immune-complex evidence may be absent.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), potentially drug-induced
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder causing abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, and elevated inflammatory markers. It may be triggered by medications, autoimmune disease, infection, or malignancy.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory panniculitis characterized by tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules, usually on the lower legs, often accompanied by fever, malaise, and ankle or knee arthralgia. It can be associated with medications, infections, inflammatory disease, and systemic autoimmune conditions.

Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bact.normalized_text: Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bacteremia
Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bact.description: Joint infection, sometimes accompanied by systemic infection and skin inflammation, causing fever, acute joint pain, swelling, and elevated inflammatory markers. Diabetes and immunosuppression increase risk.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft-tissue space after blunt neck trauma, which can expand and cause posterior pharyngeal wall swelling and delayed airway obstruction.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.description: Injury to the larynx from direct blunt force that may produce mucosal swelling, hemorrhage, cartilage injury, vocal impairment, dysphagia, and airway narrowing.

Traumatic pharyngeal soft-tissue injury.description: Contusion, edema, or hemorrhage of the pharyngeal wall following blunt neck trauma, potentially causing dysphagia and narrowing of the upper airway.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. The hypervascular pancreatic lesion and biochemical pattern strongly support this diagnosis.

Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.description: A syndrome of low blood glucose caused by inappropriate internal insulin secretion, most commonly due to insulinoma but also potentially from other pancreatic beta-cell disorders.

Sulfonylurea- or meglitinide-induced hyp.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin-secretagogue medications, which increase endogenous insulin and C-peptide levels and can biochemically resemble insulinoma.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, often without a discrete pancreatic tumor.

Adrenal insufficiency.description: Inadequate cortisol production can impair glucose maintenance during fasting and cause fatigue, weakness, and hypoglycemia, although it would not usually cause hyperinsulinemia.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility or subluxation of the false-rib costal cartilage, usually involving the 8th to 10th ribs, which can irritate an intercostal nerve and cause intermittent lower anterior chest or upper abdominal pain. The ultrasound appearance is compatible with abnormal relationship/mobility of the lower costal cartilages.

Interchondral subluxation of the 8th rib.description: Partial displacement or abnormal motion of a lower rib cartilage relative to the adjacent costal cartilage, commonly the 8th rib over or beneath the 9th rib. This is a structural mechanism underlying slipping rib syndrome.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or minor tearing of the muscles between the ribs, often after new or intense exercise, causing localized chest-wall pain that worsens with movement, coughing, deep breathing, or trunk rotation.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation or irritation of costochondral or chondrosternal junctions, producing localized reproducible chest-wall pain. It is usually benign and may follow repetitive physical activity.

Rib stress injury or stress fracture.normalized_text: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
Rib stress injury or stress fracture.description: An overuse injury of a rib caused by repetitive loading, which may occur in athletes and can cause focal chest-wall pain that gradually develops during training.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia, dysplastic or immature myeloid cells, and possible cytogenetic abnormalities, with organ infiltration that may involve the lungs.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic lung disease causing subacute respiratory symptoms, peripheral blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary infiltrates; it often responds rapidly to systemic corticosteroids.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A syndrome of persistent unexplained eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated organ damage, including pulmonary infiltrates, airway symptoms, cardiac disease, skin manifestations, or neurologic involvement.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: An eosinophil-rich necrotizing vasculitis typically associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, chronic rhinosinusitis, neuropathy, and pulmonary infiltrates; ANCA may be negative.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma,.normalized_text: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-positive (ALCL)
Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma,.description: A pediatric T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by large CD30-positive malignant lymphoid cells, often with ALK expression. It commonly causes fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, extranodal disease, and bone marrow or gastrointestinal involvement.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, usually presenting with painless lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, fatigue, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, poor growth, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease may produce fever, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gastrointestinal lesions, and elevated inflammatory markers, particularly in immunocompromised patients but occasionally in immunocompetent children.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies that causes prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias. It can occur in endemic tropical and subtropical regions.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria (severe fa.description: A mosquito-borne protozoal infection caused by P. falciparum, often producing high fever, hemolysis, jaundice, hemoglobinuria, kidney injury, and potentially cerebral or visual symptoms. The blood-smear appearance of multiple delicate ring forms, including appliqué forms, strongly supports this diagnosis.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral illness that commonly causes abrupt fever, severe headache, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally hepatic dysfunction or bleeding.

Leptospirosis.description: A zoonotic bacterial infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, myalgias, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine.

Enteric fever (typhoid fever).description: A systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi, typically acquired from contaminated food or water during travel. It causes sustained fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Acute viral hepatitis.description: Acute liver inflammation, commonly caused by hepatitis A or E after food or water exposure during travel, which may produce fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and dark urine.

Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation f.normalized_text: Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation from cervical spine hardware erosion
Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation f.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which a plate or screw erodes into the pharynx or esophagus, causing perforation, infection, and leakage into surrounding neck or mediastinal tissues.

Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.normalized_text: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with paraspinal abscess
Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and adjacent soft tissues, potentially producing a deep paraspinal abscess and spreading along fascial planes into the thoracic region.

Descending necrotizing mediastinitis.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum that spreads downward from a cervical or pharyngeal source, often causing pus collections, systemic infection, and extension into the chest.

Retropharyngeal or deep neck space absce.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal or deep neck space abscess
Retropharyngeal or deep neck space absce.description: A collection of infected fluid in the retropharyngeal or adjacent deep cervical spaces that can cause swallowing pain and may spread into the mediastinum.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus caused by a sudden rise in intraesophageal pressure, classically after forceful vomiting. It can cause pneumomediastinum, pleural contamination, pleural effusion, and life-threatening mediastinitis.

Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.normalized_text: Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophag.description: Inflammation and infection of the mediastinum, often resulting from esophageal perforation and leakage of air, gastric contents, and bacteria into mediastinal tissues.

Mallory-Weiss syndrome.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching or vomiting, typically producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than full-thickness esophageal rupture.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Free air in the mediastinum, sometimes triggered by vomiting, coughing, or increased intrathoracic pressure. In this clinical setting it should prompt evaluation for an esophageal perforation.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (funct.description: Paroxysmal seizure-like episodes caused by functional neurologic mechanisms rather than epileptic cortical discharges. They are commonly associated with trauma-related, mood, and anxiety disorders and may include prolonged shaking, stiffening, unresponsiveness, or unusual motor activity.

Generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizu.description: Epileptic seizures characterized by abrupt loss of consciousness, generalized tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, and a postictal recovery period. They may cause falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, lactate elevation, and creatine kinase elevation.

Panic attacks with functional motor mani.normalized_text: Panic attacks with functional motor manifestations
Panic attacks with functional motor mani.description: Panic attacks are abrupt surges of intense fear or distress accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as palpitations, nausea, visual disturbance, and impaired concentration. In some patients, severe anxiety can coexist with functional seizure-like motor episodes.

Obturator hernia with small-bowel obstru.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly, multiparous women and may compress the obturator nerve, causing medial thigh or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign).

Femoral hernia with small-bowel obstruct.description: A hernia passing through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in women and has a high risk of incarceration and bowel obstruction.

Incarcerated inguinal hernia with small-.normalized_text: Incarcerated inguinal hernia with small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated inguinal hernia with small-.description: An inguinal hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through the inguinal canal and can become trapped, producing bowel obstruction or strangulation.

Adhesive small-bowel obstruction.description: Mechanical obstruction caused by fibrous intra-abdominal adhesions, most often after prior abdominal or pelvic surgery.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. Corpus callosum lesions on brain MRI are characteristic.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and may cause visual, sensory, and other neurologic deficits.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (primary CNS vasculitis)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An inflammatory vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord that can produce headaches, multifocal ischemic lesions, and fluctuating neurologic deficits.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by audiovestibular dysfunction, especially sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, together with inflammatory eye disease such as interstitial keratitis; retinal vasculitis can occur in atypical cases.

Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.normalized_text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF syndrome), usually due to MT-TK m.8344A>G mutation
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder characterized by myopathy, ragged-red fibers, cerebellar ataxia, seizures or myoclonus, hearing loss, and variable cardiac and cognitive involvement. Late-onset presentations may be dominated by axial muscle weakness and paraspinal atrophy.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to mitochondr.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to mitochondrial DNA mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy due to mitochondr.description: A group of disorders caused by pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants that impair oxidative phosphorylation. Presentations can include exercise intolerance, proximal or axial myopathy, elevated CK, hearing loss, cardiac arrhythmias, cognitive changes, and neurologic manifestations such as ataxia.

Maternally inherited diabetes and deafne.normalized_text: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness / m.3243A>G-related mitochondrial disease
Maternally inherited diabetes and deafne.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder most often caused by the m.3243A>G MT-TL1 variant. It may cause sensorineural hearing loss, myopathy, exercise intolerance, cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia, cognitive impairment, diabetes, and sometimes MELAS-spectrum neurologic disease.

Myofibrillar myopathy, including desmin-.description: An inherited muscle disorder caused by disruption of structural proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle. It can produce axial and proximal weakness, dropped head or bent-spine syndrome, elevated CK, myopathic EMG changes, and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Spinocerebellar ataxia with associated m.normalized_text: Spinocerebellar ataxia with associated myopathy, such as mitochondrial recessive ataxia or selected dominant spinocerebellar ataxias
Spinocerebellar ataxia with associated m.description: Inherited ataxia disorders can cause progressive gait imbalance and cerebellar atrophy; some genetic forms also produce peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, seizures, hearing loss, or skeletal-muscle involvement.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of childhood, often involving extranodal sites and sometimes bone marrow/blood (Burkitt leukemia). It typically expresses mature B-cell markers, surface immunoglobulin, CD10, and CD20.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-center B-cell type
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-.description: A mature aggressive B-cell lymphoma composed of large B cells, often presenting as a nodal or extranodal mass. Germinal-center type tumors can express CD10 and B-cell markers, although this entity is less common than Burkitt lymphoma in very young children.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of precursor B lymphoblasts that commonly affects young children and can present with bone pain, anemia, lymphadenopathy, soft-tissue masses, and circulating blasts. Typical cases express TdT and CD34 and lack surface immunoglobulin.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis in which parasite eggs lodge in portal venules, causing granulomatous inflammation and periportal fibrosis, potentially leading to hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension.

Traumatic hepatic hematoma.description: A collection of blood within or beneath the liver capsule following blunt abdominal trauma; it can cause right upper-quadrant pain and may become infected or cause prolonged inflammatory symptoms.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing a localized collection of pus in the liver, usually presenting with fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and inflammatory illness.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: A hepatic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica, often associated with intestinal amoebiasis and characterized by fever and right upper-quadrant pain.

diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings consistent with anterior wall ischemic injury.

Essential thrombocythemia with coronary.normalized_text: Essential thrombocythemia with coronary arterial thrombosis
Essential thrombocythemia with coronary.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent thrombocytosis and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis causing myocardial infarction.

Polycythemia vera with hyperviscosity-re.normalized_text: Polycythemia vera with hyperviscosity-related coronary thrombosis
Polycythemia vera with hyperviscosity-re.description: A JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased red blood cell mass, often accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, causing thrombosis and aquagenic pruritus.

Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal/vasospast.normalized_text: Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal/vasospastic angina) causing myocardial infarction
Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal/vasospast.description: Transient coronary artery vasoconstriction, often occurring at rest or during sleep, which can cause episodic chest pain and transient ST-segment elevation; prolonged spasm can cause infarction.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease or esoph.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause burning substernal discomfort, often worse at night or when lying down, and may improve with acid-suppressive therapy.

Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.normalized_text: Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy due to severe perinatal asphyxia
Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Brain injury caused by impaired oxygen delivery and/or blood flow around the time of birth, commonly following prolonged fetal distress, difficult delivery, or cardiopulmonary arrest.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Respiratory failure caused by aspiration of meconium-containing amniotic fluid before or during delivery, leading to airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, air trapping, and possible persistent pulmonary hypertension.

Neonatal pneumothorax / pulmonary air-le.description: Air leakage from the lungs into the pleural space, potentially causing lung collapse and hemodynamic compromise. It may occur spontaneously or after positive-pressure ventilation and resuscitation.

Bronchopulmonary sequestration, possibly.normalized_text: Bronchopulmonary sequestration, possibly with an anomalous systemic arterial supply
Bronchopulmonary sequestration, possibly.description: A congenital pulmonary malformation in which nonfunctioning lung tissue lacks normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree and receives blood supply from the systemic circulation, often from the descending aorta. It can cause respiratory distress and may be identified by abnormal thoracic imaging and Doppler/CT angiography.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.normalized_text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.description: Failure of the normal postnatal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in right-to-left shunting and severe hypoxemia. It is often associated with meconium aspiration, birth asphyxia, pneumonia, or pulmonary air-leak disorders.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: A complement-dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar and glomerular thrombi, hemolysis, severe hypertension, and acute or chronic kidney failure. It may be triggered by drugs, infection, or cocaine use and can have a familial pattern.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, severe hypertension, and thrombotic microangiopathy, resulting in acute kidney injury, hemolysis, and renal vascular lesions.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: A hypertensive emergency can produce endothelial damage and fibrinoid vascular injury, causing renal failure, proteinuria, hemolysis with schistocytes, and characteristic concentric arteriolar thickening.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, often with mixed cryoglobulinemia, low complement levels, proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal impairment.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: TTP is a severe ADAMTS13-deficiency thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurologic symptoms, and variable kidney injury.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies. Lesions in the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause intractable nausea, vomiting, and hiccups, followed by brainstem neurological deficits.

Area postrema syndrome.description: A clinical syndrome caused by involvement of the area postrema in the dorsal medulla, characterized by otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and/or hiccups. It is most commonly associated with NMOSD.

Brainstem encephalitis (rhombencephaliti.description: Inflammation of the brainstem and cerebellum, which may be autoimmune, infectious, or paraneoplastic. It can cause cranial nerve dysfunction, nystagmus, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise.

Multiple sclerosis with brainstem involv.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease affecting the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. Brainstem lesions may cause nystagmus, dysphagia, weakness, and upper motor neuron signs.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare, often subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod associated with animal or animal-product exposure. It has a strong association with native aortic-valve infection and is characteristically resistant to vancomycin, while often susceptible to penicillin.

Native aortic-valve infective endocardit.description: Infection of the native cardiac valve endocardium, usually caused by bacteria, producing persistent fever, constitutional symptoms, valvular vegetations, new or changing murmurs, and valve regurgitation.

Enterococcus faecalis infective endocard.description: A subacute form of infective endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis, commonly affecting older adults or patients with cardiac disease and often involving native valves, particularly the aortic or mitral valve.

Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.normalized_text: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic embolization through a patent foramen ovale
Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.description: Air entering the venous circulation during venesection can travel to the right heart and pulmonary arteries. With a patent foramen ovale, air may cross from the right to left atrium and embolize to the cerebral and coronary circulations.

Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causin.normalized_text: Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causing transient ischemic attack
Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causin.description: A paradoxical cerebral air embolus occurs when venous air crosses a right-to-left cardiac shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale, enters the arterial circulation, and temporarily obstructs cerebral blood flow.

Coronary air embolism causing acute myoc.normalized_text: Coronary air embolism causing acute myocardial ischemia
Coronary air embolism causing acute myoc.description: Air reaching the coronary arterial circulation through a right-to-left shunt can obstruct coronary blood flow, producing acute chest pain, ECG changes, and myocardial injury despite absence of atherosclerotic coronary occlusion.

Pulmonary air embolism.description: Air introduced into a peripheral vein can enter the pulmonary arterial circulation, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxaemia, acute dyspnoea, chest pain, and potentially transient increases in right-sided cardiac pressure.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A rare, usually superficial cerebral astrocytic tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe of younger patients and commonly presents with longstanding seizures. BRAF V600E mutations are frequent.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and potential recurrence or progression from an initially lower-grade PXA. BRAF V600E may remain present.

Ganglioglioma.description: A typically slow-growing mixed neuronal-glial tumor, often located in the temporal lobe and strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some tumors harbor BRAF V600E mutations.

Diffuse low-grade glioma.description: A diffusely infiltrating primary glial tumor that may cause seizures and headaches, particularly when involving the cerebral cortex. Molecular features commonly include IDH mutation rather than BRAF V600E.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype.description: An aggressive high-grade diffuse astrocytic glioma that generally presents in older adults with progressive headaches, neurologic deficits, seizures, and rapidly enlarging infiltrative lesions.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by characteristic cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle inflammation causing weakness.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: A subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy associated with antisynthetase antibodies, inflammatory myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and mechanic's hands.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness, typically without the distinctive skin manifestations of dermatomyositis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease characterized by rapidly progressive proximal weakness and markedly elevated muscle enzymes, often associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies; skin findings are generally absent.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term enzyme-inducing antiepileptic therapy, such as phenytoin, which accelerates vitamin D metabolism and can lead to vitamin D deficiency, impaired mineralization of bone, and insufficiency fractures.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of adult bone, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency. It causes diffuse bone pain, muscle weakness, and characteristic pseudofractures known as Looser's zones.

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: A disorder of impaired bone mineralization due to chronically low phosphate, which may be inherited, medication-related, or caused by renal phosphate wasting. It produces bone pain, proximal weakness, and insufficiency fractures or Looser's zones.

Osteoporosis with bilateral femoral neck.normalized_text: Osteoporosis with bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fractures
Osteoporosis with bilateral femoral neck.description: Osteoporosis causes reduced bone mass and fragility fractures, including femoral neck insufficiency fractures. It can cause pain after fractures but usually does not itself cause diffuse muscle pain or classic Looser's zones.

Group A streptococcal infective endocard.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis of the mitral valve with septic cerebral embolic stroke
Group A streptococcal infective endocard.description: Acute bacterial infection of the mitral valve caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, producing valvular vegetation, mitral regurgitation, bacteremia, and embolization to the brain causing ischemic stroke.

Acute cardioembolic ischemic stroke.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of thrombotic or infected material from the heart, in this case most likely from mitral-valve infective endocarditis.

Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to.normalized_text: Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to infective endocarditis, with congestive heart failure
Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to.description: Mitral-valve infection can damage valve leaflets or chordae and cause significant mitral regurgitation, producing left-sided cardiac volume overload, pulmonary congestion, respiratory distress, and elevated natriuretic peptide levels.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare ciliopathy characterized by craniofacial abnormalities, ectodermal findings involving hair, teeth, and nails, skeletal dysplasia, and progressive renal disease that may present with tubulointerstitial nephropathy or nephronophthisis-like kidney failure.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: A rare SMARCAL1-related multisystem disorder featuring progressive kidney disease, skeletal dysplasia with short stature, characteristic facial features, sparse hair, and susceptibility to infections due to immune dysfunction.

Jeune syndrome / asphyxiating thoracic d.description: A skeletal ciliopathy characterized by a narrow thorax, short ribs and limbs, brachydactyly, and possible progressive renal disease, retinal disease, and liver involvement.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A ciliopathy involving renal tubulointerstitial disease or nephronophthisis, skeletal abnormalities such as cone-shaped epiphyses and short digits, and retinal dystrophy; some affected children have craniofacial abnormalities.

Orofaciodigital syndrome type 9 / renal.normalized_text: Orofaciodigital syndrome type 9 / renal skeletal ciliopathy spectrum
Orofaciodigital syndrome type 9 / renal.description: A group of ciliopathies that can produce facial dysmorphism, digital and skeletal abnormalities, renal cystic or tubulointerstitial disease, and variable eye findings. Specific subtypes may overlap with cranioectodermal dysplasia.

Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis associate.normalized_text: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis associated with oesophageal malignancy
Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis associate.description: Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory autoimmune myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin lesions. In older adults, particularly men with new-onset dermatomyositis, it may be associated with an underlying cancer; the abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and PET-CT uptake raise concern for oesophageal malignancy.

Classic dermatomyositis.description: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory disease characterized by immune-mediated skeletal-muscle inflammation, proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and distinctive cutaneous findings such as Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign, and photosensitive poikiloderma.

Polymyositis.description: Polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy that causes symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and sometimes dysphagia. Unlike dermatomyositis, it does not produce the characteristic skin manifestations.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is a severe autoimmune muscle disease causing rapidly progressive proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase levels. It may be associated with statin exposure, autoantibodies, or malignancy, but characteristic dermatomyositis skin lesions are generally absent.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in children, causing fragmentation, collapse, and remodeling of the femoral head. It most often affects boys aged 4 to 10 years.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, typically occurring in adolescents during periods of rapid growth and often associated with obesity.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often following a viral illness, that commonly causes acute hip pain and limp in children.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: Bacterial infection of the hip joint that is an orthopedic emergency and usually presents with acute severe pain, systemic illness, fever, and refusal to bear weight.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection producing a collection of pus within the liver; gas-forming organisms can create intralesional gas that may mimic free air beneath the diaphragm on radiography.

Ruptured or leaking pyogenic liver absce.normalized_text: Ruptured or leaking pyogenic liver abscess with subphrenic gas
Ruptured or leaking pyogenic liver absce.description: A liver abscess can extend to the liver surface and rupture or leak into the subphrenic/peritoneal space, causing peritonism and an apparent pneumoperitoneum.

Perforated peptic ulcer.description: A gastric or duodenal ulcer can perforate, releasing air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity and causing acute upper abdominal pain with pneumoperitoneum.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, and characteristic facial and neurologic findings.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.description: A developmental disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4, characterized by growth restriction, microcephaly, severe developmental delay, hypotonia, distinctive craniofacial features, and frequent seizures and congenital heart defects.

Angelman syndrome.description: A neurogenetic disorder usually caused by loss of maternal UBE3A expression in the 15q11-q13 region, resulting in severe developmental delay, absent or limited speech, gait impairment, hypotonia in infancy, microcephaly developing over time, seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.normalized_text: Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragonadal endodermal sinus tumor)
Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragon.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor producing alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) that can arise outside the gonads, exceptionally in the small intestine such as the jejunum.

Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk sac tum.normalized_text: Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk sac tumor differentiation
Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk sac tum.description: An extremely rare intestinal epithelial malignancy containing yolk sac-like differentiation; these tumors may produce substantial AFP and show glandular or hepatoid/yolk-sac-like pathology.

Hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the jejunum.description: A rare AFP-producing adenocarcinoma with morphologic and immunophenotypic resemblance to hepatocellular carcinoma. It may arise in the gastrointestinal tract and can cause very high AFP levels.

Primary intestinal lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm involving the bowel, often presenting as a bowel-wall mass with mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and abdominal symptoms.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the jejunum
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract that can arise in the jejunum and present as a bowel-wall mass with abdominal pain or bleeding.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and sometimes severe painless or minimally painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan can identify ectopic gastric mucosa.

Intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most commonly ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic colicky abdominal pain and may progress to bowel ischemia and bloody, mucus-containing stools.

Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead poi.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point for intussusception
Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead poi.description: A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point for intussusception. This can produce both the episodic obstructive pain characteristic of intussusception and substantial gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcerated ectopic gastric mucosa.

Acute infectious colitis or bacterial en.normalized_text: Acute infectious colitis or bacterial enteritis
Acute infectious colitis or bacterial en.description: Inflammation of the intestine caused by bacterial pathogens such as Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli. It may cause abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and leukocytosis.

Cow's milk protein-induced allergic proc.description: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy in infants, commonly triggered by cow's milk protein, causing colonic inflammation and blood-streaked stools in otherwise well-appearing infants.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare lung disorder characterized by diffuse proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, usually affecting older nonsmoking women. It commonly causes constrictive bronchiolitis, airflow obstruction, mosaic attenuation, and multiple small pulmonary nodules or carcinoid tumorlets.

Constrictive bronchiolitis (obliterative.description: A small-airway disease in which inflammation and fibrosis narrow or obliterate bronchioles, producing fixed airflow obstruction and air trapping. It may occur as part of DIPNECH or after inhalational injury, autoimmune disease, infection, transplantation, or medication exposure.

Multifocal pulmonary carcinoid tumors/tu.description: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors that can appear as enhancing lung nodules. Multiple small carcinoid tumorlets and nodules are particularly associated with DIPNECH and may coexist with bronchiolitis.

Asthma or chronic obstructive airway dis.normalized_text: Asthma or chronic obstructive airway disease
Asthma or chronic obstructive airway dis.description: Asthma and other obstructive airway diseases can cause dyspnea, reduced FEV1, and small-airway obstruction. However, the combination of severe fixed obstruction, mosaic attenuation, and multiple lung nodules in an older nonsmoking woman is more suggestive of DIPNECH-associated bronchiolitis.

Unicentric Castleman disease, hyaline-va.description: A rare benign lymphoproliferative disorder usually involving a single lymph-node region. The hyaline-vascular subtype often causes a firm, slowly fluctuating localized lymph node with few systemic symptoms; histology typically shows regressed germinal centers, concentric mantle zones, and prominent penetrating vessels.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous disorder characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes. It can produce cough, fever, pulmonary infiltrates, and extrapulmonary lymph-node enlargement.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection commonly causes upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Tissue may show granulomatous inflammation, often with caseation, although organisms can be difficult to identify.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can cause pulmonary nodules or cavitary lesions, cough, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous inflammation. Kidney and upper-airway involvement are common but may not always be present initially.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that often presents in young adults with painless rubbery cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and may cause fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus reactivation
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, usually occurring in patients with impaired cellular immunity or exposure to immunomodulatory therapies such as natalizumab or fingolimod.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute inflammatory demyelinating episode causing new or worsening neurologic deficits in a patient with multiple sclerosis.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, often affecting posterior brain regions, that can cause seizures and visual disturbances; it is associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, immunosuppressive medications, and systemic illness.

Viral encephalitis, including herpes sim.normalized_text: Viral encephalitis, including herpes simplex virus encephalitis
Viral encephalitis, including herpes sim.description: Inflammation of the brain caused by viral infection, often presenting with seizures, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits, and inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid findings.

Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.normalized_text: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular, neural, renal, cardiac, skin, and ocular tissues.

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid deposition, often producing concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, and angina-like chest symptoms.

Fabry nephropathy.description: Renal involvement in Fabry disease due to glycosphingolipid accumulation in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and other renal cells, causing proteinuria and progressive chronic kidney disease.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy that can cause chest pain, exertional dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, and abnormal ECG findings. Fabry disease can mimic or cause a hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy phenotype.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: A traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected during ICU hospitalization, producing a localized hepatic infection and systemic inflammatory response.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a localized collection of pus within the liver, which may occur after liver trauma, biliary infection, or infection of a pre-existing hematoma.

Post-traumatic biloma with secondary inf.description: A biloma is a localized collection of bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts after liver trauma; it may become infected and mimic a hepatic abscess.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, commonly occurring in critically ill trauma or ICU patients because of gallbladder ischemia and bile stasis.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.normalized_text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast media
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe, usually drug-induced pustular eruption characterized by abrupt onset of numerous sterile nonfollicular pustules, often accompanied by neutrophilia. Iodinated radiographic contrast is a recognized trigger.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.normalized_text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-like severe cutaneous adverse reaction to iodinated contrast
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.description: TEN is a life-threatening medication-related mucocutaneous reaction marked by widespread keratinocyte death, epidermal detachment, bullae, and full-thickness epidermal necrosis. Rarely, it may have pustular or AGEP-overlap features.

Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.normalized_text: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption due to iodinated contrast media
Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption.description: A drug eruption in which sharply demarcated erythematous or violaceous plaques develop bullae and epidermal necrosis after medication exposure; iodinated contrast can cause recurrent or generalized bullous forms.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.description: A rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by a gram-negative rod carried in dog saliva. It can cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrotic purpura, and multiorgan failure, particularly in people with heavy alcohol use or impaired splenic function.

Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associat.normalized_text: Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation
Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associat.description: Purpura fulminans is a severe thrombotic skin manifestation of disseminated intravascular coagulation, usually triggered by overwhelming bacterial sepsis. It causes rapidly expanding purple skin lesions, hemorrhage, tissue necrosis, and possible limb ischemia.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection follow.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection following dog bites
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection follow.description: A deep, rapidly progressive bacterial infection of fascia and soft tissue that can follow traumatic wounds or animal bites. It may produce severe systemic toxicity, skin discoloration, bullae, necrosis, and septic shock.

Severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome.description: Alcohol withdrawal occurs after abrupt reduction or cessation of heavy alcohol intake. Severe cases can cause autonomic hyperactivity, agitation, tremor, hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens.

Clostridial myonecrosis or tetanus relat.normalized_text: Clostridial myonecrosis or tetanus related to contaminated traumatic wounds
Clostridial myonecrosis or tetanus relat.description: Clostridial wound infections can follow contaminated trauma and may cause severe systemic illness and tissue necrosis. Tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, causes painful muscle rigidity and spasms after contaminated wounds rather than purpuric septic shock.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder commonly caused by mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes, including MT-TL1. It causes impaired energy production, myopathy, lactic acidosis, and recurrent neurologic stroke-like episodes at a young age.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mut.description: A mitochondrial muscle disease caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, producing chronic weakness, exercise intolerance, hypotonia, muscle wasting, and elevated lactate. MT-TL1 mutations can produce isolated myopathy or overlap with MELAS.

Acute ischemic stroke, likely cardioembo.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke, likely cardioembolic in the setting of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy/intracardiac thrombus
Acute ischemic stroke, likely cardioembo.description: An ischemic stroke results from arterial occlusion and causes sudden focal neurologic deficits. The brain imaging is compatible with a large right hemispheric infarction, and the echocardiographic images suggest a potential intracardiac thrombotic embolic source.

Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin t.description: A malignancy of the bile ducts near the hepatic hilum that obstructs bile flow, producing cholestatic liver injury and obstructive jaundice. Imaging and adenocarcinoma-like histology are consistent with this diagnosis.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A bile-duct adenocarcinoma arising in the lower common bile duct. It can cause progressive mechanical biliary obstruction, cholestatic liver tests, pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice.

Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.description: Cancer arising in the head of the pancreas can compress the distal common bile duct and cause painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice. CA 19-9 may be elevated, although this cancer is uncommon at age 29.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive cho.description: A stone in the common bile duct can obstruct bile drainage, causing jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.

Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.normalized_text: Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatitis A or hepatitis E
Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatit.description: Viral inflammation of the liver can cause nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and elevated aminotransferases. Food exposure can raise concern for hepatitis A or E, although the marked obstructive pattern suggests another cause.

Gallstone ileus with distal migration of.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus with distal migration of a gallstone to the rectum
Gallstone ileus with distal migration of.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone that enters the bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula and migrates distally; in this case, the stone reached and became impacted in the rectum.

Cholecystoenteric fistula with enteric p.normalized_text: Cholecystoenteric fistula with enteric passage of a gallstone
Cholecystoenteric fistula with enteric p.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and gastrointestinal tract, most often caused by chronic gallstone disease, allowing a gallstone to pass directly into the intestine and potentially lodge in the distal bowel.

Rectal fecal impaction.description: Accumulation of hard stool in the rectum causing obstructed defecation, rectal pressure, and sometimes minor mucosal bleeding. It may resemble obstruction caused by another impacted intrarectal object.

Crohn's disease with anorectal involveme.description: Inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the rectum and anus, producing inflammation, ulceration, strictures, bleeding, pain, and obstructive defecatory symptoms.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella laterally out of the trochlear groove, often occurring after a twisting injury or minor trauma in adolescents with ligamentous laxity.

Osteochondral fracture associated with p.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture associated with patellar dislocation
Osteochondral fracture associated with p.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, commonly from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation; the fragment may become an intra-articular loose body.

Patellofemoral instability related to ge.normalized_text: Patellofemoral instability related to generalized joint hypermobility
Patellofemoral instability related to ge.description: Recurrent or first-time patellar maltracking/dislocation due to increased ligamentous laxity, often affecting adolescents and increasing the risk of medial patellofemoral ligament injury and patellar dislocation.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring alopecia of the axillary and pubic areas, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules on the trunk and limbs.

Lichen planopilaris.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory disorder of hair follicles that causes scarring alopecia of the scalp, often with perifollicular scale, erythema, itching, and follicular keratotic lesions.

Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalva.description: A rare follicular keratinization disorder characterized by widespread follicular hyperkeratotic spiny papules and progressive scarring alopecia, usually beginning in childhood and more commonly affecting males.

Lichen spinulosus.description: A follicular keratinization disorder causing grouped rough, pinpoint, spiny follicular papules, often on the trunk, buttocks, and extremities; it is usually benign and occurs in children or young adults.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.normalized_text: Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), postpartum-associated
Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It produces microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and prominent acute kidney injury, and may cause skin vascular thrombosis and ulceration.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A severe thrombotic microangiopathy, usually due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, and febrile manifestations. Pregnancy can precipitate an episode.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can injure renal arterioles and small vessels, producing renal failure, hematuria, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. It may overlap with or trigger complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.

Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated.normalized_text: Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome (HELLP syndrome)
Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated.description: A severe pregnancy complication related to preeclampsia, defined by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia. Kidney injury and hypertension may occur, but the syndrome generally occurs during late pregnancy or shortly after delivery.

Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli-a.normalized_text: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli-associated typical hemolytic uremic syndrome
Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli-a.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy most often triggered by Shiga toxin-producing bacterial gastroenteritis. It causes acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Small-intestinal gastrointestinal stroma.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells. Ileal GISTs commonly harbor activating KIT mutations, particularly in exon 11, and may cause mucosal ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tum.normalized_text: Epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tumor (epithelioid GIST) of the ileum
Epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tum.description: A morphologic subtype of GIST composed predominantly of rounded or epithelioid tumor cells rather than spindle cells. Like other GISTs, it may express KIT and harbor activating KIT mutations.

Small-bowel leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the small bowel and present as an enhancing mass with bleeding, anemia, pain, obstruction, or metastatic spread. It is generally not driven by KIT exon 11 mutations.

Small-bowel adenocarcinoma.description: An epithelial malignancy arising from the mucosa of the small intestine. It may cause occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, obstruction, and an ileal mass, but it does not typically contain activating KIT exon 11 mutations.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor characterized by solid and pseudopapillary architecture, often with hemorrhagic and cystic degeneration. It usually occurs in young women but can rarely occur in elderly men.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells; nonfunctioning tumors may grow large before causing mass effect, while functioning tumors cause hormone-related syndromes.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare exocrine pancreatic malignancy composed of acinar-type cells. It can form a large, relatively well-defined mass and may present with nonspecific abdominal symptoms.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic cancer, typically an infiltrative ductal tumor that causes biliary obstruction, abdominal pain, weight loss, or new/worsening diabetes.

Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasm with.normalized_text: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasm with invasive carcinoma
Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasm with.description: A mucin-producing cystic pancreatic tumor that can become very large and may develop invasive cancer; it is usually found in the pancreatic body or tail and occurs predominantly in women.

Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign c.description: An autosomal-dominant acantholytic skin disorder causing recurrent painful, pruritic, erosive or blistering plaques in intertriginous areas. Flares are commonly triggered by heat, sweating, friction, and humidity.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited disorder of keratinization and acantholysis characterized by greasy, crusted keratotic papules, often in seborrheic or flexural areas; heat and sweating may worsen disease.

Acanthosis nigricans with superimposed i.description: Acanthosis nigricans is velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity and insulin resistance. Moisture and friction can produce secondary intertrigo with maceration, odor, erosions, or infection.

Candidal intertrigo.description: A yeast infection of moist skin folds causing erythema, maceration, soreness, pruritus, fissuring, and sometimes malodor. Obesity and possible insulin resistance increase risk.

Inverse psoriasis.description: Psoriasis affecting intertriginous areas, producing smooth, erythematous to hyperpigmented, painful or pruritic plaques that may fissure or erode because of friction and moisture.

Myositis ossificans circumscripta (idiop.normalized_text: Myositis ossificans circumscripta (idiopathic pelvic/iliacus muscle myositis ossificans)
Myositis ossificans circumscripta (idiop.description: A benign reactive process in which bone forms within soft tissue or muscle, often after trauma but sometimes without an identifiable precipitating event. Imaging commonly shows peripheral zonal ossification around a soft-tissue mass.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or mineralized matrix in soft tissues without primary origin from bone. It may present as a progressively enlarging painful calcified soft-tissue mass.

Synovial sarcoma with calcification.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that commonly affects adolescents and young adults and can contain calcifications. It usually presents as a slowly enlarging deep soft-tissue mass with pain or tenderness.

Parosteal osteosarcoma.description: A low-grade bone-forming osteosarcoma arising from the external surface of a bone, typically producing a densely ossified mass attached to cortex. Pelvic involvement is uncommon but possible.

Anti-GAD65 positive classical stiff-pers.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated reflex responses, and continuous motor-unit activity; it is commonly associated with anti-GAD antibodies.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum autoimmune disorder causing rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms, myoclonus, brainstem dysfunction, autonomic instability, and sometimes respiratory compromise; it is often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies but can overlap with anti-GAD autoimmunity.

Tetanus.description: An acute toxin-mediated infection caused by Clostridium tetani that produces painful generalized muscle rigidity, spasms, hyperreflexia, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.

Cervical or thoracic myelopathy with upp.normalized_text: Cervical or thoracic myelopathy with upper motor-neuron spasticity
Cervical or thoracic myelopathy with upp.description: Spinal cord disease, such as compressive myelopathy, inflammatory myelitis, or other cord pathology, can cause progressive leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and impaired walking.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in younger women. Carotid and subclavian artery stenosis can cause cerebral hypoperfusion, syncope, stroke, and rarely scalp ischemia with ulceration or necrosis.

Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlus.normalized_text: Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlusion due to premature atherosclerotic disease
Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlus.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion of the carotid arteries can reduce cerebral perfusion and cause transient ischemic symptoms, syncope-like episodes, or stroke. In severe multivessel disease, reduced external carotid circulation can rarely lead to scalp ischemia and tissue necrosis.

Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia
Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.description: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, especially branches of the external carotid artery. It can cause scalp tenderness, scalp ulceration or necrosis, visual loss, and ischemic neurologic complications.

Traumatic scalp hematoma or laceration r.normalized_text: Traumatic scalp hematoma or laceration related to recurrent falls and dual antiplatelet therapy
Traumatic scalp hematoma or laceration r.description: Repeated collapse can cause scalp trauma. Aspirin and clopidogrel increase bleeding and bruising risk, so a minor injury may evolve into a large hematoma, skin breakdown, or necrotic-appearing wound.

Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infan.description: A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, often associated with dog reservoirs in Mediterranean regions. In immunosuppressed patients, it can cause fever, cytopenias, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoimmune-like serology, and may lack splenomegaly. The marrow image is compatible with intracellular amastigotes.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, anti-dsDNA positivity, and immune-complex vasculitic skin findings.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized classically by neutropenia and splenomegaly, sometimes with anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and recurrent infections.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, commonly associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders, or chronic infections. It can produce purpura, livedo, arthralgia, and low complement levels.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder characterized by yellow-brown to red plaques with central atrophy, induration, telangiectasia, and occasional ulceration. It most often affects the pretibial area and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory granulomatous dermatosis that commonly presents as annular papules or plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common benign diabetic skin manifestation consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, thought to reflect diabetic microangiopathy or repeated minor trauma.

Pretibial myxedema.description: Localized dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, usually associated with Graves disease. It produces nonpitting edema, waxy thickening, peau d'orange texture, and red-brown or violaceous plaques on the shins.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can cause papules, plaques, nodules, or scars in the skin. Skin lesions may be red-brown or violaceous and can occur without systemic symptoms.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).description: A disorder of resistance to parathyroid hormone, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated parathyroid hormone, and may also cause resistance to thyroid-stimulating hormone.

Hypocalcemic tetany with possible laryng.description: Neuromuscular irritability caused by low serum calcium. It can cause muscle stiffness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek sign, dysphagia, stridor, and potentially life-threatening laryngospasm.

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.normalized_text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), choking-phobia presentation
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.description: An eating or feeding disorder characterized by avoidance of food because of fear of aversive consequences, such as choking or vomiting, resulting in inadequate intake and possible dehydration or nutritional complications.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with lar.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with laryngopharyngeal reflux
Gastroesophageal reflux disease with lar.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus and upper airway can cause regurgitation, vomiting, throat discomfort, dysphagia, excessive belching, drooling, and nocturnal upper-airway symptoms such as stridor or cough.

Dabrafenib-trametinib associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills or diaphoresis, fatigue, nausea, and sometimes hypotension or dehydration; it often begins soon after treatment initiation and improves when the drugs are withheld.

Dabrafenib-trametinib induced sarcoid-li.description: BRAF and MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger a systemic sarcoid-like inflammatory reaction with noncaseating granulomas affecting skin, lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, or other organs. It may mimic metastatic melanoma or infection.

Granulomatous hepatitis due to drug-indu.normalized_text: Granulomatous hepatitis due to drug-induced liver injury
Granulomatous hepatitis due to drug-indu.description: A medication-related hepatic inflammatory reaction that can produce granulomas, fever, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and abnormal liver imaging or liver tests. Targeted anticancer agents can rarely cause this pattern of liver injury.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can cause persistent fever, constitutional symptoms, pulmonary disease, hepatosplenic involvement, and granulomatous inflammation. It is more likely in immunocompromised patients but can occur in others depending on exposure and geography.

Metastatic melanoma with visceral involv.description: Melanoma may recur or metastasize to lymph nodes, lung, liver, spleen, bone, brain, and other organs. Visceral metastatic disease can cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal pain, although high acute fever is less typical unless there is extensive disease or another complication.

Gallbladder metastasis from prostate ade.description: Rare metastatic involvement of the gallbladder by prostate cancer, potentially producing cystic-duct or biliary obstruction and presenting as cholecystitis or pancreatitis.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly due to obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone, sludge, or malignant lesion.

Gallbladder carcinoma.description: Primary malignant tumor of the gallbladder that may obstruct the cystic duct or biliary tree and cause abdominal pain, cholecystitis-like symptoms, and cholestatic liver-test abnormalities.

Acute biliary pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation caused by transient or persistent obstruction at the ampulla or distal bile duct, usually from gallstones, sludge, or malignant biliary obstruction.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AA.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AAAS-related disease)
