Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AA.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia/dysphagia, and ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency; progressive neurologic and autonomic abnormalities are common.

Four A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with.normalized_text: Four A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with autonomic and neurologic involvement)
Four A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with.description: An expanded phenotype of Allgrove syndrome in which the classic triad of alacrima, achalasia, and adrenal insufficiency is accompanied by prominent autonomic neuropathy and progressive central or peripheral neurologic dysfunction.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy/adrenomyel.description: A peroxisomal ABCD1-related disorder causing primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive myelopathy or cerebral white-matter disease, typically in boys. It is usually associated with elevated very-long-chain fatty acids.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of acute encephalopathy caused by vasogenic edema, often in posterior cerebral regions. It can occur with cancer therapies, renal dysfunction, hypertension, endothelial injury, or severe systemic illness and may include restricted diffusion or small hemorrhages.

Multifocal ischemic stroke due to cancer.normalized_text: Multifocal ischemic stroke due to cancer-associated hypercoagulability or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
Multifocal ischemic stroke due to cancer.description: Advanced metastatic adenocarcinoma can produce a hypercoagulable state or sterile valvular thrombi, resulting in multiple embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories, sometimes with hemorrhagic transformation.

Cerebral aspergillosis with angioinvasiv.normalized_text: Cerebral aspergillosis with angioinvasive fungal infarcts
Cerebral aspergillosis with angioinvasiv.description: Invasive Aspergillus infection in immunocompromised patients can invade cerebral blood vessels, causing multifocal infarctions, hemorrhagic lesions, abscesses, and rapidly progressive encephalopathy. Fever may be absent in severely immunocompromised patients.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: PML is a JC-virus demyelinating brain infection occurring in immunosuppressed individuals. It produces progressive cognitive, behavioral, motor, and visual deficits with multifocal white-matter MRI lesions, usually without mass effect or enhancement.

Central nervous system metastases with h.normalized_text: Central nervous system metastases with hemorrhagic metastatic lesions
Central nervous system metastases with h.description: Breast cancer can metastasize to the brain, causing cognitive changes, weakness, seizures, focal deficits, and sometimes hemorrhage. Leptomeningeal involvement can also cause diffuse encephalopathy and weakness.

Isolated spinal cord neurosarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord without evident systemic disease. It can cause enhancing cervical cord lesions and a progressive myelopathy; biopsy typically shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.

Cervical spinal cord tumor (ependymoma o.normalized_text: Cervical spinal cord tumor (ependymoma or astrocytoma)
Cervical spinal cord tumor (ependymoma o.description: An intramedullary neoplasm of the cervical spinal cord that may progressively compress or infiltrate corticospinal and sensory tracts, producing myelopathy and bladder dysfunction.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disease that commonly causes acute or subacute myelitis, often with longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions; optic neuritis may or may not be present initially.

Spinal tuberculosis (intramedullary tube.normalized_text: Spinal tuberculosis (intramedullary tuberculoma or tuberculous myelitis)
Spinal tuberculosis (intramedullary tube.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce granulomatous inflammation within or around the spinal cord, causing subacute myelopathy. Pathology usually shows caseating granulomas and acid-fast organisms may be detectable.

Primary CNS lymphoma or inflammatory lym.normalized_text: Primary CNS lymphoma or inflammatory lymphoma mimic
Primary CNS lymphoma or inflammatory lym.description: Lymphoma involving the spinal cord can cause an enhancing intramedullary lesion and progressive myelopathy, although biopsy generally demonstrates atypical monoclonal lymphoid cells rather than granulomas.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.description: A severe bacterial lower-respiratory infection causing consolidation and tissue necrosis with formation of one or more cavitary abscesses, often involving dependent portions of the lung.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic suppurative infection caused by Actinomyces species that can produce mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and chest discomfort; it may be mistaken for cancer or tuberculosis.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with cavitary dis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, lung consolidation, and cavitation, although upper-lobe disease is more typical in immunocompetent adults.

Pulmonary nocardiosis.description: An infection caused by Nocardia species that may produce subacute cough, consolidation, nodules, and cavitary lesions; it is more common in immunocompromised patients but can occur in apparently healthy individuals.

Cavitary lung malignancy, especially squ.normalized_text: Cavitary lung malignancy, especially squamous cell carcinoma with post-obstructive infection
Cavitary lung malignancy, especially squ.description: A lung cancer can obstruct a bronchus and lead to persistent cough, localized infection, necrosis, and cavitary consolidation. Smoking is an important risk factor, although this is less common at age 33.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A zoonotic filarial infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually from infected dogs. In humans, immature worms can produce isolated painless or migrating subcutaneous nodules; Dirofilaria repens is endemic in parts of Croatia and the Mediterranean region.

Subcutaneous cysticercosis.description: Infection with larval Taenia solium cysts, which may form painless subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules. Lesions are generally fixed rather than migratory and may be associated with neurologic disease if cysts involve the central nervous system.

Subcutaneous sparganosis.description: A tissue infection caused by migrating Spirometra larvae, usually acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or raw/undercooked amphibian or reptile meat. It can cause slowly migrating painless subcutaneous nodules.

Loiasis.description: A filarial infection caused by Loa loa, transmitted by Chrysops deer flies in West and Central Africa. It may cause transient migratory subcutaneous swellings known as Calabar swellings.

Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richards.description: A progressive tau-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early unexplained falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. Midbrain atrophy may produce the characteristic 'hummingbird' appearance on MRI.

Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian ty.description: A synucleinopathy causing rapidly progressive parkinsonism with autonomic failure, gait impairment, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes abnormal eye movements. Axial rigidity and falls can occur, but a marked early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical than in PSP.

Corticobasal syndrome / corticobasal deg.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually presents with asymmetric parkinsonism, limb dystonia, apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, myoclonus, and cognitive-language dysfunction. Eye movement abnormalities and falls can develop later.

Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.normalized_text: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset form
Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.description: A rare lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can present in adolescents or adults with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive decline. It may mimic PSP but usually has earlier onset or systemic/psychiatric clues.

Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus ne.description: A subacute fungal meningitis caused by Cryptococcus, occurring most commonly in advanced HIV/AIDS. Encapsulated budding yeasts can be seen with India ink staining, and elevated opening pressure is characteristic.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose.

Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, or HIV itself. CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.

Neurosyphilis (syphilitic meningitis).description: Central nervous system infection with Treponema pallidum that can cause aseptic meningitis, especially during early disseminated syphilis or in people with HIV.

Acute bacterial meningitis.description: Rapidly progressive infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. CSF classically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and high protein.

Acute ischemic stroke of the left medial.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute ischemic stroke of the left medial.description: A small brainstem infarction affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), disrupting coordination between the abducens and oculomotor nuclei. This produces ipsilateral impaired eye adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia.description: A gaze disorder caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, characterized by impaired adduction of the eye on the side of the lesion and nystagmus of the opposite abducting eye.

Posterior circulation transient ischemic.normalized_text: Posterior circulation transient ischemic attack or small pontomesencephalic infarction
Posterior circulation transient ischemic.description: Transient or permanent ischemia in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect ocular motor pathways in the pons or midbrain, including the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce demyelinating lesions of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, particularly in younger adults.

Ocular myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, often without generalized weakness.

Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium fal.normalized_text: Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum
Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium fal.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery, presenting in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly produces high parasitemia with multiple delicate ring forms in individual erythrocytes and can cause severe hemolysis and organ dysfunction.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne or rarely transfusion-associated intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and ring-form parasites on peripheral smear. Multiple parasites in a red cell can occur, although Maltese-cross tetrads are more characteristic.

Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.normalized_text: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.description: Systemic bacterial infection in a young infant can cause fever, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and shock. Severe sepsis may also cause anemia through hemolysis, bleeding, or marrow suppression.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic.normalized_text: Hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic microangiopathy
Hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy causes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury, often with hematuria or proteinuria. In infants, atypical complement-mediated HUS may occur without diarrheal illness.

Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with local rectal invasion
Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with pelvic/rectal involvement and distant metastases such as lung and liver lesions.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.normalized_text: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.description: A malignant tumor arising from the rectum that may cause tenesmus and pelvic pain and can metastasize to the liver and lungs.

Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation.normalized_text: Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation of recurrent prostate cancer
Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation.description: An aggressive variant of prostate cancer that may emerge after prior treatment, often progresses rapidly, and can produce visceral metastases involving the liver and lungs.

Pelvic lymphoma with gastrointestinal an.normalized_text: Pelvic lymphoma with gastrointestinal and extranodal involvement
Pelvic lymphoma with gastrointestinal an.description: Lymphoma can involve the rectum or pelvic tissues and may cause constitutional symptoms, abdominal or rectal pain, and lesions in organs such as the liver or lungs.

Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysi.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysi.description: An acquired form of hypokalemic periodic paralysis caused by thyrotoxicosis, most often Graves disease. Thyroid hormone excess drives potassium into cells, producing profound hypokalemia and acute muscle weakness; episodes can be precipitated by medications, supplements, carbohydrate intake, or exertion.

Graves disease with thyrotoxicosis.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, causing diffuse thyroid hyperfunction, hypervascular goiter, and clinical hyperthyroidism. It can precipitate thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder that causes episodic weakness or paralysis associated with low serum potassium, often triggered by rest after exercise, carbohydrate intake, stress, or certain medications.

Hypokalemic paralysis from gastrointesti.normalized_text: Hypokalemic paralysis from gastrointestinal potassium loss due to diarrhea
Hypokalemic paralysis from gastrointesti.description: Diarrhea can cause potassium depletion and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. Severe potassium depletion may lead to generalized weakness or paralysis.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, noncancerous bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is often lobulated, slowly enlarging, and usually requires no treatment unless it interferes with hygiene, prostheses, or speech.

Congenital palatal hamartoma.description: A hamartoma is a benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components in an abnormal arrangement. In the palate, it may present as a longstanding, asymptomatic congenital mass.

Palatal fibroma (focal fibrous hyperplas.description: A benign localized overgrowth of fibrous connective tissue, often caused by chronic irritation or trauma. It usually appears as a painless, firm, smooth mucosal nodule.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.normalized_text: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.description: Herniation of lumbar disc material, commonly at L4-L5 or L5-S1, causing compression or irritation of a lumbar nerve root. The MRI appearance is compatible with degenerative disc disease and a posterior disc protrusion/extrusion causing canal or nerve-root compression.

Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to dege.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to degenerative disc disease
Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to dege.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal from degenerative disc bulging, facet arthropathy, and ligament thickening, potentially compressing nerve roots and producing radicular symptoms or weakness.

Lumbar disc extrusion with sequestrated.normalized_text: Lumbar disc extrusion with sequestrated disc fragment
Lumbar disc extrusion with sequestrated.description: A more severe form of disc herniation in which disc material extends through the annulus and may migrate within the epidural space, causing abrupt nerve-root compression and neurological deficit.

Cauda equina compression syndrome second.normalized_text: Cauda equina compression syndrome secondary to a large lumbar disc herniation
Cauda equina compression syndrome second.description: Compression of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots in the cauda equina, often caused by a large central lumbar disc extrusion. It is an emergency when associated with bladder, bowel, saddle sensory, or progressive bilateral motor symptoms.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with neurologic and cardiac involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A multisystem disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia and eosinophil-mediated organ injury after secondary causes such as parasites, allergy, malignancy, and vasculitis have been excluded. It can cause thromboembolic stroke, encephalopathy, myocardial injury, and pulmonary lesions.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A necrotizing eosinophil-rich small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes asthma, chronic sinus disease, eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, cardiac involvement, and occasionally central nervous system ischemic events.

Eosinophilic myocarditis associated with.description: Inflammatory myocardial damage caused by eosinophilic infiltration, often occurring as part of hypereosinophilic syndrome or EGPA. It may cause myocardial necrosis, ventricular dysfunction, mural thrombus formation, and embolic cerebral infarctions.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia / myeloid.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia / myeloid neoplasm with eosinophilia
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia / myeloid.description: A clonal hematologic disorder causing sustained eosinophilia that can produce end-organ damage through eosinophilic infiltration and thrombosis. Molecular testing, bone-marrow examination, and evaluation for rearrangements such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA are needed to distinguish it from idiopathic HES.

Parasitic helminth infection with second.normalized_text: Parasitic helminth infection with secondary hypereosinophilia
Parasitic helminth infection with second.description: Helminthic infections can produce marked eosinophilia and pulmonary infiltrates or nodules; some infections may also involve the central nervous system. This is an important cause to exclude in patients with eosinophilia.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and the lungs.

Sarcoid-like reaction associated with br.normalized_text: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with breast cancer
Sarcoid-like reaction associated with br.description: A noninfectious granulomatous reaction resembling sarcoidosis that may occur in lymph nodes or organs of patients with malignancy, sometimes after chemotherapy or radiation, and can mimic metastatic disease on FDG-PET.

Metastatic breast cancer involving media.normalized_text: Metastatic breast cancer involving mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes
Metastatic breast cancer involving media.description: Recurrence or spread of breast carcinoma can produce FDG-avid lymphadenopathy and may involve mediastinal lymph nodes, particularly in patients with prior node-positive breast cancer.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause mediastinal or hilar lymph-node enlargement and granulomatous inflammation, often with caseating necrosis but occasionally with noncaseating granulomas.

Active IgG kappa multiple myeloma.description: A malignant clonal plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin, commonly causing anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone disease, and markedly abnormal serum free light chains.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic precursor plasma-cell neoplasm with a significant monoclonal protein and/or increased marrow plasma cells but without myeloma-defining end-organ injury.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A common premalignant condition characterized by a small stable monoclonal protein without significant marrow infiltration, organ damage, or myeloma-defining biomarkers.

AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated.normalized_text: AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell dyscrasia
AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated.description: A disorder in which monoclonal light chains form amyloid deposits in tissues, potentially causing renal, cardiac, neurologic, gastrointestinal, or hepatic dysfunction.

Intracranial germinoma (suprasellar/pine.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescents and young adults and may arise in the suprasellar region, pineal region, or both. Suprasellar involvement can disrupt hypothalamic-pituitary function and cause diabetes insipidus, hypogonadism, and visual symptoms.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign epithelial tumor arising near the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus. It can impair pituitary hormone production, cause diabetes insipidus, visual-field deficits, headache, and delayed or impaired sexual development.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.description: A rare inflammatory histiocytic disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus. Central diabetes insipidus is a classic endocrine manifestation; additional pituitary deficits may cause delayed puberty or hypogonadism.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.normalized_text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infective endocarditis of the aortic valve
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, caused here by MRSA. Injection drug use, persistent bacteremia, embolic phenomena, new valvular regurgitation, and peripheral stigmata strongly support this diagnosis.

Aortic root abscess complicating aortic.normalized_text: Aortic root abscess complicating aortic valve infective endocarditis
Aortic root abscess complicating aortic.description: A periannular abscess is a destructive extension of infective endocarditis into tissue around the aortic valve. It can cause new aortic regurgitation and conduction delay or heart block because of involvement of the nearby cardiac conduction system.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.normalized_text: Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.description: Infected valvular vegetations can embolize to cerebral arteries, causing ischemic stroke and sometimes brain abscess, hemorrhage, or mycotic aneurysm. This is a common serious complication of left-sided infective endocarditis.

Acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembol.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism from paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembol.description: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation can cause left atrial thrombus formation and embolic ischemic stroke, particularly when anticoagulation is absent or inadequate. It is an alternative contributor to the focal neurological deficit but does not explain the infectious and peripheral features as well as endocarditis.

Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (g.normalized_text: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (g.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in glycogen accumulation, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile disease typically presents in the first months of life with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and elevated muscle enzymes.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal glycogen-storage and cardiomyopathy disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, elevated CK, and later intellectual or developmental impairment; males are generally more severely affected.

PRKAG2 syndrome.description: An autosomal-dominant glycogen-storage cardiomyopathy caused by pathogenic PRKAG2 variants. It is characterized by cardiac hypertrophy, ventricular pre-excitation, conduction-system disease, and arrhythmias, usually presenting later in childhood or adulthood.

Primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due.normalized_text: Primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to a sarcomeric gene disorder
Primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due.description: Genetic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can occur in infants and may cause ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomegaly, cardiac dysfunction, and elevated natriuretic peptides. It is generally caused by variants in sarcomeric cardiac-muscle genes rather than lysosomal enzyme deficiency.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and potentially presenting with multifocal bone, soft-tissue, renal, or other extramedullary lesions. It is the most common childhood leukemia.

Neuroblastoma.description: A childhood embryonal tumor arising from sympathetic nervous system tissue, commonly in the adrenal glands or retroperitoneum, which can metastasize to bone and bone marrow and cause periorbital ecchymoses.

Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarcoma
Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarc.description: A hematologic malignancy of myeloid precursor cells that can infiltrate bone marrow and form extramedullary tumor masses, including orbital, bone, and soft-tissue lesions.

Ewing sarcoma with multifocal osseous di.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma with multifocal osseous disease
Ewing sarcoma with multifocal osseous di.description: An aggressive small round cell sarcoma of bone or soft tissue in children and adolescents that may cause localized bone pain, fever, limp, and metastatic bone marrow or soft-tissue involvement.

Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.normalized_text: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) / chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis
Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.description: An autoinflammatory bone disorder causing recurrent sterile inflammation at multiple skeletal sites, often producing episodic bone pain and limping in children.

Bacterial cellulitis.description: An acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, commonly causing localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain; ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema without a drainable collection.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necro.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection involving deep fascia and soft tissue, often causing severe pain, swelling, erythema, systemic toxicity, and later skin discoloration, bullae, or necrosis.

Gluteal soft-tissue abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in skin or subcutaneous tissue, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing focal pain, erythema, swelling, warmth, and sometimes fluctuance or drainage.

Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tis.normalized_text: Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tissue bleeding
Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tis.description: Bleeding into subcutaneous tissue or muscle, usually after trauma, injections, anticoagulant use, or a bleeding disorder; it may cause pain, swelling, and bruising-like discoloration.

Superficial thrombophlebitis of a glutea.normalized_text: Superficial thrombophlebitis of a gluteal superficial vein
Superficial thrombophlebitis of a glutea.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein, causing localized pain, redness, warmth, swelling, and occasionally a palpable tender cord along the involved vein.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), sclerodermatous/dermatomyositis-like cutaneous phenotype
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. It can cause lichenoid or sclerotic skin disease, fascial tightening and joint contractures, muscle involvement, and liver enzyme abnormalities.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions, including facial erythema, shawl-sign rash, and Gottron papules over the knuckles.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with cutaneous and musculoskeletal manifestations
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause photosensitive facial or generalized rash, fever, arthralgia or myalgia, muscle symptoms, autoantibodies, and possible liver test abnormalities.

Systemic sclerosis or scleroderma-like a.normalized_text: Systemic sclerosis or scleroderma-like autoimmune disease
Systemic sclerosis or scleroderma-like a.description: A connective-tissue disease characterized by skin thickening, fibrosis, reduced joint mobility, and possible muscle or internal-organ involvement. A similar scleroderma-like syndrome may occur as chronic GVHD after transplantation.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma (Gr.description: A rare disorder characterized by the rapid appearance of numerous keratoacanthomas, which are crateriform keratinizing tumors often considered to lie on the squamous-cell-carcinoma spectrum.

Multiple keratoacanthomas associated wit.normalized_text: Multiple keratoacanthomas associated with chronic renal failure and dialysis
Multiple keratoacanthomas associated wit.description: Multiple keratoacanthomas may occur in patients with chronic kidney disease, prior transplantation, immunologic dysregulation, or long-term dialysis; lesions are rapidly growing keratinizing papules or nodules.

Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.description: A hereditary keratoacanthoma syndrome causing recurrent crops of crateriform squamous tumors that may spontaneously regress and leave scars.

Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease/reactive perforating collagenosis)
Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle d.description: A pruritic perforating skin disorder common in diabetes and chronic renal failure, especially in dialysis patients, producing excoriated hyperkeratotic papules with central plugs.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.normalized_text: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: A keratinizing skin cancer that can present as a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug; multiple lesions can occur in patients with cumulative sun damage or immune dysfunction.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: An acute inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing motor weakness, sensory-level deficits, pain, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.

Acute partial transverse myelitis.description: A focal or asymmetric form of transverse myelitis, often involving only part of the spinal cord and producing unilateral weakness and asymmetric sensory deficits.

Spinal cord infarction.description: Ischemic injury of the spinal cord, often presenting with sudden severe spinal pain followed by weakness, dissociated sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disease that can cause severe myelitis with weakness, sensory deficits, neuropathic pain, and bladder dysfunction; spinal lesions are often longitudinally extensive.

Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervica.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervical myelitis
Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervica.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that may initially present with partial myelitis, asymmetric weakness, sensory symptoms, and urinary dysfunction.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), likely IRS4-rearranged T-ALL with t(X;14)
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive precursor T-cell neoplasm characterized by marrow and blood replacement by T-lymphoblasts. The reported X-chromosome/14q11 T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus rearrangement may involve IRS4 and supports a T-ALL subtype.

T-prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia that usually affects older adults and produces marked lymphocytosis, often with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and expression of mature T-cell markers.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: An aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). It commonly presents with leukemic peripheral-blood involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and CD4-positive mature T-cell phenotype.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, extreme hyperferritinemia, organ enlargement, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with seconda.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease may involve the lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow and can trigger HLH, particularly in severely ill patients. Bone marrow may show intracellular yeast-like organisms within macrophages.

Disseminated tuberculosis with secondary.description: Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis is widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving multiple organs, including lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It can cause pancytopenia and may trigger secondary HLH.

Talaromyces marneffei disseminated infec.normalized_text: Talaromyces marneffei disseminated infection with secondary HLH
Talaromyces marneffei disseminated infec.description: Talaromyces marneffei is a dimorphic fungal infection endemic in parts of southern China and Southeast Asia. Disseminated infection can affect the lungs, reticuloendothelial system, and bone marrow and may produce severe cytopenias and HLH.

Aggressive lymphoma-associated HLH.description: Lymphomas, especially T-cell/NK-cell lymphomas and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, can trigger HLH through cytokine-driven immune activation. This produces fever, cytopenias, coagulopathy, very high ferritin, and liver or spleen enlargement.

Dengue encephalitis with cerebral vascul.description: A rare neurologic complication of dengue virus infection in which viral infection and immune-mediated vascular inflammation cause meningoencephalitis, focal neurologic deficits, and ischemic brain lesions.

Japanese encephalitis.description: Mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis endemic in parts of Asia and the western Pacific that can cause fever, coma, movement abnormalities, and focal neurologic deficits.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that can cause meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, rash, and severe altered consciousness, particularly in older adults.

Rickettsial meningoencephalitis with cer.description: Infection with rickettsial organisms, including scrub typhus or spotted-fever group rickettsioses, can produce fever, rash, meningoencephalitis, small-vessel vasculitis, and cerebral infarction.

Acute bacterial meningitis with infectio.normalized_text: Acute bacterial meningitis with infectious cerebral vasculitis
Acute bacterial meningitis with infectio.description: Bacterial meningitis, especially pneumococcal meningitis, can cause fever, coma, neutrophilic CSF inflammation, cerebral arteritis, thrombosis, and ischemic focal deficits.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An IgA immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that commonly follows an upper respiratory infection and causes palpable purpura, joint symptoms, gastrointestinal involvement, and sometimes kidney disease. The biopsy pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vascular IgA, C3, and fibrin deposition strongly supports this diagnosis.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.description: A small-vessel vasculitis of the skin caused by immune-complex deposition, often triggered by infection, inflammatory disease, or medication. It typically presents with palpable purpura on dependent areas of the lower extremities and may cause arthralgia or arthritis.

Adalimumab-associated vasculitis.description: Anti-tumor necrosis factor medications such as adalimumab can rarely induce immune-mediated vasculitis, most often cutaneous small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis, sometimes with systemic manifestations. Drug-induced cases may occur after prolonged exposure.

Crohn's disease-associated peripheral ar.normalized_text: Crohn's disease-associated peripheral arthritis with cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis
Crohn's disease-associated peripheral ar.description: Crohn's disease can have extraintestinal inflammatory manifestations, including peripheral arthritis and, less commonly, cutaneous vasculitis. These manifestations may occur independently of overt gastrointestinal symptoms.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing small- and medium-vessel vasculitis, often associated with PR3-ANCA, that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and joints. It can cause purpura and arthralgia but usually has more destructive sinonasal, pulmonary, or renal findings.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsil or base of tongue) with cervical nodal metastasis
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A squamous cell cancer arising in the oropharynx, commonly from the palatine tonsil or base of tongue. HPV-associated disease often occurs in relatively younger patients without heavy tobacco or alcohol exposure and commonly presents with an upper-neck metastatic lymph node.

Non-HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamou.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the tonsil, tongue base, pharyngeal wall, or other oropharyngeal mucosa that may spread to upper cervical lymph nodes. Traditional risk factors include smoking and substantial alcohol exposure.

Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma w.normalized_text: Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with cervical nodal metastasis
Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma w.description: Squamous cell carcinoma arising from the hypopharynx, including the pyriform sinus or posterior pharyngeal wall, often presenting late with cervical lymph-node metastases and throat or ear pain.

Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes.normalized_text: Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes and Waldeyer ring
Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve cervical lymph nodes and lymphoid tissue of the tonsils or tongue base, producing neck masses and sometimes throat symptoms.

Chronic infectious cervical lymphadeniti.normalized_text: Chronic infectious cervical lymphadenitis or deep neck infection
Chronic infectious cervical lymphadeniti.description: Bacterial, mycobacterial, or other infectious inflammation of cervical lymph nodes can cause a neck mass and throat pain, although persistent fixed nodes with a pharyngeal mass are concerning for malignancy instead.

Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.normalized_text: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, rarely involving the bladder. It is often associated with longstanding chronic cystitis and may remain localized without systemic disease.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can rarely present as a primary bladder mass or develop through transformation of an indolent lymphoma such as MALT lymphoma.

Chronic follicular cystitis.description: A benign reactive inflammatory condition of the bladder characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, commonly occurring with recurrent urinary tract infection or chronic bladder irritation.

Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary blad.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary blad.description: A malignant tumor arising from the bladder urothelium. It commonly presents with hematuria and may be accompanied by chronic inflammation, but it is not typically driven by recurrent bacterial cystitis alone.

Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the left.normalized_text: Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the left proximal femur
Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the left.description: A rare, severe bone infection characterized by gas-forming bacteria within bone; Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause this condition, particularly in older patients with diabetes.

Septic arthritis of the hip due to Klebs.normalized_text: Septic arthritis of the hip due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Septic arthritis of the hip due to Klebs.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint that causes inflammation, joint destruction, pain, and systemic inflammatory-marker elevation. It may occur through spread from a urinary infection, especially in frail older adults with diabetes.

Hip fracture, likely femoral neck fractu.normalized_text: Hip fracture, likely femoral neck fracture
Hip fracture, likely femoral neck fractu.description: A fracture involving the femoral neck or proximal femur, commonly occurring after a fall in elderly people with osteoporosis or frailty.

Complicated Klebsiella pneumoniae urinar.normalized_text: Complicated Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infection
Complicated Klebsiella pneumoniae urinar.description: A urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, which can produce a significant inflammatory response and may present atypically in elderly patients, including falls or functional decline.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with detached osteochondral loose body
Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.description: A focal area of subchondral bone and overlying cartilage becomes damaged, often in active adolescents or young adults, and may detach into the joint as an osteochondral fragment. It can cause mechanical knee symptoms and a visible loose body on radiographs.

Post-traumatic osteochondral fracture wi.normalized_text: Post-traumatic osteochondral fracture with intra-articular loose body
Post-traumatic osteochondral fracture wi.description: A prior injury can damage articular cartilage and underlying bone, leaving an osteochondral fragment free within the knee. The fragment may intermittently obstruct motion and cause effusions and locking.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A benign proliferative synovial disorder in which cartilaginous nodules form within a joint and may detach, calcify, and become loose bodies. It commonly affects the knee and can produce pain, swelling, and locking.

Meniscal tear with mechanical knee locki.normalized_text: Meniscal tear with mechanical knee locking
Meniscal tear with mechanical knee locki.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus can cause pain, recurrent joint swelling, catching, and locking, particularly in athletes or after prior knee injury.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the pancreas, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which can form a pancreatic-head mass and cause biliary obstruction.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy; tumors in the pancreatic head frequently obstruct the common bile duct and produce painless obstructive jaundice.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignancy of the distal common bile duct that causes mechanical obstruction of bile flow and can mimic a pancreatic-head tumor.

Autoimmune pancreatitis with obstructive.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory pancreatic disorder, often IgG4-related, that may cause focal pancreatic enlargement or a mass-like lesion and obstruct the distal bile duct.

Secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chro.normalized_text: Secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chronic renal failure
Secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chro.description: Periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of large lobulated calcium-phosphate masses, commonly occurring in patients with long-standing dialysis, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Calcinosis cutis, metastatic type.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by systemic disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism, including renal failure and hyperphosphatemia.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolo.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small cutaneous vessels, typically causing painful ischemic skin lesions and necrosis.

Gouty tophus.description: A nodular deposit of monosodium urate crystals caused by chronic hyperuricemia, usually affecting joints, ears, fingers, toes, and pressure areas.

Soft-tissue sarcoma.description: A malignant tumor arising from connective tissues such as fat, muscle, fibrous tissue, or blood vessels, often presenting as a progressively enlarging deep soft-tissue mass.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.description: An intra-articular fracture of the upper tibia involving the lateral weight-bearing surface of the knee, commonly caused by high-energy valgus or axial-loading trauma. The radiographs show a fracture involving the lateral tibial plateau with articular surface depression.

Bicondylar tibial plateau fracture.description: A more extensive proximal tibial intra-articular fracture involving both medial and lateral tibial condyles, typically occurring after substantial force and often associated with ligamentous injury or soft-tissue compromise.

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear wi.normalized_text: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear with traumatic hemarthrosis
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear wi.description: A tear of the ACL caused by pivoting, hyperextension, or high-energy knee trauma. It can produce immediate swelling from bleeding into the joint and difficulty bearing weight; it may coexist with a tibial plateau fracture.

Acute meniscal tear.description: A traumatic tear of the medial or lateral knee meniscus, often caused by twisting or impact. It can cause pain, swelling, and impaired weight bearing and may occur together with tibial plateau fractures or ligament injuries.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A rare mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal; rectal GISTs are usually submucosal spindle-cell masses and may harbor KIT or PDGFRA mutations.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the rectal wall and typically presents as a large intramural or submucosal mass composed of spindle cells.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that usually appears as a circumscribed submucosal mass and can cause obstructive symptoms when large.

Rectal schwannoma.description: An uncommon nerve-sheath tumor of the rectum, usually benign, that forms a slow-growing submucosal spindle-cell mass and may produce obstructive or pressure-related symptoms.

Rectal endometriosis (deep infiltrating.description: Ectopic endometrial tissue involving the rectovaginal septum or rectal wall, often producing a fibrotic mass and bowel symptoms in women of reproductive or perimenopausal age.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related SHORT syn.description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic triangular/progeroid facial appearance, and variably insulin resistance, eye abnormalities, dental anomalies, and hearing loss. The acronym SHORT refers to short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A genetic imprinting disorder, most often related to chromosome 11p15 alterations or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7, causing fetal and postnatal growth restriction, relative macrocephaly at birth, feeding difficulty, body asymmetry, and a triangular facial appearance.

3M syndrome.description: A primordial growth-restriction syndrome caused by biallelic variants in genes such as CUL7, OBSL1, or CCDC8. It produces severe prenatal and postnatal short stature, low birth weight, characteristic facial features, and usually normal intelligence.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: A rare adult-onset combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by profound B-cell depletion, hypogammaglobulinemia, impaired T-cell function, recurrent bacterial infections, and opportunistic infections.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A primary antibody deficiency causing low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine responses, commonly presenting with recurrent respiratory infections, chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, and sometimes autoimmune or granulomatous disease.

HIV infection/AIDS.description: Advanced HIV infection causes progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and predisposes to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, constitutional symptoms, and recurrent bacterial respiratory infections.

Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia.description: A rare non-HIV immunodeficiency defined by persistent low CD4 T-cell counts without another identified cause, leading to opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii infection.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring primarily in patients with impaired cellular immunity, especially CD4 lymphocytopenia or combined immunodeficiency.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic ne.description: A benign, self-limited inflammatory lymphadenitis that typically affects young adults and most often presents with cervical lymph-node enlargement. Histology characteristically shows patchy necrosis with karyorrhectic debris, histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and relative absence of neutrophils.

Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated.description: Autoimmune lupus can cause necrotizing lymphadenitis that may closely resemble Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically. It is usually accompanied by systemic autoimmune manifestations and serologic evidence of lupus.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Mycobacterial tuberculosis may cause chronic cervical or mediastinal lymph-node enlargement, often with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy that commonly presents with persistent painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, often in young adults.

Fulminant viral myocarditis (possibly ad.description: Acute inflammation of the heart muscle, often following a viral respiratory illness, which can rapidly cause severe ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, chest pain, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure occurring in the last month of pregnancy or within several months after delivery. It can cause severe left ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock.

Massive pulmonary embolism from pregnanc.normalized_text: Massive pulmonary embolism from pregnancy-associated deep-vein thrombosis
Massive pulmonary embolism from pregnanc.description: A clot originating in the deep veins, often in the legs, that embolizes to the pulmonary arteries. Pregnancy, obesity, and immobility or venous stasis increase risk; massive embolism can cause shock and cardiac arrest.

Pregnancy-associated acute coronary synd.normalized_text: Pregnancy-associated acute coronary syndrome, including spontaneous coronary artery dissection
Pregnancy-associated acute coronary synd.description: Acute myocardial ischemia caused by coronary artery obstruction; spontaneous coronary artery dissection is an important nonatherosclerotic cause in pregnant and postpartum women and may trigger ventricular tachycardia or sudden cardiac arrest.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract.

Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.normalized_text: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.description: Abnormal direct vascular communications in the liver, often involving hepatic arterial, portal venous, and hepatic venous circulations. In HHT, these can produce high-output heart failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischemia, and portosystemic shunting.

Hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemi.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired hepatic detoxification or diversion of portal blood around the liver. It may be precipitated by dehydration, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, or increased nitrogen load.

Macular juvenile xanthogranuloma.description: A rare flat (macular) variant of juvenile xanthogranuloma, a benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis of infancy/childhood. Lesions may be yellow-orange to brown, irregularly shaped macules rather than the usual papules or nodules.

Urticaria pigmentosa (maculopapular cuta.description: The most common form of childhood cutaneous mastocytosis, characterized by tan-brown to reddish-brown macules or papules caused by increased skin mast cells. Lesions may urticate after rubbing (Darier sign).

Café-au-lait macules.description: Benign, sharply circumscribed hyperpigmented patches that may occur alone or as part of genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type 1. Isolated lesions are common in healthy children.

Benign cephalic histiocytosis.description: A benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis occurring mainly in infants and young children, usually causing asymptomatic red-yellow to red-brown papules that may spread from the head to the upper trunk.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.description: Residual darkening of the skin after inflammation, injury, dermatitis, infection, or insect bites. It may persist after the original inflammatory lesion resolves.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMA.normalized_text: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMAS, Wilkie syndrome)
Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMA.description: Mechanical obstruction of the third portion of the duodenum caused by compression between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after severe weight loss and loss of retroperitoneal fat.

Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive.normalized_text: Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive eating disorder with severe malnutrition
Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive.description: An eating disorder characterized by inadequate caloric intake and markedly low body weight; severe malnutrition can cause amenorrhea, constipation, fatigue, and can precipitate superior mesenteric artery syndrome.

Mechanical proximal small-bowel obstruct.description: Partial or complete blockage of the duodenum or proximal small bowel causing upstream gastric and bowel dilatation, vomiting, reduced intestinal transit, and constipation. In this case, SMAS would be a likely specific cause.

Gastrocolic fistula (gastric pouch-to-tr.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula (gastric pouch-to-transverse colon fistula) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Gastrocolic fistula (gastric pouch-to-tr.description: An abnormal connection between the gastric pouch and colon, allowing food to bypass normal intestinal digestion and enter the colon directly. It can occur as a late complication of bariatric surgery, often related to marginal ulceration or chronic inflammation.

Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anas.normalized_text: Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with fistulization
Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anas.description: A marginal ulcer is peptic ulceration near the gastrojejunal surgical connection after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Severe or chronic ulcers can erode into adjacent structures, including the colon, producing a gastrocolic fistula.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.normalized_text: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.description: Excessive bacterial colonization of the small intestine can occur after altered gastrointestinal anatomy and may cause diarrhea, gas, malabsorption, nutritional deficiencies, and weight loss.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Air leaking into the mediastinum, often caused by increased intrathoracic pressure from coughing or an asthma exacerbation. It can cause sharp chest pain radiating to the neck and may be subtle on chest radiography.

Acute asthma exacerbation.description: An acute worsening of reversible airway obstruction, commonly triggered by poor adherence to inhaled therapy, respiratory infection, or environmental exposure.

Acute bronchitis or viral lower respirat.normalized_text: Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
Acute bronchitis or viral lower respirat.description: Inflammation of the bronchial airways, usually viral, causing cough and sputum production and potentially triggering bronchospasm in a person with asthma.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow, usually by thrombus, which can produce acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. It is an important alternative diagnosis in acute pleuritic chest pain.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial lung collapse, which can present with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Small pneumothoraces may have normal oxygen saturation.

Leprosy (Hansen disease), likely multiba.description: A chronic infection with Mycobacterium leprae that affects skin and peripheral nerves, causing sensory loss, neuropathic pain, and characteristic plaques, papules, or diffuse infiltrative skin lesions.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis associated with chronic hepatitis C infection that can cause palpable purpura, painful peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia, renal disease, and systemic symptoms.

HIV-associated distal symmetric polyneur.description: A painful, length-dependent sensory neuropathy that may occur in untreated HIV infection or from neurotoxic antiretroviral medications, typically beginning in the feet and progressing proximally.

Secondary syphilis with possible syphili.normalized_text: Secondary syphilis with possible syphilitic peripheral neuropathy
Secondary syphilis with possible syphili.description: The disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection, commonly producing a diffuse papulosquamous rash and generalized symptoms; neurologic involvement can occur but peripheral neuropathy is less common.

Nutritional deficiency neuropathy (espec.normalized_text: Nutritional deficiency neuropathy (especially vitamin B12, thiamine, or vitamin B6 deficiency)
Nutritional deficiency neuropathy (espec.description: Deficiency of essential vitamins, often related to malnutrition or substance use, can cause a symmetric distal polyneuropathy with sensory loss, paresthesias, pain, and gait difficulty.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agam.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, resulting in failure of B-cell maturation, markedly reduced immunoglobulins, and susceptibility to recurrent bacterial respiratory infections after maternal antibodies decline.

Autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia.description: A group of rare inherited disorders affecting B-cell development through genes other than BTK, such as IGHM, CD79A, CD79B, BLNK, or PIK3R1. These conditions produce absent or markedly reduced B cells and severe hypogammaglobulinemia.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).description: A group of severe primary immunodeficiencies characterized by profound T-cell dysfunction, often with impaired B-cell function and low immunoglobulin concentrations, causing severe and recurrent infections in infancy.

Penile fracture (rupture of the tunica a.normalized_text: Penile fracture (rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum)
Penile fracture (rupture of the tunica a.description: An acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually occurring during sexual intercourse. Blood can escape into adjacent soft tissues and track into the perineum and scrotum.

Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/pe.normalized_text: Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/perineal hematoma
Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/pe.description: A subtype of penile fracture in which a corporal tear is located near the penile root. Hemorrhage may predominantly present in the perineum and scrotum rather than causing marked swelling of the penile shaft.

Rupture of the superficial or deep dorsa.normalized_text: Rupture of the superficial or deep dorsal penile vein
Rupture of the superficial or deep dorsa.description: Traumatic tearing of a dorsal penile vein during intercourse can cause penile-base, perineal, and scrotal bruising. It may clinically resemble penile fracture but generally lacks a corpus cavernosum tunical tear.

Scrotal hematoma secondary to genital tr.normalized_text: Scrotal hematoma secondary to genital trauma
Scrotal hematoma secondary to genital tr.description: A collection of blood within scrotal soft tissues caused by trauma to adjacent genital structures, including the penis, perineum, spermatic cord, or scrotal wall.

Testicular torsion.description: Twisting of the spermatic cord that compromises testicular blood supply and produces a surgical acute-scrotum emergency.

Muscle-eye-brain disease (POMGNT1-relate.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused by abnormal glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, producing congenital hypotonia and weakness together with intellectual disability, structural brain abnormalities, and ocular findings.

Walker-Warburg syndrome.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy characterized by congenital hypotonia, marked developmental impairment, eye abnormalities, elevated CK, and severe brain malformations such as cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, and cerebellar or brainstem abnormalities.

Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy.description: An autosomal-recessive dystroglycanopathy causing congenital muscular dystrophy, intellectual disability, brain malformations, seizures in many patients, and sometimes ocular involvement. It is most commonly reported in Japanese populations but can occur elsewhere.

LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.normalized_text: LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystrophy (merosin-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy)
LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystro.description: A congenital muscular dystrophy caused by LAMA2 deficiency, typically presenting in infancy with profound hypotonia, weakness, absent reflexes, delayed motor development, contractures, elevated CK, and characteristic diffuse cerebral white-matter abnormalities on MRI.

Primary bladder adenocarcinoma.description: A rare malignant epithelial tumor arising from the urinary bladder, usually in older adults. It may form gland-like structures and can present as a pelvic or lower abdominal mass.

Urachal adenocarcinoma.description: A gland-forming adenocarcinoma arising from embryologic urachal remnants, most often near the bladder dome or anterior midline pelvis. It commonly affects middle-aged or older adults and can form a palpable lower abdominal mass.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma, including sig.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, including sigmoid colon carcinoma
Colorectal adenocarcinoma, including sig.description: A malignant glandular tumor of the colon that is common in older adults. A sigmoid or rectosigmoid tumor may cause left lower abdominal pain and a palpable pelvic mass, and can extend into adjacent pelvic organs.

Prostatic adenocarcinoma with local pelv.normalized_text: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with local pelvic extension
Prostatic adenocarcinoma with local pelv.description: A common malignancy in older men that originates in the prostate and may invade the bladder base, seminal vesicles, or adjacent pelvic tissues in advanced disease, producing a pelvic mass.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion, commonly from antifreeze, causing high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolality gap, neurologic depression, and later renal injury from calcium oxalate crystal deposition.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion that is metabolized to formic acid, producing severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolality gap, central nervous system depression, and potentially visual injury.

Propylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxicity from propylene glycol, a solvent found in some intravenous and oral medication formulations, which can cause elevated osmolality gap, lactic acidosis, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and depressed consciousness.

Cyanide poisoning.description: Cyanide inhibits cellular oxygen utilization, rapidly causing profound lactic acidosis, metabolic acidosis, altered mental status, cardiovascular collapse, and potentially death.

Salicylate poisoning.description: Aspirin or salicylate overdose can cause altered mental status, elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, hyperthermia, tinnitus, and elevated lactate in severe poisoning.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Ovarian torsion with massive ovarian ede.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion with massive ovarian edema
Ovarian torsion with massive ovarian ede.description: Partial or intermittent twisting of the ovarian pedicle impairs venous and lymphatic drainage, producing marked ovarian enlargement and edema; it can mimic an ovarian tumor and cause recurrent abdominal pain.

Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.normalized_text: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.description: A rare sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor occurring mainly in children and adolescents. It may become very large, cause abdominal pain or distension, and may hemorrhage or undergo torsion. Many tumors produce estrogen, although not all do.

Ovarian dysgerminoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor most commonly seen in adolescents and young women. It usually presents as a unilateral, solid, enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass with pain or pressure symptoms.

Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst or ruptured ova.normalized_text: Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst or ruptured ovarian cyst
Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst or ruptured ova.description: Bleeding into or rupture of a functional ovarian cyst can cause sudden unilateral pelvic pain and, when bleeding is substantial, anemia and peritoneal irritation. Functional cysts are less likely before menarche.

Appendicitis with appendiceal phlegmon o.normalized_text: Appendicitis with appendiceal phlegmon or abscess
Appendicitis with appendiceal phlegmon o.description: Appendicitis classically begins with central abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant. Complicated or contained appendicitis may form an inflammatory mass and cause elevated inflammatory markers.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency, leading to accumulation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides. It can cause developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, skeletal abnormalities, coarse facial features, hearing problems, and vacuolated blood cells.

Fucosidosis.description: A rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency. It produces progressive neurodevelopmental impairment, hypotonia, seizures, coarse facial appearance, skeletal deformities, behavioral changes, and cytoplasmic vacuoles in leukocytes.

Aspartylglucosaminuria.description: A lysosomal storage disease caused by aspartylglucosaminidase deficiency. Affected children develop progressive intellectual and motor impairment, hypotonia, seizures, behavioral difficulties, facial coarsening, skeletal findings, and vacuolated lymphocytes.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. It causes progressive developmental delay, coarse facial features, skeletal disease, joint contractures, behavioral abnormalities, and sometimes seizures.

Smith-Magenis syndrome.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder most often caused by deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 or pathogenic variants in RAI1. It is characterized by developmental delay, hypotonia, distinctive facial features, sleep disturbance, behavioral dysregulation, and stereotyped or self-injurious behaviors.

Pyogenic spondylodiscitis with iliopsoas.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies that can extend into the psoas muscle, causing a retroperitoneal abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause.

Primary iliopsoas abscess.description: A deep abscess within the iliopsoas muscle, usually caused by hematogenous bacterial seeding, commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus. It may cause back, hip, flank, or abdominal pain and systemic sepsis.

Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.normalized_text: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with metastatic infection
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.description: Bloodstream infection with S. aureus can seed distant sites, producing vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, psoas abscesses, septic thrombophlebitis, and pulmonary infection or septic emboli.

Septic thrombophlebitis of the iliac vei.normalized_text: Septic thrombophlebitis of the iliac vein associated with psoas abscess
Septic thrombophlebitis of the iliac vei.description: Infection and thrombosis of a deep pelvic vein can occur adjacent to a psoas abscess or spinal infection. It may produce leg swelling and can cause septic pulmonary embolic complications.

Pyogenic liver abscess with systemic sep.normalized_text: Pyogenic liver abscess with systemic sepsis and metastatic musculoskeletal infection
Pyogenic liver abscess with systemic sep.description: A bacterial liver abscess can cause fever, leukocytosis, cholestatic liver abnormalities, and bacteremia; in severe cases, organisms may seed distant tissues such as the spine, psoas muscle, lungs, or veins.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema.description: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that can occur after rapid drainage of a large pleural effusion or pneumothorax, typically affecting the re-expanded lung.

Aspiration pneumonia.description: Infection or chemical lung injury caused by inhalation of gastric or oropharyngeal contents, often producing dependent unilateral infiltrates and hypoxemic respiratory symptoms.

Hospital-acquired or community-acquired.description: Acute infectious inflammation of lung parenchyma that commonly causes cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and focal consolidation.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Pulmonary fluid accumulation caused by elevated cardiac filling pressures, usually due to acute heart failure; it typically produces bilateral interstitial or alveolar edema.

Iliac artery fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder causing alternating stenosis and dilation ('string-of-beads' appearance), which can involve renal and iliac arteries. Iliac involvement can cause exertional claudication, while renal involvement can cause hypertension.

External iliac artery endofibrosis.description: A nonatherosclerotic fibrotic narrowing of the external iliac artery, classically occurring in endurance athletes and producing exercise-induced buttock, thigh, or leg claudication with near-normal resting vascular testing.

Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease cau.normalized_text: Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease causing vascular claudication
Aortoiliac peripheral artery disease cau.description: Narrowing of the aortoiliac arteries reduces blood flow during exertion, producing buttock, hip, or thigh claudication. It is most commonly due to atherosclerosis but may also result from nonatherosclerotic arterial disease.

Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic c.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic c.description: Degenerative narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal can cause exertional buttock and thigh discomfort, often worsened by standing or walking and relieved by sitting or spinal flexion.

Drug-induced acquired long QT syndrome w.normalized_text: Drug-induced acquired long QT syndrome with torsades de pointes
Drug-induced acquired long QT syndrome w.description: A potentially life-threatening polymorphic ventricular tachycardia caused by QT prolongation, commonly triggered by QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic drugs such as sotalol. Concomitant rate-slowing therapy and post-cardioversion bradycardia can increase risk.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.description: A rapid ventricular rhythm with beat-to-beat variation in QRS morphology. When associated with prolonged QT interval it is termed torsades de pointes; it can cause hypotension, syncope, or sudden cardiac arrest.

Sotalol-associated proarrhythmia.description: An adverse antiarrhythmic effect in which sotalol prolongs ventricular repolarization and may provoke marked QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, bradyarrhythmia, or other ventricular arrhythmias.

Recurrent atrial tachycardia.description: A supraventricular tachyarrhythmia arising from the atria, often causing palpitations, lightheadedness, and reduced exercise tolerance. Prior atrial surgery can predispose to recurrent atrial tachycardia.

Systemic sarcoidosis with acute sarcoid.normalized_text: Systemic sarcoidosis with acute sarcoid arthritis (Lofgren-spectrum presentation)
Systemic sarcoidosis with acute sarcoid.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving intrathoracic lymph nodes, skin, joints, liver, and lymph nodes. Acute sarcoid arthritis can present with fever, erythematous nodules, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and polyarthritis.

Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and r.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and reactive polyarthritis
Tuberculosis with erythema nodosum and r.description: Tuberculosis can cause constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, granulomatous inflammation, erythema nodosum, and inflammatory arthritis. Tuberculous arthritis is usually chronic and commonly affects one joint, while reactive arthritis may be polyarticular.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: An autoinflammatory systemic disorder causing fever, inflammatory polyarthritis, rash, lymphadenopathy, and hepatomegaly. It typically produces high spiking quotidian fever and a transient salmon-pink rash.

Reactive arthritis.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis occurring after gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, usually affecting lower-limb joints asymmetrically and sometimes accompanied by mucocutaneous findings.

Disseminated fungal infection with granu.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection with granulomatous disease (for example histoplasmosis)
Disseminated fungal infection with granu.description: Disseminated fungal infections can produce prolonged fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, pulmonary hilar lymph node enlargement, skin lesions, and granulomatous inflammation, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Bevacizumab-associated physeal abnormali.description: Anti-VEGF therapy such as bevacizumab can disrupt endochondral bone formation in growing children, producing widened, irregular, or painful physes, often involving the distal radius or other rapidly growing bones.
