Distal radial physeal stress injury.description: A repetitive mechanical stress injury of the distal radial growth plate that can cause physeal widening, irregularity, local pain, and reduced wrist motion. It is classically seen in young athletes but may also occur in medically vulnerable children with altered bone health.

Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) invol.normalized_text: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) involving the distal radius/carpal region
Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) invol.description: Osteonecrosis is bone death caused by impaired blood supply. It can occur in children receiving cancer therapy, particularly with corticosteroid exposure, and may present with focal joint pain and restricted motion; MRI can detect early changes.

Menkes disease (ATP7A-related copper tra.description: An X-linked disorder of impaired intestinal copper transport causing severe systemic copper deficiency, neurodegeneration, connective-tissue abnormalities, characteristic sparse kinky hair, and tortuous cerebral vessels.

Occipital horn syndrome (milder ATP7A-re.normalized_text: Occipital horn syndrome (milder ATP7A-related copper transport disorder)
Occipital horn syndrome (milder ATP7A-re.description: A milder allelic form of ATP7A-related copper transport disease characterized primarily by connective-tissue manifestations, vascular tortuosity, bladder diverticula, joint laxity, and occipital bone exostoses.

Acquired copper deficiency due to malnut.normalized_text: Acquired copper deficiency due to malnutrition or impaired intestinal absorption
Acquired copper deficiency due to malnut.description: Low copper levels can result from inadequate dietary intake, prolonged parenteral nutrition without adequate supplementation, malabsorption, or intestinal disease; it may cause anemia, neutropenia, poor growth, and neurologic dysfunction.

Mitochondrial membrane protein-associate.normalized_text: Mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration / mitochondrial disorder with secondary copper abnormalities
Mitochondrial membrane protein-associate.description: Mitochondrial disorders may present in infancy with failure to thrive, hypotonia, developmental delay, recurrent illness, and neuroimaging abnormalities, although they do not usually cause the distinctive Menkes hair phenotype or profound copper transport defect.

Adrenocortical oncocytoma.description: A rare adrenal cortical tumor composed of oncocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Most are nonfunctioning and incidentally discovered, although some can enlarge substantially and require surgical removal to exclude malignant potential.

Adrenal cortical adenoma.description: A common benign tumor of the adrenal cortex. Many adenomas are nonfunctioning incidental findings, while some produce cortisol or aldosterone.

Adrenocortical carcinoma.description: A rare malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that may be hormonally functional or nonfunctional. It often presents as a large, enlarging adrenal mass and can be asymptomatic when nonfunctional.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing tumor of adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. Some pheochromocytomas are clinically silent, but most cause episodic or persistent catecholamine-related symptoms.

Adrenal cavernous hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular adrenal lesion that is often nonfunctioning and incidentally found. It can become large and may show heterogeneous imaging features due to hemorrhage, thrombosis, or calcification.

Linear morphea (en coup de sabre).description: A localized scleroderma subtype causing a linear, indurated, sclerotic plaque on the forehead and scalp, often associated with scalp atrophy and scarring alopecia.

Morphea profunda.description: A deeper variant of localized scleroderma involving the deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, or muscle, producing marked induration and tethering of skin.

Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus manifestation characterized by inflammation of subcutaneous fat, which can cause firm plaques, lipoatrophy, and scarring alopecia when affecting the scalp.

Systemic sclerosis.description: An autoimmune connective-tissue disorder characterized by widespread skin thickening and fibrosis, vascular abnormalities, and potential internal-organ involvement.

ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.normalized_text: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis (mesenteric vasculitis)
ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus is a multisystem autoimmune disease. Rarely, ANA can be negative despite strongly positive anti-dsDNA/anti-Ro antibodies. Lupus enteritis, often due to immune-complex-mediated mesenteric vasculitis, causes acute abdominal pain, vomiting, bowel-wall edema, and possible ileus.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus serositis and intestinal pseudo-obstruction
Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus.description: Lupus can cause inflammation of serosal surfaces, including pericarditis and peritonitis, and can occasionally produce intestinal pseudo-obstruction from intestinal smooth-muscle dysfunction, vasculitis, or associated bowel-wall edema.

Behçet disease with gastrointestinal vas.description: Behçet disease is an inflammatory vasculitic disorder characterized by recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin lesions, and sometimes gastrointestinal ulceration or vascular inflammation causing abdominal pain.

Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-v.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-vessel systemic vasculitis with mesenteric involvement
Polyarteritis nodosa or another medium-v.description: Medium-vessel vasculitis can affect mesenteric arteries, producing severe abdominal pain, vomiting, intestinal ischemia, bowel-wall edema, and inflammatory marker elevation.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma in a coronary artery causing narrowing of the vessel lumen and acute myocardial ischemia; it is more common in younger women and may be associated with pregnancy-related hormonal changes and connective-tissue disorders.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) secondary to SCAD
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction without persistent ST-segment elevation, caused here most plausibly by reduced coronary blood flow from spontaneous coronary artery dissection rather than plaque rupture.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS).description: A heritable connective-tissue disorder, usually related to pathogenic COL3A1 variants, characterized by arterial fragility, arterial aneurysm or dissection, organ rupture, and pregnancy-related complications. Coronary and renal/visceral arterial involvement can occur.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD).description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arteriopathy of medium-sized arteries, particularly renal and carotid arteries, that can cause arterial stenosis, aneurysm, dissection, and tortuosity. It has a strong association with SCAD in women.

Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.normalized_text: Intestinal malrotation with intermittent midgut volvulus
Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.description: Congenital abnormal positioning and fixation of the intestine that can predispose to twisting of the midgut around the mesenteric vessels. Upper GI contrast studies may show an abnormal duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew configuration of the proximal small bowel.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: Progressive thickening of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, usually affecting young male infants between 2 and 8 weeks of age. It can lead to poor intake, dehydration, and poor weight gain.

Congenital duodenal web or partial duode.normalized_text: Congenital duodenal web or partial duodenal obstruction
Congenital duodenal web or partial duode.description: A congenital membrane within the duodenum that partially obstructs passage of feeds. Partial webs may present later than complete duodenal atresia with chronic feeding intolerance and poor growth.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with fee.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with feeding aversion
Gastroesophageal reflux disease with fee.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus can cause feeding refusal, irritability, recurrent regurgitation, and inadequate caloric intake. Severe cases may lead to poor weight gain.

Edematous dermatomyositis.description: A rare, severe variant of dermatomyositis characterized by inflammatory myopathy with prominent subcutaneous edema, often involving the face, limbs, and neck, with possible bulbar and respiratory muscle involvement.

Polymyositis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes; dysphagia may occur due to pharyngeal muscle involvement.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy that usually produces marked proximal weakness and substantial creatine kinase elevation, sometimes with dysphagia; biopsy typically shows prominent muscle necrosis with relatively little inflammation.

Angioedema.description: Acute localized swelling of the skin and mucosal tissues, often affecting the face, tongue, and upper airway; it may be histamine-mediated or bradykinin-mediated, including medication-associated angioedema.

Allergic contact dermatitis to parapheny.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis to paraphenylenediamine (PPD) in black henna tattoo
Allergic contact dermatitis to parapheny.description: A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction caused by PPD, a chemical commonly added to black henna to darken the color and shorten application time. It often produces a sharply localized eczematous or blistering eruption matching the tattoo design.

Allergic contact dermatitis to black hen.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis to black henna with secondary impetiginization
Allergic contact dermatitis to black hen.description: Severe PPD-induced allergic contact dermatitis that has become secondarily infected with bacteria, commonly Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. This can cause weeping, yellow discharge, and honey-colored crusts over an eczematous tattoo-shaped rash.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, characterized by fragile blisters that rupture and leave erosions with yellow or golden crusting.

Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.normalized_text: Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo dye or application chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis from tattoo.description: Inflammation caused by direct chemical injury to the skin from substances in tattoo dye, solvents, or additives. It can produce redness, burning, swelling, and occasionally blistering at the contact site.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by chronic deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, producing visible tophi, joint destruction, and loss of function.

Tophaceous gout with severe gouty arthro.normalized_text: Tophaceous gout with severe gouty arthropathy of the hands
Tophaceous gout with severe gouty arthro.description: A severe deforming form of chronic gout in which large urate tophi accumulate around the small joints, tendons, and soft tissues of the hands, causing deformity and major restriction of motion.

Rheumatoid arthritis.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that commonly affects the small joints of the hands symmetrically and can cause deformity, nodules, and impaired hand function.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.description: A crystal deposition disorder caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, usually producing acute or chronic arthritis and occasionally mass-like periarticular deposits.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A B-cell-derived lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background; nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymphoma commonly affects young adults and often presents with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the anterior mediastinum, usually in young adults, often causing a bulky mediastinal mass and respiratory symptoms.

Mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A tumor derived from germ cells that can arise in the anterior mediastinum of young men and present as a mediastinal mass with respiratory symptoms and supraclavicular lymph node enlargement.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP/PC.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring most often in advanced HIV infection, typically causing diffuse bilateral interstitial or perihilar pulmonary infiltrates and progressive respiratory symptoms.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lungs, which is common in people with HIV and may have atypical radiographic appearances, including diffuse infiltrates or hilar involvement.

Community-acquired atypical pneumonia.description: A lower respiratory infection caused by organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, or respiratory viruses, often producing dry cough and diffuse or patchy interstitial infiltrates.

Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.description: An opportunistic viral lung infection occurring primarily in severely immunocompromised individuals, including advanced HIV, and capable of causing diffuse interstitial lung infiltrates and hypoxemic breathlessness.

Pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma.description: A malignancy associated with human herpesvirus 8 in advanced HIV infection that can involve the lungs, producing cough, dyspnea, and bilateral perihilar or interstitial radiographic opacities.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis.description: Diffuse infiltration of pulmonary lymphatic vessels by metastatic carcinoma, often from lung, breast, stomach, pancreas, or prostate cancer. It commonly produces interlobular septal thickening and progressive breathlessness.

Pulmonary tumor thrombotic microangiopat.description: A rare cancer-related condition in which microscopic tumor emboli obstruct small pulmonary arteries and trigger vascular remodeling, causing rapidly progressive dyspnea, pulmonary hypertension, and elevated coagulation markers.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, usually originating from deep veins, producing acute or subacute dyspnea, pleuritic or nonspecific chest pain, and occasionally syncope.

Primary bronchogenic carcinoma with lymp.normalized_text: Primary bronchogenic carcinoma with lymphangitic spread
Primary bronchogenic carcinoma with lymp.description: Lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma in a smoker, may spread through pulmonary lymphatics before a dominant lung mass is apparent, causing progressive dyspnea and unilateral interstitial lung changes.

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Fluid accumulation in the lung interstitium and alveoli due to elevated cardiac filling pressures, commonly from left ventricular dysfunction or acute ischemic heart disease.

Right unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.description: Loss of right phrenic nerve function causes elevation and reduced movement of the right hemidiaphragm, leading to compression of the right lung base and hypoxemic breathlessness. It may occur after viral illness or from other phrenic nerve injury.

Diaphragmatic eventration.description: Diaphragmatic eventration is abnormal permanent elevation of part or all of a hemidiaphragm due to thinning or weakness of diaphragmatic muscle. It can reduce lung volume and cause dyspnea, particularly in obesity.

Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructiv.normalized_text: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructiv.description: COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of airflow limitation, often triggered by viral respiratory infection. Smoking is a major risk factor and patients may have wheeze, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Pulmonary embolism is obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow, usually by thrombus, and may cause acute dyspnea and severe hypoxemia with relatively few chest examination findings.

Community-acquired pneumonia, including.description: Community-acquired pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma and can produce dyspnea, hypoxemia, focal reduced air entry, and aegophony. Viral infection can occur without fever or leukocytosis.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS) of the maxilla/oral cavity
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may present as a rapidly enlarging extranodal mass in the oral cavity or jaw. The histology and BCL6/MUM1-positive, CD10-negative immunophenotype are compatible with an activated B-cell phenotype of DLBCL.

Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the oral cavity
Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoma arising primarily in oral soft tissues, gingiva, palate, maxilla, or jaw rather than initially presenting in lymph nodes. DLBCL is the most common histologic subtype in the oral cavity.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla/oral cavity
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Colorectal carcinoma can rarely metastasize to the jaws or oral soft tissues, producing swelling, bone destruction, tooth mobility, and nonhealing extraction wounds. A prior history of colorectal cancer makes this an important alternative diagnosis.

Odontogenic infection with maxillary ost.description: A bacterial infection of the maxilla and adjacent soft tissues, often following dental extraction, that can cause swelling, delayed socket healing, local inflammation, and bone destruction.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary gingiva/alveolus
Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary.description: An oral cavity malignancy arising from squamous epithelium that can present as an ulcerative or exophytic gingival mass, persistent extraction-site nonhealing, local bone invasion, and cheek swelling.

Tinea incognito (steroid-modified extens.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection whose typical ring-like appearance has been altered, masked, and allowed to spread by use of potent topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol.

Tinea corporis with tinea cruris.description: A superficial dermatophyte infection of glabrous skin and the groin, producing itchy, expanding scaly annular plaques with an active raised border and central clearing.

Nummular dermatitis (discoid eczema).description: A chronic inflammatory eczema characterized by itchy coin-shaped scaly plaques, often on the extremities; lesions may become extensive or secondarily irritated.

Plaque psoriasis.description: A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease causing well-demarcated erythematous plaques with scale; inverse psoriasis can affect the groin with less scale.

Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.normalized_text: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica, often signet-ring cell carcinoma)
Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.description: An infiltrative gastric cancer that spreads diffusely through the stomach wall, causing marked wall thickening, poor distensibility, and gastric outlet obstruction; mucosal endoscopy may initially fail to show a discrete intraluminal mass.

Gastric plexiform fibromyxoma.description: A rare, usually benign mesenchymal tumor arising predominantly in the gastric antrum or pylorus. It can infiltrate the gastric wall and produce gastric outlet obstruction, often without a prominent mucosal mass.

Primary gastric lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the stomach that can cause diffuse gastric-wall thickening, enlarged folds, submucosal infiltration, and occasionally gastric outlet obstruction.

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from the muscularis propria of the stomach. An antral or pyloric GIST may compress or obstruct the gastric outlet, although many GISTs form a localized exophytic mass.

Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NA.description: A condition in which maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets, causing severe thrombocytopenia and bleeding manifestations in an otherwise well newborn.

Congenital thrombocytopenia due to inher.normalized_text: Congenital thrombocytopenia due to inherited platelet-production disorder
Congenital thrombocytopenia due to inher.description: A group of genetic disorders causing reduced platelet number or abnormal platelet production, which may present at birth with petechiae, purpura, and excessive bruising.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia.description: An inherited platelet function disorder caused by defective or absent platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, resulting in impaired platelet aggregation despite a potentially normal platelet count.

Congenital factor XIII deficiency.description: A rare autosomal recessive coagulation disorder in which clots are unstable because factor XIII cannot adequately cross-link fibrin. It can cause neonatal bruising, bleeding after procedures, and later severe hemorrhage.

Hemophilia A or Hemophilia B.description: X-linked deficiencies of factor VIII or factor IX that primarily affect male infants and can cause excessive bleeding after trauma, injections, or invasive procedures.

Chronic subdural hematoma.description: A collection of blood products between the dura and arachnoid membranes, often developing gradually over days to weeks after minor or repetitive head trauma. It may cause progressive headache and mass effect despite a normal neurological examination initially.

Acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma.description: A chronic subdural collection with newer bleeding into it, potentially following repeated minor trauma. It can produce an increasingly severe headache and radiological evidence of mixed-age blood products.

Traumatic cerebral contusion with associ.normalized_text: Traumatic cerebral contusion with associated subdural hematoma
Traumatic cerebral contusion with associ.description: A cerebral contusion is bruising and bleeding within brain tissue after acceleration-deceleration injury; temporal and frontal regions are common sites. It may coexist with a subdural hematoma after repetitive head movements.

Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.normalized_text: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET)
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.description: A malignant small round cell sarcoma arising in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly has EWSR1 rearrangement, often involving an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion, and may show neural or neuroendocrine differentiation.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSR.description: An aggressive small round cell sarcoma that usually develops in the abdominal or pelvic peritoneum of young people. It is characterized by an EWSR1-WT1 fusion and often presents with peritoneal masses.

Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue.normalized_text: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue
Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue.description: A rare malignant soft-tissue sarcoma, sometimes called melanoma of soft parts, most often arising in tendons or aponeuroses of the extremities. It may harbor EWSR1-ATF1 or EWSR1-CREB1 rearrangements.

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.description: A high-grade epithelial malignancy composed of neuroendocrine cells, often arising in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, lung, or gynecologic organs and commonly expressing synaptophysin.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, resulting in cytokine excess, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, and coagulopathy.

Dabrafenib/trametinib-associated hemopha.description: Secondary HLH triggered by BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy. Dabrafenib plus trametinib can rarely provoke severe systemic inflammatory reactions, including HLH, often shortly after treatment initiation.

Pembrolizumab-associated immune-related.description: HLH can rarely occur as a severe immune-related adverse event of PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab, due to excessive immune activation.

Malignancy-associated hemophagocytic lym.description: Secondary HLH may be triggered by advanced malignancy, including metastatic solid tumors, although it is more commonly associated with hematologic cancers.

Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to hypo.normalized_text: Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to hypothalamic-pituitary injury
Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to hypo.description: Deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones caused by trauma to the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, or pituitary gland. The transorbital gunshot trajectory and retained metallic foreign body near the skull base may have injured these structures.

Post-traumatic central adrenal insuffici.description: Adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency from hypothalamic or pituitary injury causes inadequate cortisol production. This can be life-threatening, particularly during acute trauma or infection.

Post-traumatic hypogonadotropic hypogona.description: Deficient hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone or pituitary gonadotropin secretion results in low luteinising hormone and low testosterone, causing delayed or arrested puberty.

Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic.normalized_text: Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction
Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic.description: Central hypothyroidism occurs when pituitary thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion is inadequate for the circulating thyroid hormone level, usually because of pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congenital aqueductal stenosis
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congeni.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct causes impaired cerebrospinal-fluid flow, progressive enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles, and raised intracranial pressure.

Hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal plat.normalized_text: Hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal plate glioma
Hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal plat.description: A low-grade tumor of the tectal region can compress the cerebral aqueduct and produce obstructive hydrocephalus, often presenting with vomiting, macrocephaly, and developmental decline in young children.

Dandy-Walker malformation or other poste.normalized_text: Dandy-Walker malformation or other posterior fossa cerebrospinal-fluid outflow abnormality
Dandy-Walker malformation or other poste.description: Congenital posterior fossa malformations can disrupt cerebrospinal-fluid circulation and lead to hydrocephalus, macrocephaly, developmental delay, and impaired motor development.

Intracranial mass causing raised intracr.normalized_text: Intracranial mass causing raised intracranial pressure
Intracranial mass causing raised intracr.description: Brain tumors or other intracranial masses can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid pathways or increase intracranial pressure, causing vomiting, lethargy, developmental loss, and enlarged head size in infants with open sutures.

Cyclic vomiting syndrome.description: Cyclic vomiting syndrome causes recurrent stereotyped episodes of severe vomiting separated by periods of relative wellness, often associated with lethargy and poor intake.

Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome).description: A cause of secondary hypertension due to autonomous aldosterone production, leading to suppressed renin and an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Potassium may be normal.

Obstructive sleep apnea-associated hyper.description: Obstructive sleep apnea can cause resistant or newly recognized hypertension through recurrent nocturnal hypoxia and sympathetic nervous system activation. It is commonly associated with obesity.

Essential (primary) hypertension.description: The most common form of hypertension, caused by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors such as obesity, smoking, and sleep apnea.

Cushing syndrome.description: A disorder of chronic excess cortisol production that can cause hypertension, central obesity, fatigue, glucose intolerance, skin changes, and muscle weakness.

Pseudo-Cushing state related to obesity.normalized_text: Pseudo-Cushing state related to obesity and obstructive sleep apnea
Pseudo-Cushing state related to obesity.description: Obesity, chronic stress, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea may cause mild elevation of cortisol testing without true autonomous cortisol excess; dexamethasone suppression is usually preserved.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) c.normalized_text: Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) causing coronary vasospasm and myocardial infarction
Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) c.description: Transient epicardial coronary artery spasm can cause severe ischemia, ST-segment elevation, myocardial infarction, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias despite otherwise normal or minimally diseased coronary arteries. Triptans such as sumatriptan can precipitate vasospasm.

Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.description: An acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary occlusion produces chest pain, ST-segment elevation, elevated cardiac troponin, and may lead to ventricular arrhythmia and cardiac arrest. The ECG pattern shown is consistent with prominent anterior precordial ST-segment elevation.

Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospas.description: Sumatriptan is a serotonin receptor agonist used for migraine that can rarely cause coronary vasoconstriction or vasospasm, resulting in chest pain, transient ST elevation, myocardial infarction, and potentially life-threatening arrhythmias.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.normalized_text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) with impending or actual colonic perforation
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.description: Acute massive dilatation of the colon without a mechanical blockage, often occurring in patients with severe neurologic disease, immobility, metabolic illness, or medications affecting bowel motility. Marked dilatation can cause ischemia and perforation.

Stercoral colitis with stercoral colonic.normalized_text: Stercoral colitis with stercoral colonic perforation
Stercoral colitis with stercoral colonic.description: Inflammation, ischemic pressure injury, ulceration, and possible perforation of the colon caused by impacted stool (fecaloma). It occurs most often in patients with chronic constipation, immobility, or neurologic impairment.

Mechanical large-bowel obstruction due t.normalized_text: Mechanical large-bowel obstruction due to fecal impaction
Mechanical large-bowel obstruction due t.description: A distal fecal impaction can function as a mechanical obstruction, producing proximal colonic dilatation, abdominal distension, vomiting, and potentially ischemia or perforation if untreated.

Sigmoid volvulus.description: Twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesenteric attachment causes closed-loop large-bowel obstruction. It is associated with chronic constipation, neurologic disease, reduced mobility, and a redundant sigmoid colon; ischemia and perforation may occur.

Cryptococcal pneumonia with cryptococcal.description: Infection with Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii that can involve the lungs and disseminate to the central nervous system, causing subacute meningitis. Pulmonary disease may produce nodules, cough, dyspnea, and constitutional symptoms.

Histoplasmosis with pulmonary and centra.normalized_text: Histoplasmosis with pulmonary and central nervous system involvement
Histoplasmosis with pulmonary and centra.description: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that can cause chronic pulmonary disease, diffuse or nodular lung infiltrates, constitutional symptoms, and, less commonly, chronic meningitis.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with tuberculous.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause a chronic respiratory illness with constitutional symptoms and may spread hematogenously to the meninges, producing subacute meningitis with headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.

Nocardiosis with pulmonary and central n.normalized_text: Nocardiosis with pulmonary and central nervous system dissemination
Nocardiosis with pulmonary and central n.description: Nocardia species are aerobic filamentous bacteria that can cause subacute pulmonary infection with nodules or consolidation and can disseminate to the brain or meninges, particularly in immunocompromised patients but occasionally in immunocompetent hosts.

Legionella pneumonia with neurologic inv.description: Legionella pneumophila causes an atypical pneumonia associated with fever, cough, myalgias, headache, and systemic symptoms. Neurologic manifestations can occur, although true meningitis is uncommon.

Renal-limited thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A microvascular renal injury characterized by endothelial damage, arteriolar or glomerular thrombosis, and ischemic vascular changes. It may occur without the full systemic features of hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A complement-driven thrombotic microangiopathy that predominantly affects the kidneys and can present in adulthood, sometimes without a clear infectious trigger or prominent gastrointestinal symptoms.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A systemic thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, leading to platelet-rich microvascular thrombi, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and possible neurologic or renal involvement.

Antiphospholipid syndrome nephropathy.description: Renal vascular injury caused by antiphospholipid-associated thrombosis, often producing thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrous intimal hyperplasia, and chronic ischemic renal changes.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can cause endothelial injury, arteriolar fibrinoid damage, hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, and secondary thrombotic microangiopathy in the kidney.

Uterine arteriovenous malformation (uter.description: An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, often acquired after pregnancy-related uterine trauma, miscarriage, curettage, or other uterine procedures. It can cause sudden, recurrent, life-threatening uterine bleeding.

Retained products of conception.description: Persistence of placental or fetal tissue in the uterus after miscarriage or pregnancy termination, causing ongoing or delayed vaginal bleeding and sometimes infection.

Gestational trophoblastic disease.description: A spectrum of abnormal trophoblastic proliferation after pregnancy, including molar pregnancy and gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which may present with abnormal uterine bleeding after a pregnancy loss.

Submucosal uterine leiomyoma (fibroid).description: A benign smooth-muscle tumour of the uterus; fibroids that project into the uterine cavity commonly cause heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia.

Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.description: A functional bowel disorder that can develop after an episode of infectious or antibiotic-associated diarrhea, causing recurrent abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits without systemic illness.

Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infec.description: Recurrent C. difficile infection is return of antibiotic-associated diarrhea after apparent improvement, usually causing frequent unformed stools and abdominal cramping.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhea (non-C. d.description: Diarrhea caused by disruption of normal intestinal microbiota during or shortly after antibiotic treatment, often mild and self-limited.

Inflammatory bowel disease.description: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are chronic inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract that may cause abdominal pain and increased stool frequency.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often occurring in advanced HIV infection and involving lungs, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and adrenal glands.

Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis wit.normalized_text: Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis with abdominal tuberculosis
Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis wit.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing diffuse pulmonary micronodules and possible involvement of lymph nodes, peritoneum, intestines, and other organs; risk is increased in advanced HIV infection.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: Opportunistic disseminated infection caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria, usually in patients with very low CD4 counts; it commonly causes fever, wasting, anemia, lymphadenopathy, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Talaromycosis (disseminated Talaromyces.description: A disseminated fungal opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, particularly in endemic regions of Southeast and East Asia, causing fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary disease, cytopenias, and gastrointestinal involvement.

AIDS with opportunistic esophagitis, mos.normalized_text: AIDS with opportunistic esophagitis, most likely Candida esophagitis
AIDS with opportunistic esophagitis, mos.description: Candida infection of the oral cavity and esophagus is common in advanced HIV and can cause painful swallowing, retrosternal or epigastric pain, nausea, poor intake, and occasionally bleeding from severe mucosal inflammation.

HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/.normalized_text: HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), cutaneous presentation
HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/.description: An aggressive mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection. It can present with pruritic papules, patches, plaques, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, and skin histology resembling cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymp.description: The most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, typically causing chronic pruritic patches and plaques that may progress to tumors, erythroderma, and lymph-node involvement. Histology often shows epidermotropism of atypical T lymphocytes.

Secondary syphilis.description: The disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection, classically producing a diffuse maculopapular or papulosquamous eruption involving the palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms.

Crusted scabies.description: A severe infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei characterized by widespread hyperkeratotic, scaly, and often intensely pruritic plaques. It is more common in immunocompromised or chronically ill patients and may involve the palms, soles, and flexural regions.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized by myocardial inflammation, myocyte injury, and multinucleated giant cells. It commonly presents with ventricular arrhythmias, heart failure, or rapidly worsening cardiac function.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Inflammatory granulomatous involvement of the heart due to sarcoidosis, which can cause conduction disease, ventricular tachycardia, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. Histology typically shows noncaseating granulomas, sometimes with giant cells.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often with myocyte disarray and fibrosis. It can cause exertional chest symptoms, dyspnea, and ventricular arrhythmias.

Coronary artery disease with exertional.normalized_text: Coronary artery disease with exertional angina
Coronary artery disease with exertional.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries causing myocardial ischemia during exertion. Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity substantially increase risk.

Postoperative pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A rare neutrophilic dermatosis causing rapidly progressive painful ulceration and wound breakdown after trauma or surgery (pathergy), often mistaken for infection; debridement may worsen the lesion.

Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.normalized_text: Post-cesarean surgical-site infection with wound dehiscence
Post-cesarean surgical-site infection wi.description: A bacterial infection involving the cesarean incision that can cause fever, leukocytosis, purulent drainage, tissue separation, and delayed healing.

Necrotizing fasciitis of the cesarean wo.normalized_text: Necrotizing fasciitis of the cesarean wound
Necrotizing fasciitis of the cesarean wo.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft-tissue infection involving fascia, usually producing severe pain, systemic toxicity, tissue necrosis, and worsening postoperative wound destruction.

Intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionit.description: Infection and inflammation of the amniotic fluid, placenta, and fetal membranes, typically associated with maternal fever, uterine tenderness, maternal leukocytosis, fetal tachycardia, and preterm labor.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), including postoperative pathergy
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: An inflammatory neutrophilic skin disorder characterized by fever, neutrophilia, elevated inflammatory markers, and painful inflammatory skin lesions that can occasionally arise at sites of trauma or surgery.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) with large anterior cervical osteophytes
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.description: A noninflammatory disorder characterized by flowing calcification and ossification along spinal ligaments, often producing large anterior cervical osteophytes that can compress the pharynx or esophagus.

Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.normalized_text: Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervical osteophyte formation
Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.description: Degenerative disease of the cervical spine in which osteophytes form at vertebral margins; very large anterior osteophytes can mechanically compress the hypopharynx or esophagus and cause swallowing difficulty.

Ossification of the anterior longitudina.normalized_text: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament
Ossification of the anterior longitudina.description: Abnormal calcification or ossification of the anterior longitudinal spinal ligament, often associated with DISH, which may create a bulky anterior cervical mass effect on the pharynx and esophagus.

Hypopharyngeal or cervical esophageal ma.normalized_text: Hypopharyngeal or cervical esophageal malignancy causing extrinsic compression
Hypopharyngeal or cervical esophageal ma.description: Tumors involving the hypopharynx, cervical esophagus, or nearby structures can produce progressive dysphagia and aspiration, although they more often cause an intrinsic mucosal lesion rather than a bony posterior compression.

Primary mediastinal (thymic) large B-cel.description: An aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma arising in the anterior mediastinum, classically affecting young women and often presenting as a bulky mediastinal mass causing respiratory symptoms.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A rare malignant epithelial tumor of the thymus that usually presents as an anterior mediastinal mass and may invade or compress nearby thoracic structures.

NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma).description: A rare, highly aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma driven by NUTM1 rearrangement, often arising in midline thoracic structures and commonly mistaken for thymic carcinoma or other undifferentiated cancers.

Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type.description: A lymphoma frequently affecting young adults and commonly presenting with mediastinal lymphadenopathy; the nodular sclerosis subtype is especially common in young women.

Mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A germ cell tumor arising in the anterior mediastinum, including teratoma, seminoma, or nonseminomatous germ cell tumor; large tumors can cause cough and dyspnea by compressing lung and mediastinal structures.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.normalized_text: Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (PBMAH) causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: A rare cause of endogenous cortisol excess in which both adrenal glands develop multiple nodules and autonomously produce cortisol, often presenting gradually in older adults.

Cushing syndrome.description: A clinical state of chronic cortisol excess that can result from adrenal, pituitary, or ectopic ACTH-dependent causes. Cortisol excess causes skin fragility, bruising, bone loss, and increased risk of kidney stones.

Adrenal Cushing syndrome due to bilatera.normalized_text: Adrenal Cushing syndrome due to bilateral cortisol-secreting adrenal adenomas
Adrenal Cushing syndrome due to bilatera.description: Autonomous cortisol production from adrenal adenomas can produce ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. Bilateral adrenal nodules are less common than a single adrenal adenoma but may cause mild or overt cortisol excess.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A fibroinflammatory disorder causing plaque-like retroperitoneal soft-tissue thickening that can encase the ureters, inferior vena cava, and iliac vessels, producing venous obstruction and flank or abdominal pain.

Inferior vena cava and iliac venous obst.normalized_text: Inferior vena cava and iliac venous obstruction (inferior vena cava syndrome)
Inferior vena cava and iliac venous obst.description: Obstruction or compression of the inferior vena cava or iliac veins, often from thrombosis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or a mass, causes impaired venous return from the legs and abdominal wall.

Retroperitoneal malignancy causing venou.normalized_text: Retroperitoneal malignancy causing venous compression (such as lymphoma)
Retroperitoneal malignancy causing venou.description: Lymphoma or another retroperitoneal tumor can form infiltrative soft tissue around major abdominal vessels and lymphatic channels, resulting in inferior vena cava or iliac venous compression, edema, and abdominal or back pain.

Abdominopelvic tuberculosis with retrope.normalized_text: Abdominopelvic tuberculosis with retroperitoneal lymphadenitis or fibrosis
Abdominopelvic tuberculosis with retrope.description: Tuberculosis can involve abdominal lymph nodes and the retroperitoneum, occasionally causing fibrotic tissue, vascular compression, abdominal pain, and edema. A history of latent tuberculosis increases consideration of this cause.

Bilateral lower-extremity lymphedema due.normalized_text: Bilateral lower-extremity lymphedema due to pelvic or retroperitoneal lymphatic obstruction
Bilateral lower-extremity lymphedema due.description: Obstruction of pelvic or retroperitoneal lymphatic drainage by fibrosis, malignancy, inflammation, or prior pelvic surgery can cause chronic progressive swelling of both legs and sometimes abdominal wall edema.

Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleo.normalized_text: Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis with cholestatic hepatitis
Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleo.description: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection causing infectious mononucleosis, with hepatic involvement producing cholestasis, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes.

Epstein-Barr virus-associated acute acal.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, occasionally occurring during Epstein-Barr virus infection and associated with gallbladder wall edema and right-upper-quadrant pain.

Acute ascending cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tract, usually caused by obstruction of the common bile duct; classically presents with fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by cystic-duct obstruction from gallstones.

Acute viral hepatitis.description: Acute liver inflammation caused by hepatotropic viruses or systemic viral infections, which may cause jaundice, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools, and elevated aminotransferases.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal artery involvement
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause renal arterial stenoses, microaneurysms, thrombosis, and renal infarctions. Angiography often shows multiple small aneurysms and irregular vessel narrowing.

Bilateral renal infarction.description: Acute interruption of renal arterial blood flow causing ischemic necrosis of renal tissue. It may result from vasculitis, arterial dissection, embolism, thrombosis, or severe atherosclerotic disease.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory disorder of medium-sized arteries that produces alternating stenosis and dilation, often described as a 'string-of-beads' appearance. Renal involvement can cause hypertension, dissection, thrombosis, or renal infarction.

Cardioembolic or thromboembolic renal in.description: Renal infarction can occur when an embolus from the heart or a proximal artery obstructs a renal artery branch. Common causes include atrial fibrillation, endocarditis, ventricular thrombus, or hypercoagulable states.

Ureteral nephrolithiasis.description: A urinary tract stone obstructing the ureter commonly causes acute colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, often with nausea and vomiting.

Intestinal tuberculosis with possible di.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis with possible disseminated tuberculosis
Intestinal tuberculosis with possible di.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the ileocecal region, sometimes accompanied by pulmonary or disseminated disease. It can cause chronic constitutional and abdominal symptoms.

Colorectal carcinoma, particularly right.description: Cancer of the colon can produce progressive weight loss, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, altered bowel habits, and an obstructing or ulcerated lesion in the cecum or ascending colon.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia / ischemic c.description: Insufficient intestinal blood flow due to severe atherosclerotic disease can cause postprandial abdominal pain, food avoidance, weight loss, diarrhea, and colonic ischemic injury.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm with inflammat.normalized_text: Abdominal aortic aneurysm with inflammatory involvement or impending complication
Abdominal aortic aneurysm with inflammat.description: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation of the abdominal aorta, usually caused by atherosclerosis. Large or inflammatory aneurysms may cause abdominal or back pain, constitutional symptoms, and may coexist with widespread vascular disease.

Gastrointestinal histoplasmosis or anoth.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal histoplasmosis or another disseminated fungal infection
Gastrointestinal histoplasmosis or anoth.description: Disseminated fungal infection can involve the lungs and gastrointestinal tract, producing chronic constitutional symptoms, abdominal pain, diarrhea, ulcerated intestinal lesions, and weight loss, especially in frail or immunocompromised patients.

Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.normalized_text: Pancreatic panniculitis associated with acute pancreatitis
Pancreatic panniculitis associated with.description: A rare form of lobular panniculitis caused by release of pancreatic enzymes into the bloodstream, resulting in enzymatic fat necrosis in subcutaneous tissue. Histology typically shows lobular fat necrosis with "ghost" adipocytes.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, commonly caused by alcohol use or gallstone disease, characterized by abdominal pain and elevated pancreatic enzymes. It can produce systemic complications, including pancreatic panniculitis.

Pancreatitis, panniculitis, and polyarth.description: A rare systemic syndrome in which pancreatic disease causes enzymatic fat necrosis, painful subcutaneous nodules, and inflammatory arthritis due to periarticular fat necrosis. It may occur with acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, or pancreatic malignancy.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory panniculitis that causes painful erythematous subcutaneous nodules, most often on the anterior lower legs. It can be associated with infections, medications, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, and other systemic conditions.

Multiple myeloma with extensive osseous.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with extensive osseous and extramedullary plasmacytomas
Multiple myeloma with extensive osseous.description: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy characterized by monoclonal light-chain production, marrow involvement, lytic bone disease or plasmacytomas, and end-organ damage including renal dysfunction, hypercalcaemia, and anaemia.

Multiple myeloma with diffuse calvarial.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with diffuse calvarial involvement (myeloma skull lesions)
Multiple myeloma with diffuse calvarial.description: A presentation of multiple myeloma in which clonal plasma cells extensively infiltrate skull bone, producing expansile lytic lesions and a visible or palpable cranial mass.

Multiple solitary plasmacytomas / multif.description: Plasmacytomas are localized masses of monoclonal plasma cells involving bone or soft tissue. Multiple lesions can occur and may represent or progress to systemic multiple myeloma.

Light-chain multiple myeloma.description: A subtype of multiple myeloma in which the malignant plasma-cell clone predominantly secretes free immunoglobulin light chains rather than an intact monoclonal immunoglobulin, often causing renal injury.

Hepatic tuberculosis (hepatic tuberculom.normalized_text: Hepatic tuberculosis (hepatic tuberculoma or focal hepatic TB)
Hepatic tuberculosis (hepatic tuberculom.description: A focal form of abdominal tuberculosis in which granulomatous tuberculomas or microabscesses develop in the liver; it may occur as recurrent or reactivated disease after prior tuberculosis.

Hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor (inflam.description: A rare benign-to-intermediate fibroinflammatory liver mass that can occur in children and adolescents and may mimic infection or malignancy on imaging.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver producing one or more pus-filled lesions, usually associated with fever, abdominal pain, and inflammatory markers.

Hepatic lymphoma.description: Lymphomatous involvement of the liver can produce focal or multiple liver lesions and constitutional symptoms; it may be associated with lymphadenopathy or systemic lymphoma.

Hepatoblastoma or hepatocellular carcino.description: Primary malignant liver tumors that can present as hepatic masses with abdominal pain, anorexia, or an abdominal mass; hepatoblastoma is usually seen in younger children, while hepatocellular carcinoma may occur in older children with chronic liver disease.

Cholesterol embolization syndrome (ather.description: Systemic embolization of cholesterol crystals from disrupted atherosclerotic plaques, often occurring days to weeks after angiography, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation. It commonly affects the kidneys, skin, gastrointestinal tract, and central nervous system.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause renal ischemia, hypertension, livedo reticularis, painful skin nodules, digital ischemia, neuropathy, and systemic inflammation.

ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.normalized_text: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis)
ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.description: A small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis that may cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, systemic inflammation, skin purpura, neuropathy, and pulmonary disease.

Acute interstitial nephritis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory injury of the renal interstitium, commonly caused by medications such as antibiotics, proton-pump inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or diuretics. Eosinophilia and acute kidney injury are characteristic clues.

Acute limb ischemia from thromboembolism.normalized_text: Acute limb ischemia from thromboembolism or severe peripheral arterial disease
Acute limb ischemia from thromboembolism.description: Arterial occlusion from thrombus or embolus causes abrupt distal ischemia, pain, cyanosis, tissue necrosis, and potentially gangrene. It may occur after cardiac procedures or in patients with diffuse atherosclerosis.

Severe accidental hypothermia.description: A dangerous reduction in core body temperature, usually from environmental exposure or impaired thermoregulation, causing cardiovascular depression, altered consciousness, and characteristic ECG changes such as Osborn (J) waves.

Myxedema coma.description: A life-threatening presentation of severe hypothyroidism characterized by hypothermia, depressed mental status, bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoventilation.

Sepsis with hypothermia.description: Severe systemic infection can cause altered mental status and circulatory instability; elderly patients may present with hypothermia rather than fever.

Adrenal crisis.description: Acute adrenal insufficiency causing hypotension, weakness, altered mental status, and sometimes hypothermia, often precipitated by illness or physiologic stress.

Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.normalized_text: Seronegative anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (seronegative Goodpasture syndrome)
Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome in which antibodies target basement membranes in the lung and kidney. Some patients have negative circulating anti-GBM antibody tests despite tissue evidence of disease.

Anti-GBM disease with immune-complex glo.normalized_text: Anti-GBM disease with immune-complex glomerulonephritis overlap
Anti-GBM disease with immune-complex glo.description: A pulmonary-renal autoimmune syndrome with features of both anti-GBM disease and immune-complex-mediated renal disease, potentially producing both linear and granular immunoglobulin staining.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and neuropsychiatric involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, pulmonary capillaritis with hemoptysis, anemia, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that can cause pulmonary capillaritis with hemoptysis, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and neurologic manifestations.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with.normalized_text: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with coincidental or early glomerular immune disease
Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis with.description: A rare cause of recurrent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage characterized by hemoptysis and iron-deficiency anemia, usually without a defined systemic autoimmune disorder.

Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.normalized_text: Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor (mixed germ cell tumor) with gastrointestinal metastasis
Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.description: A malignant testicular germ cell tumor containing nonseminomatous elements, commonly embryonal carcinoma and/or yolk sac tumor. These tumors can markedly elevate alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin and may metastasize to retroperitoneal lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract, causing bleeding.

Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastati.normalized_text: Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastatic gastrointestinal involvement
Testicular yolk sac tumor with metastati.description: A nonseminomatous germ cell tumor characterized by substantial alpha-fetoprotein production. In adults it may occur as part of a mixed testicular germ cell tumor and can metastasize through retroperitoneal lymphatic pathways, occasionally involving the duodenum or other gastrointestinal sites.

NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with.normalized_text: NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease with.description: Gastric or duodenal mucosal ulceration caused by inhibition of protective prostaglandins from NSAID exposure. It commonly produces epigastric pain and may cause chronic or acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Testicular seminoma.description: A malignant germ cell tumor of the testis that usually presents as painless testicular enlargement and may metastasize to retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Some seminomas cause mild human chorionic gonadotropin elevation, but alpha-fetoprotein should remain normal.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens.description: A limb-threatening form of extensive deep venous thrombosis causing near-total venous outflow obstruction, severe edema, cyanosis, and secondary arterial compromise.

Extensive acute deep vein thrombosis of.normalized_text: Extensive acute deep vein thrombosis of the right lower extremity
Extensive acute deep vein thrombosis of.description: Formation of a thrombus in the deep veins of the leg, potentially extending into the femoral or iliac veins and causing painful unilateral swelling.

Acute limb ischemia from arterial emboli.normalized_text: Acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism
Acute limb ischemia from arterial emboli.description: Sudden reduction in arterial blood flow to a limb, often caused by an embolus from atrial fibrillation, resulting in pain, pallor or cyanosis, coolness, and diminished pulses.

Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-a.normalized_text: Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-associated hypercoagulability (Trousseau syndrome)
Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-a.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the stomach that can create a hypercoagulable state and predispose to unprovoked extensive venous thrombosis; the provided endoscopic and histologic images are consistent with gastric adenocarcinoma.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVL.normalized_text: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL) involving the penis
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVL.description: A rare aggressive extranodal B-cell lymphoma in which malignant large B cells proliferate predominantly within small blood vessels, often causing fever and organ-specific ischemic or vascular symptoms without lymphadenopathy.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) wi.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with penile/cavernosal involvement
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) wi.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that may rarely involve the penis or corpora cavernosa, causing malignant priapism through infiltration or obstruction of venous drainage.

Leukemia-associated malignant priapism.description: Priapism may occur in hematologic malignancies, especially chronic myeloid leukemia or acute leukemia, due to hyperleukocytosis, leukostasis, and impaired venous drainage from the corpora cavernosa.

Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous gen.normalized_text: Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous genital infection
Penile tuberculosis or granulomatous gen.description: Tuberculosis can cause fever and genital involvement in patients from endemic regions, although penile disease is rare and typically produces ulcers, nodules, or destructive skin lesions rather than isolated priapism.

Struma ovarii with pseudo-Meigs syndrome.description: A specialized ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue. It can cause ascites, pleural effusion, and marked CA-125 elevation despite benign cytology and normal thyroid function.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.description: A malignant ovarian tumor, commonly high-grade serous carcinoma, which often presents after menopause with an adnexal mass, ascites, abdominal symptoms, and elevated CA-125.

Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or.normalized_text: Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma
Meigs syndrome due to ovarian fibroma or.description: A benign ovarian fibroma, thecoma, or fibrothecoma associated with ascites and pleural effusion; CA-125 can rise substantially because of peritoneal and pleural irritation.

Mucinous borderline ovarian tumor.description: A low-malignant-potential epithelial ovarian neoplasm that may appear as a large multiloculated cystic adnexal mass with septa and can cause abdominal distention.

Ovarian endometrioma with severe endomet.normalized_text: Ovarian endometrioma with severe endometriosis-related ascites
Ovarian endometrioma with severe endomet.description: Endometriosis can produce ovarian cystic lesions, elevated CA-125, and rarely massive hemorrhagic ascites with pleural effusion, although this is unusual after menopause.

Cervical spinal tuberculosis (tuberculou.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the cervical vertebrae, often producing vertebral marrow involvement and a prevertebral or epidural soft-tissue abscess. Plain radiographs may be normal early in the disease.

Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.normalized_text: Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis with prevertebral abscess
Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.description: A bacterial infection involving cervical vertebral marrow and often the adjacent intervertebral disc, potentially extending into prevertebral and epidural soft tissues. MRI is much more sensitive than radiographs early in infection.

Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical.normalized_text: Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical spine
Primary osseous lymphoma of the cervical.description: Lymphoma may involve vertebral bone and create an infiltrative paraspinal or epidural soft-tissue mass. It can present with persistent localized pain and may be occult on early plain radiographs.

Cervical chordoma.description: Chordoma is a rare, slow-growing malignant tumor derived from notochord remnants. It commonly arises in the sacrum or clivus but can occur in the upper cervical spine, causing destructive osseous and prevertebral soft-tissue masses.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A rare benign childhood soft-tissue hamartoma, usually presenting before age 2 years as a painless, firm, slowly enlarging subcutaneous mass or plaque on the trunk, axilla, shoulder, or upper arm. It is composed of fibrous tissue, primitive mesenchyme, and fat.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign congenital proliferation of dermal smooth muscle, commonly involving the lumbosacral region. It usually appears as a skin-colored or hyperpigmented plaque and may become more prominent with growth; hypertrichosis is common.

Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma.description: A benign hamartoma containing eccrine sweat glands and vascular structures. It often presents in childhood as a solitary nodule or plaque and may be associated with focal hyperhidrosis, hypertrichosis, discoloration, or pain.

Eccrine nevus.description: A localized benign hamartoma characterized by an increased number or size of eccrine sweat glands. It generally presents as a localized plaque with focal hyperhidrosis, often beginning in childhood.

Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.normalized_text: Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with pulmonary involvement
Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.description: A clonal inflammatory disorder characterized by infiltration of tissues by Langerhans cells. In children it can involve skin, bone, lungs, liver, and other organs. Pulmonary disease may produce nodules and cystic or cavitary changes, while scalp lesions can resemble seborrheic dermatitis.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia with bronchie.description: An inherited disorder of impaired mucociliary clearance that causes recurrent respiratory infections, chronic sinus disease, and progressive bronchiectasis. Some affected patients have situs inversus, known as Kartagener syndrome.

Hyper-IgE syndrome.description: A primary immunodeficiency, often caused by STAT3 pathway abnormalities, characterized by eczema-like dermatitis, recurrent bacterial lung infections, lung cysts or pneumatoceles, and bronchiectasis.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with post-infecti.normalized_text: Pulmonary tuberculosis with post-infectious bronchiectatic or cavitary disease
Pulmonary tuberculosis with post-infecti.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause constitutional symptoms, chronic pulmonary inflammation, upper-lobe cavitation, and bronchiectasis. Cutaneous tuberculosis or a coincidental scalp infection may cause skin lesions.

Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.normalized_text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 2
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.description: The most common form of invasive breast cancer, previously termed invasive ductal carcinoma. Grade 2 indicates intermediate histologic differentiation.

Multifocal or multicentric invasive brea.normalized_text: Multifocal or multicentric invasive breast carcinoma
Multifocal or multicentric invasive brea.description: Breast cancer involving more than one malignant focus in the same breast; MRI is often used to assess the full extent of disease when mammography is limited by dense tissue or occult lesions.

Breast carcinoma with possible internal.normalized_text: Breast carcinoma with possible internal mammary lymph node metastasis
Breast carcinoma with possible internal.description: Invasive breast cancer can spread to regional lymph nodes, including axillary and internal mammary nodes. MRI may identify suspicious enhancing internal mammary-chain nodes during staging.

Hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy (.description: A toxic maculopathy caused by long-term hydroxychloroquine exposure, producing parafoveal retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor damage. Risk rises substantially with prolonged treatment and high cumulative dose.

Autoimmune retinopathy associated with i.normalized_text: Autoimmune retinopathy associated with inflammatory arthritis
Autoimmune retinopathy associated with i.description: An immune-mediated retinal degeneration that may occur with systemic autoimmune disease and can cause photoreceptor dysfunction, visual-field loss, reduced color vision, photopsias, and progressive visual impairment.

Retinitis pigmentosa or a related inheri.normalized_text: Retinitis pigmentosa or a related inherited retinal dystrophy
Retinitis pigmentosa or a related inheri.description: A group of inherited retinal degenerations characterized by progressive photoreceptor loss, often beginning with night blindness and peripheral field constriction, with possible later central visual and color-vision impairment.

Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lym.normalized_text: Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lymphoma of the nasopharynx, likely lymphocyte-rich subtype
Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lym.description: A rare localized form of classical Hodgkin lymphoma arising in nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue. It is characterized by rare Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background; the malignant cells typically express CD30 and CD15.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin l.description: An indolent Hodgkin lymphoma composed of neoplastic lymphocyte-predominant cells in a background of small B lymphocytes. It usually involves peripheral lymph nodes and typically expresses CD20 and B-cell markers rather than CD15/CD30.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma composed of large pleomorphic anaplastic lymphoid cells. It may arise in lymph nodes or extranodal tissues and can mimic classical Hodgkin lymphoma histologically.

EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer.description: A localized Epstein-Barr virus-associated B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder that usually occurs in immunosuppressed or elderly patients and produces sharply circumscribed mucosal ulcers containing Hodgkin-like CD30-positive atypical cells.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: An epithelial malignancy arising from the nasopharyngeal mucosa, often associated with EBV in endemic populations. It commonly presents with nasal obstruction, neck lymphadenopathy, otologic symptoms, or cranial neuropathies.

Ipilimumab-induced immune-mediated myoca.description: Inflammatory myocardial injury caused by immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy; it can present with chest pain, troponin elevation, ECG changes, heart failure symptoms, and nonobstructive coronary arteries.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated c.normalized_text: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated cardiac sarcoid-like granulomatous inflammation
Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated c.description: A sarcoid-like immune reaction induced by checkpoint blockade can cause granulomatous inflammation involving the myocardium, producing inflammatory cardiac uptake on PET imaging, myocardial injury, and conduction or functional abnormalities.

Acute coronary syndrome with myocardial.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome with myocardial infarction and nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Acute coronary syndrome with myocardial.description: Myocardial infarction can occur despite the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary disease, including from coronary vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, or transient plaque disruption.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.normalized_text: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy or dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.description: Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract occurs when systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve narrows the outflow tract; it may be due to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or be provoked by hypercontractility, dehydration, or systemic illness.

Syphilitic proctitis (rectal secondary s.description: Sexually transmitted Treponema pallidum infection involving the rectum, which can cause inflammatory proctitis, rectal bleeding, pain, fissures, and ulcerative lesions. The histology and spirochete immunostaining are strongly supportive.

Chlamydia trachomatis proctitis, includi.normalized_text: Chlamydia trachomatis proctitis, including lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)
Chlamydia trachomatis proctitis, includi.description: Sexually acquired rectal infection, particularly common after receptive anal exposure, that may cause proctitis with rectal pain, bleeding, discharge, mucosal inflammation, and occasionally ulceration or fissuring. LGV serovars can cause more severe inflammatory disease.

Gonococcal proctitis.description: Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of the rectum acquired through sexual contact. It commonly causes anorectal discomfort, tenesmus, rectal discharge, mucosal erythema, and sometimes bleeding.

Herpes simplex virus proctitis.description: HSV infection of the anorectum, usually sexually acquired, can cause severe anorectal pain, painful defecation, bleeding, ulcerations, and inflammatory proctitis.

Inflammatory bowel disease, especially u.normalized_text: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative proctitis or Crohn disease involving the anus
Inflammatory bowel disease, especially u.description: Inflammatory bowel disease can involve the rectum and anus. Ulcerative proctitis typically causes rectal bleeding and mucosal inflammation, while Crohn disease can produce anal fissures and skin tags.

Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria.description: The presence of a small amount of blood in urine detected on dipstick testing without urinary symptoms; it may be benign or require evaluation for urinary tract, kidney, or prostate causes.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.description: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that commonly affects older men and can cause lower urinary tract symptoms or occasionally hematuria.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or u.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or urinary tract
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or u.description: A cancer arising from the lining of the bladder or upper urinary tract, often presenting with painless microscopic or visible hematuria, particularly in older adults.

Nephrolithiasis.description: Kidney or ureteral stones can cause blood in the urine, often with sudden flank pain, nausea, or urinary discomfort.

Urinary tract infection.description: An infection of the bladder, urethra, or kidneys that may cause dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, fever, and occasionally microscopic hematuria.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia.description: An inherited qualitative fibrinogen disorder in which fibrinogen antigen concentration is normal or near normal, but the fibrinogen molecule has impaired function, causing reduced functional fibrinogen activity and variable bleeding or thrombosis risk.

Congenital hypodysfibrinogenemia.description: An inherited fibrinogen disorder characterized by both reduced fibrinogen quantity and impaired fibrinogen function. It may cause bleeding, thrombosis, or be discovered during preoperative coagulation screening.

Congenital afibrinogenemia or hypofibrin.description: An inherited quantitative fibrinogen deficiency caused by absent or reduced production of fibrinogen, typically producing low fibrinogen antigen and activity with bleeding beginning early in life.

Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver.normalized_text: Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver disease or systemic illness
Acquired dysfibrinogenemia due to liver.description: A secondary qualitative fibrinogen abnormality that can occur with liver disease, malignancy, autoimmune disease, or other systemic disorders and may lead to discordance between fibrinogen activity and antigen levels.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
