Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (giant c.normalized_text: Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (giant cell carcinoma of the lung)
Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (giant c.description: A rare, aggressive non-small-cell lung carcinoma composed of poorly differentiated spindle and/or giant tumor cells, strongly associated with heavy smoking and often presenting as a large central lung mass.

Small-cell lung carcinoma.description: An aggressive neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly linked to smoking. It commonly arises centrally, grows rapidly, causes bulky mediastinal adenopathy, and may compress or invade the superior vena cava.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.description: A non-small-cell lung cancer strongly associated with tobacco use that often develops as a central bronchial mass and can obstruct an airway or invade mediastinal structures.

Primary lung adenocarcinoma.description: The most common non-small-cell lung cancer, usually peripheral but sometimes central; advanced disease can involve mediastinal lymph nodes and produce superior vena cava obstruction.

Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.normalized_text: Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to an intrathoracic malignancy
Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.description: A clinical syndrome caused by obstruction of the superior vena cava, most often from lung cancer or mediastinal malignancy, resulting in impaired venous drainage from the head, neck, and upper extremities.

BCL11B-related disorder with severe T-ce.normalized_text: BCL11B-related disorder with severe T-cell immunodeficiency
BCL11B-related disorder with severe T-ce.description: A de novo BCL11B-related developmental and immune disorder that can cause severe T-cell lymphopenia or SCID, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, craniofacial/skeletal findings, and skin disease.

Complete DiGeorge syndrome / congenital.normalized_text: Complete DiGeorge syndrome / congenital athymia due to 22q11.2 deletion or related thymic-development defect
Complete DiGeorge syndrome / congenital.description: A disorder of thymic development causing profound T-cell deficiency, often detected by absent TRECs. It may occur with congenital heart defects and developmental abnormalities.

PAX1 deficiency / otofaciocervical syndr.normalized_text: PAX1 deficiency / otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 with severe combined immunodeficiency
PAX1 deficiency / otofaciocervical syndr.description: A rare disorder caused by biallelic PAX1 variants that impairs thymic development and can produce profound T-cell immunodeficiency together with craniofacial, skeletal, and congenital structural abnormalities.

CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia o.normalized_text: CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia or athymia
CHARGE syndrome with thymic hypoplasia o.description: A CHD7-related multisystem developmental syndrome that can include impaired thymic development with T-cell lymphopenia, congenital heart disease, hypotonia, and brain abnormalities.

FOXN1 deficiency (nude SCID).description: A thymic epithelial-cell developmental disorder causing severe T-cell immunodeficiency, classically associated with congenital alopecia and nail dystrophy.

Primary colorectal extranodal marginal z.normalized_text: Primary colorectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary colorectal extranodal marginal z.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. In the colon or rectum it may present as localized mucosal nodules, polyps, ulcerated lesions, or a mass, with histology showing small lymphoid-cell infiltration and lymphoepithelial lesions.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the col.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the colon or rectum
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the col.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can involve the gastrointestinal tract and cause a colorectal mass, altered bowel habits, bleeding, abdominal pain, or obstructive symptoms. It may arise de novo or by transformation of an indolent lymphoma.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the colon or rectum. Rectal tumors commonly cause tenesmus, mucus discharge, bleeding, altered stool caliber, and bowel-habit changes.

Ulcerative proctitis or ulcerative colit.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum. Proctitis can produce urgency, tenesmus, mucus discharge, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding.

Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep ve.normalized_text: Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep ve.description: A blood clot in the deep veins of the left leg and pelvis, often causing unilateral swelling, pain, erythema, and warmth. In this case, risk factors include estrogen-containing oral contraceptives and possible inherited predisposition.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Pulmonary embolism is obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, most commonly originating from a lower-extremity DVT. The chest CT image is consistent with emboli in pulmonary arterial branches.

May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.normalized_text: May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compression syndrome) with iliofemoral DVT
May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein co.description: May-Thurner syndrome is compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery, predisposing young women to extensive left-sided pelvic and leg DVT. The pelvic CT finding is compatible with left iliac venous thrombosis.

Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.normalized_text: Cellulitis of the left lower extremity
Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.description: Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that can cause localized warmth, redness, swelling, tenderness, and leukocytosis.

Superficial thrombophlebitis.description: Superficial thrombophlebitis is inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein, producing localized pain, redness, warmth, and sometimes a palpable tender cord.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.normalized_text: X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (CGD; CYBB/gp91phox deficiency)
X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by impaired NADPH oxidase function in phagocytes, resulting in defective oxidative burst and susceptibility to recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections. The absent oxidative-burst pattern and possible carrier pattern in a female relative strongly support X-linked CGD.

Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatou.normalized_text: Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatous disease (NCF1, NCF2, NCF4, or CYBA deficiency)
Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatou.description: A form of CGD caused by defects in other components of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, also producing an absent or markedly reduced neutrophil oxidative burst and recurrent severe infections.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by defective leukocyte adhesion and migration, leading to recurrent severe bacterial infections, poor wound healing, impaired pus formation, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary adenocarcinoma arising from bile ducts within the liver, often associated with elevated CA 19-9 and a desmoplastic, gland-forming histologic pattern.

Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma to the liver
Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma to.description: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a gland-forming malignancy that commonly elevates CA 19-9 and frequently spreads to the liver.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the liver
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Colorectal cancer commonly metastasizes to the liver and can show gland-forming adenocarcinoma on biopsy; hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes may cause disease at young ages.

Gallbladder or extrahepatic biliary trac.normalized_text: Gallbladder or extrahepatic biliary tract adenocarcinoma with liver involvement
Gallbladder or extrahepatic biliary trac.description: Adenocarcinoma arising from the gallbladder or extrahepatic bile ducts may invade or metastasize to the liver and is often associated with increased CA 19-9.

Angioleiomyoma of the parotid region.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor arising from vascular smooth muscle, often presenting as a slow-growing, painful, well-circumscribed mass. Histology typically shows interlacing bundles of bland spindle cells around vascular channels, with smooth-muscle-marker positivity.

Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.description: The most common benign salivary-gland tumor, usually a slowly enlarging, well-circumscribed and mobile parotid mass. It is generally painless and contains epithelial and myoepithelial elements in a variable stromal background.

Schwannoma of the facial nerve or great.normalized_text: Schwannoma of the facial nerve or great auricular nerve
Schwannoma of the facial nerve or great.description: A benign peripheral-nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells. It can produce a slowly growing, mobile mass and pain or paresthesia from nerve involvement; histology may show spindle cells in Antoni A and Antoni B areas.

Parotid gland leiomyoma.description: A rare benign tumor of smooth-muscle differentiation arising in or near the parotid gland, potentially from vascular smooth muscle. It usually forms a circumscribed spindle-cell mass and may be painful when vascular in origin.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid.normalized_text: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid gland
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the parotid.description: A malignant salivary-gland tumor composed of mucous, intermediate, and epidermoid cells. Low-grade tumors may be slow growing, whereas higher-grade tumors may cause pain, fixation, facial nerve dysfunction, or nodal disease.

Fucosidosis.description: A rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency, leading to progressive neurodegeneration, coarse facial appearance, dysostosis, and variable hearing loss.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilip.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by impaired degradation of heparan sulfate. It is characterized predominantly by progressive cognitive decline and neurological deterioration, often with mild coarse facial features and hearing impairment.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. It can cause coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, developmental delay, and progressive neurological disease in severe forms.

GM1 gangliosidosis type II.description: A beta-galactosidase deficiency causing accumulation of GM1 ganglioside, with infantile or late-infantile developmental regression, progressive motor impairment, coarse facial features, and skeletal or brain abnormalities.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: A lysosomal storage disorder due to alpha-mannosidase deficiency, characterized by intellectual disability, hearing loss, coarse facial features, speech impairment, skeletal disease, and progressive motor dysfunction.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Impaired movement of both vocal folds, typically leaving them near the midline and causing marked upper-airway obstruction in neonates. It may be congenital or associated with neurologic injury such as hypoxic-ischemic injury after severe asphyxia.

Congenital bilateral vocal fold paralysi.description: A congenital form of bilateral vocal-fold immobility presenting in the neonatal period with stridor and airway obstruction; it may be isolated or associated with central nervous system abnormalities or syndromes.

Posterior glottic stenosis with vocal-fo.normalized_text: Posterior glottic stenosis with vocal-fold fixation
Posterior glottic stenosis with vocal-fo.description: Scar formation or fixation in the posterior glottis can prevent vocal-fold abduction and mimic bilateral vocal-fold paralysis. It is often acquired after airway trauma or prolonged endotracheal intubation.

Subglottic stenosis due to post-intubati.normalized_text: Subglottic stenosis due to post-intubation airway injury
Subglottic stenosis due to post-intubati.description: Narrowing below the vocal folds caused by congenital small airway caliber or acquired mucosal injury and scarring after intubation. It commonly causes biphasic or inspiratory stridor after extubation.

Laryngomalacia.description: The most common congenital cause of neonatal stridor, caused by dynamic collapse of immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. Symptoms are usually worse with feeding, crying, or supine positioning.

Fourth branchial pouch anomaly with pyri.normalized_text: Fourth branchial pouch anomaly with pyriform sinus fistula
Fourth branchial pouch anomaly with pyri.description: A congenital tract arising from the pyriform sinus that commonly causes recurrent infected left-sided neck abscesses, often near the thyroid gland or thyroid cartilage.

Infected third branchial cleft anomaly.description: A rare congenital branchial apparatus anomaly that can form a sinus or fistula in the lower anterior neck and become repeatedly infected, sometimes communicating with the pyriform sinus.

Infected second branchial cleft cyst.description: A congenital epithelial cyst of the lateral neck that may enlarge or become infected, producing a painful neck mass and fever.

Acute suppurative cervical lymphadenitis.normalized_text: Acute suppurative cervical lymphadenitis or deep neck abscess
Acute suppurative cervical lymphadenitis.description: Bacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes or deep neck spaces causing a painful swollen neck mass, fever, and possible abscess formation.

Drug-induced serum sickness-like reactio.description: A delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a medication, commonly occurring 1–3 weeks after exposure, characterized by urticarial rash, fever, joint symptoms, and edema. Unlike true serum sickness, complement levels are usually normal and significant immune-complex organ injury is absent.

Normocomplementemic urticarial vasculiti.description: A small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis that presents with urticarial-appearing lesions that are often painful or burning, persist longer than ordinary hives, and may leave bruising or hyperpigmentation. Complement levels may be normal or low.

Drug-induced acute urticaria with angioe.description: An allergic or nonallergic medication-related mast-cell reaction causing transient pruritic wheals and swelling of deeper tissues, often after exposure to a new drug or supplement.

DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosin.normalized_text: DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosin.description: A severe delayed drug hypersensitivity reaction that usually develops 2–8 weeks after medication exposure and may cause fever, rash, facial edema, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and internal-organ involvement.

Adult-onset Still disease.description: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent high spiking fevers, inflammatory arthritis or arthralgia, and a transient salmon-pink rash, often with markedly elevated inflammatory markers.

Rapunzel syndrome.description: A large gastric trichobezoar (mass of swallowed hair) that extends from the stomach into the small intestine, potentially causing gastric outlet or intestinal obstruction. The imaging and endoscopic images are characteristic of a hair-containing bezoar with intestinal extension.

Gastric trichobezoar.description: A compact mass of ingested hair retained in the stomach. It may produce chronic abdominal pain, vomiting, poor intake, anemia, and gastric outlet obstruction; it is the gastric component of Rapunzel syndrome.

Gastric outlet obstruction due to bezoar.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction due to bezoar
Gastric outlet obstruction due to bezoar.description: Mechanical obstruction at the stomach outlet caused by a large bezoar, leading to retained gastric contents, postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dehydration, and poor oral intake.

Peptic ulcer disease or NSAID-associated.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease or NSAID-associated gastritis
Peptic ulcer disease or NSAID-associated.description: Inflammation or ulceration of the stomach or duodenal lining, which can be worsened by ibuprofen and can cause epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and anemia.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: Systemic infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving multiple organs. It can produce pulmonary nodules, granulomatous lesions in the kidney, and ulcerative intestinal disease that may perforate and cause fatal peritonitis.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: A disseminated infection caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria, most often M. avium or M. intracellulare, typically occurring in patients with significant immune impairment. It may involve the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.

Disseminated Mycobacterium kansasii infe.description: A nontuberculous mycobacterial infection that commonly causes chronic pulmonary disease resembling tuberculosis; disseminated disease can occur in immunocompromised individuals and may involve extrapulmonary organs.

Intestinal tuberculosis causing ileal pe.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis causing ileal perforation and generalized peritonitis
Intestinal tuberculosis causing ileal pe.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, usually affecting the ileocecal region but potentially involving the ileum. Ulceration can progress through the bowel wall, producing perforation and severe purulent peritonitis.

Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (vaso.normalized_text: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (vasovagal reflex with sinus pause)
Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (vaso.description: A neurally mediated reflex causing increased vagal tone, leading to hypotension, bradycardia, or transient sinus arrest. It is commonly triggered by pain, nausea, emotional stress, medical procedures, or gastrointestinal illness.

Acute coronary syndrome (including unsta.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome (including unstable angina or myocardial infarction)
Acute coronary syndrome (including unsta.description: Acute coronary syndrome results from reduced blood flow to the heart, typically due to coronary artery plaque rupture or spasm, and can cause chest pain with autonomic symptoms.

Brugada syndrome.description: Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiac sodium-channel disorder associated with characteristic right-precordial ECG abnormalities and increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, and sudden cardiac death. Fever or viral illness can unmask ECG changes.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Myopericarditis is inflammation of the myocardium and/or pericardium, often occurring after a viral illness. It can cause chest pain, ECG changes, arrhythmias, and occasionally impaired cardiac function.

Acute gastroenteritis or viral illness t.normalized_text: Acute gastroenteritis or viral illness triggering a vagal episode
Acute gastroenteritis or viral illness t.description: A viral gastrointestinal illness can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and dehydration; pain, vomiting, and nausea may trigger a strong vagal reflex resulting in hypotension and bradycardia.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Free air within the mediastinum occurring without trauma or an obvious precipitating event, often due to rupture of small alveoli with air tracking along bronchovascular structures. It can cause subcutaneous emphysema and Hamman sign (precordial crepitus).

Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndro.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus that can permit air and gastrointestinal contents to enter the mediastinum, causing pneumomediastinum, severe chest pain, systemic inflammation, and potentially mediastinitis.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, commonly presenting in young men with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. It may occasionally coexist with pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the pericardium that typically causes sharp chest pain, often worse with inspiration or lying flat and relieved by sitting forward. A pericardial friction rub may be heard.

Erythema migrans due to Lyme disease.normalized_text: Erythema migrans due to Lyme disease
Erythema migrans due to Lyme disease.description: The characteristic expanding skin lesion of early Lyme borreliosis, caused by Borrelia infection transmitted by Ixodes ticks. A recalled tick bite is often absent, and early serology may be negative.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection that commonly produces an itchy, enlarging ring-shaped rash with a more active red border and relative central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory skin eruption characterized by slowly enlarging annular red plaques, often with central clearing; it may be itchy and can persist for weeks to months.

Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis.description: Inflammation of the skin after exposure to an allergen or irritant, often causing an itchy red patch or plaque. It may persist if exposure continues.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis that causes annular plaques, usually with a smooth raised border and central clearing. Localized lesions commonly occur on hands and feet but can occur elsewhere.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina).description: Transient coronary artery spasm causing episodic myocardial ischemia, often occurring at rest in the early morning and triggered by smoking or alcohol.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction with myocardial injury indicated by elevated troponin but without persistent ST-segment elevation; it may result from plaque disruption, coronary spasm, or another ischemic mechanism.

Unstable angina.description: Acute coronary syndrome characterized by new, worsening, or rest angina due to transient myocardial ischemia, traditionally without a significant rise in cardiac biomarkers.

Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.description: Myocardial infarction with elevated cardiac troponin and ischemic symptoms despite no major obstructive epicardial coronary lesion; possible mechanisms include coronary spasm, plaque erosion, embolism, or spontaneous coronary artery dissection.

Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxyg.normalized_text: Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxygen supply-demand mismatch from anemia
Type 2 myocardial infarction due to oxyg.description: Myocardial injury caused by inadequate oxygen supply relative to myocardial demand rather than acute coronary thrombosis; significant anemia can contribute to ischemia, especially in the presence of coronary spasm or underlying coronary disease.

Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.description: A TP63-related disorder characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformations (ectrodactyly), variable tooth-development defects, ectodermal abnormalities, and sometimes cleft lip or palate.

Nonsyndromic split-hand/foot malformatio.normalized_text: Nonsyndromic split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) with tooth agenesis
Nonsyndromic split-hand/foot malformatio.description: A congenital limb-malformation disorder featuring central absence or hypoplasia of digits, producing split hands and/or feet; some genetic forms are associated with hypodontia or oligodontia without prominent ectodermal or craniofacial findings.

Acetazolamide-associated fetal limb and.normalized_text: Acetazolamide-associated fetal limb and dental developmental anomaly (teratogenic embryopathy)
Acetazolamide-associated fetal limb and.description: Prenatal exposure to acetazolamide has been suspected, though not conclusively proven in humans, to contribute to congenital malformations including limb defects and growth restriction; exposure during organogenesis could potentially contribute to the observed abnormalities.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: An intermittent supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity and an irregular, often rapid ventricular rhythm that terminates spontaneously.

Frequent premature atrial contractions (.description: Early atrial beats arising outside the sinus node that may cause skipped beats, fluttering, palpitations, and may precipitate atrial tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.description: An episodic rapid heart rhythm originating above the ventricles, usually causing sudden palpitations and a regular rapid heartbeat; atrial tachycardia may occur in association with frequent atrial ectopy.

Alcohol-triggered atrial arrhythmia (hol.description: Atrial arrhythmias, most commonly atrial fibrillation, precipitated by acute alcohol intake, often in people without severe structural heart disease but more likely in those with cardiovascular risk factors.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, typically beginning in the rectum and extending proximally; severe disease can produce diffuse ulceration and purulent exudate.

Crohn disease involving the colon.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract and often causes patchy, deep, irregular ulcers with intervening granular or relatively normal mucosa.

Intestinal tuberculosis with possible ge.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis with possible genitourinary tuberculosis
Intestinal tuberculosis with possible ge.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can involve the gastrointestinal tract, producing chronic abdominal symptoms, weight loss, ulceration, and granulomatous colitis. Genitourinary involvement may cause dysuria, frequency, and urgency.

Amebic colitis.description: Colonic infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica that may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and discrete flask-shaped or irregular ulcers covered by exudate.

Primary colorectal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma involving the colon, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or other lymphoproliferative disorders, may cause weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhea, mucosal infiltration, ulceration, and abnormal vascular patterns.

Left hydropneumothorax.description: Accumulation of both air and fluid in the pleural space, producing an air-fluid level and partial collapse of the adjacent lung.

Spontaneous pneumothorax with pleural ef.description: Air in the pleural cavity causes lung collapse and pleuritic pain; associated pleural fluid creates a hydropneumothorax appearance on radiography.

Pyopneumothorax (empyema with bronchople.description: Infected pleural fluid together with pleural air, usually resulting from pneumonia, empyema, trauma, or communication between an airway and pleural space.

Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst.description: A pulmonary echinococcal cyst can rupture into a bronchus or pleural cavity, causing sudden chest pain, dyspnea, pneumothorax, hydropneumothorax, or an intrapulmonary air-fluid level.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation with infection or rupture
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A congenital cystic lung lesion may remain silent until childhood and can present with infection, air trapping, pneumothorax, or an air-fluid level if a cyst communicates with the airway.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of.description: A localized tumor of monoclonal plasma cells arising outside the bone marrow; hepatic involvement is rare. It is diagnosed when there is a solitary lesion without significant marrow plasmacytosis, myeloma-defining bone lesions, or a monoclonal protein.

Multiple myeloma with extramedullary hep.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with extramedullary hepatic involvement
Multiple myeloma with extramedullary hep.description: A systemic plasma-cell malignancy usually characterized by clonal bone marrow plasma cells, monoclonal immunoglobulin production, lytic bone lesions, anemia, renal dysfunction, and/or hypercalcemia. Liver masses can rarely represent extramedullary involvement.

Primary hepatic lymphoma.description: A lymphoma predominantly involving the liver, often presenting as a solitary or multifocal hepatic mass. Most cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, although other lymphoid neoplasms may occur.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes, most often arising in the setting of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C infection. It may be detected incidentally as a liver mass.

Gonorrhea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae cervici.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that can infect the cervix and cause increased or abnormal vaginal discharge, often developing within days to a week after exposure.

Chlamydia (Chlamydia trachomatis cervici.description: A common sexually transmitted bacterial infection of the cervix that is frequently asymptomatic but can cause vaginal discharge and cervical inflammation.

Trichomoniasis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, which can cause vaginal discharge, irritation, odor, and discomfort with urination or intercourse.

Bacterial vaginosis.description: A disruption of normal vaginal bacterial flora that commonly causes thin vaginal discharge and a fishy odor; it is associated with sexual activity but is not necessarily sexually transmitted.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis.description: A yeast infection of the vagina, usually caused by Candida species, which often causes thick vaginal discharge along with vulvar itching and irritation.

Giant bullous emphysema (vanishing lung.description: A severe form of bullous emphysema characterized by large air-filled bullae, often upper-lobe predominant, that compress adjacent functional lung tissue. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and cannabis use in younger patients.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.normalized_text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to bullous emphysema
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.description: Collapse of the lung from air entering the pleural space, occurring in a patient with underlying lung disease such as emphysema or giant bullae. Rupture of a bulla can precipitate sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness.

Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.normalized_text: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema
Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulm.description: A chronic progressive airflow-limiting disorder caused most commonly by tobacco exposure. Emphysema involves destruction of alveolar walls and may lead to hyperinflation, bullae, and secondary pneumothorax.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax associa.normalized_text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax associated with apical blebs or bullae
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax associa.description: A spontaneous pneumothorax usually occurring in thin individuals, often from rupture of subpleural blebs or bullae. Smoking substantially increases risk, and large bullae may complicate interpretation of chest imaging.

Multiple myeloma with aggressive extrame.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with aggressive extramedullary plasmacytoma
Multiple myeloma with aggressive extrame.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder characterized by monoclonal protein production, marrow infiltration, renal injury, anemia, hypercalcemia, and sometimes bulky extramedullary soft-tissue masses.

Plasma cell leukemia.description: An aggressive plasma-cell neoplasm in which malignant plasma cells circulate in peripheral blood, often causing severe marrow failure, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, high LDH, and extramedullary disease.

High-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma, such as.normalized_text: High-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
High-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma, such as.description: An aggressive lymphoid malignancy that can present with bulky abdominal or retroperitoneal masses, constitutional symptoms, marrow involvement, tumor lysis syndrome, and occasionally hypercalcemia.

Burkitt lymphoma or other highly prolife.normalized_text: Burkitt lymphoma or other highly proliferative B-cell lymphoma
Burkitt lymphoma or other highly prolife.description: A rapidly growing high-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with very high tumor burden, markedly elevated LDH, spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, abdominal masses, and possible marrow involvement.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.normalized_text: Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous PAN) with mononeuritis multiplex
Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries primarily affecting the skin, sometimes associated with peripheral nerve involvement. It commonly produces livedo racemosa, nodules, purpura, ulcers, and asymmetric peripheral neuropathy without major internal-organ disease.

Systemic polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause livedo reticularis or racemosa, mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension, renal ischemia, abdominal pain, and systemic inflammatory symptoms.

ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy, s.normalized_text: ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy, such as microscopic polyangiitis
ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy, s.description: Small-vessel systemic vasculitis may cause palpable purpura or other skin lesions and an asymmetric axonal neuropathy, often presenting as mononeuritis multiplex. It commonly has renal, pulmonary, constitutional, or inflammatory manifestations.

Classic homocystinuria due to cystathion.normalized_text: Classic homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
Classic homocystinuria due to cystathion.description: An autosomal recessive disorder of methionine metabolism causing markedly elevated homocysteine and methionine. It commonly produces a marfanoid skeletal habitus, ectopia lentis, myopia, osteoporosis, and thromboembolic risk.

Marfan syndrome.description: An autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by FBN1 variants, characterized by skeletal overgrowth, pectus deformity, scoliosis, ocular abnormalities including myopia and ectopia lentis, and aortic-root disease.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome.description: A hereditary connective-tissue disorder involving TGF-beta signaling, associated with arterial aneurysms and tortuosity, pectus deformity, scoliosis, craniofacial differences, and sometimes myopia.

Cobalamin-remethylation defect (for exam.normalized_text: Cobalamin-remethylation defect (for example, cblC disease or severe methionine synthase deficiency)
Cobalamin-remethylation defect (for exam.description: An inherited disorder of intracellular cobalamin processing or homocysteine remethylation that can cause severe hyperhomocysteinemia, neurologic disease, eye disease, and hematologic abnormalities.

Pontine cavernous malformation with acut.normalized_text: Pontine cavernous malformation with acute hemorrhage
Pontine cavernous malformation with acut.description: A cavernous malformation is a cluster of fragile abnormal blood vessels that can bleed. Hemorrhage within a pontine cavernoma can cause focal brainstem and long-tract neurological deficits and may obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow, producing hydrocephalus.

Spontaneous pontine intracerebral hemorr.description: Pontine hemorrhage is bleeding into the pons, which can injure corticospinal, sensory, cerebellar, and ocular-motor pathways. In a young adult without hypertension, an underlying vascular lesion such as a cavernoma or arteriovenous malformation should be considered.

Brainstem arteriovenous malformation wit.description: A brain arteriovenous malformation is an abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins. It can bleed into the pons and cause acute or subacute focal brainstem deficits, headache, and hydrocephalus.

Vertebral artery dissection with posteri.normalized_text: Vertebral artery dissection with posterior-circulation ischemic stroke
Vertebral artery dissection with posteri.description: Vertebral artery dissection is a tear in the arterial wall that can cause neck pain or headache and lead to ischemia in the brainstem or cerebellum. It is an important consideration in a young person with neck pain and posterior-circulation neurological deficits.

Brainstem glioma or other hemorrhagic po.normalized_text: Brainstem glioma or other hemorrhagic pontine tumor
Brainstem glioma or other hemorrhagic po.description: A pontine tumor can produce progressive cranial-nerve, long-tract, and cerebellar signs. Some tumors may bleed, but a focal hyperdense lesion with acute neurological deterioration is more suggestive of a vascular hemorrhagic lesion.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, transmitted by sandflies; amastigotes may be seen within macrophages in bone marrow and other reticuloendothelial tissues. It is endemic in parts of Central America.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. Small intracellular yeasts can resemble Leishmania in macrophages on bone marrow examination, and disease may cause fever, constitutional symptoms, and gastrointestinal involvement.

Acute pyelonephritis with sepsis.description: A bacterial kidney infection, often ascending from the urinary tract, that can produce high fever, systemic inflammatory symptoms, vomiting, dysuria, and flank or back pain.

Iliopsoas abscess or infectious myositis.description: A deep bacterial infection of the iliopsoas or adjacent pelvic musculature that may cause fever, sepsis, lower back pain, abdominal pain, and pain radiating to the groin.

Acute bacterial prostatitis with epididy.description: A genitourinary bacterial infection involving the prostate and possibly epididymis or testis. It commonly causes fever, dysuria, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, and scrotal or groin discomfort.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.normalized_text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), likely bisphosphonate- or denosumab-associated
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Progressive exposed necrotic jaw bone in a patient receiving antiresorptive therapy, commonly used for skeletal metastases. It may occur after oral surgery or reconstruction and can affect vascularized bone grafts.

Chronic osteomyelitis of the mandibular.normalized_text: Chronic osteomyelitis of the mandibular fibular free flap
Chronic osteomyelitis of the mandibular.description: Persistent infection and inflammation of bone that can cause devitalized bone, sequestration, mucosal breakdown, and exposed bone after mandibular reconstruction.

Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.normalized_text: Recurrent or progressive metastatic clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma involving the mandibular reconstruction
Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.description: Clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma can metastasize to bone, including the mandible, producing destructive osteolytic lesions and occasionally soft-tissue ulceration or pathologic bone exposure.

Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible.description: Radiation-induced hypovascular, hypocellular bone injury causing delayed bone exposure and necrosis, often after dental trauma or surgery in a previously irradiated jaw.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by myocyte necrosis, lymphocytic inflammation, and multinucleated giant cells. It often causes fulminant heart failure, ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, and cardiogenic shock.

Acute eosinophilic myocarditis.description: An inflammatory myocardial disorder caused by eosinophil-rich infiltration of the heart, sometimes related to hypersensitivity, medications, infection, or systemic eosinophilic disease. It can present abruptly with chest pain, heart failure, and cardiogenic shock.

Acute coronary syndrome with acute myoca.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock
Acute coronary syndrome with acute myoca.description: Acute myocardial infarction results from coronary artery occlusion and can cause ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation, and cardiogenic shock.

Acute viral lymphocytic myocarditis.description: Myocardial inflammation, commonly following a viral illness, that can cause chest pain resembling myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, impaired ventricular function, acute heart failure, and occasionally cardiogenic shock.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (ATS type 1, KCN.description: A rare autosomal-dominant channelopathy caused most often by KCNJ2 variants. It is characterized by ventricular arrhythmias, prominent U waves/QU prolongation, episodic periodic paralysis, and distinctive craniofacial and skeletal features. The reported KCNJ2 p.Gly406Arg variant is a classic pathogenic ATS-associated variant.

Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (LQT1.normalized_text: Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (LQT1, KCNQ1-related)
Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (LQT1.description: An inherited cardiac repolarization disorder in which adrenergic stimulation can trigger marked QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, syncope, or cardiac arrest. Events are often provoked by exercise, emotional stress, or catecholamine exposure.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricula.description: An inherited arrhythmia disorder, usually related to RYR2 or CASQ2, causing bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia during catecholamine stimulation, exercise, emotional stress, or anesthesia. The resting ECG and cardiac structure are often normal.

Timothy syndrome (LQT8, CACNA1C-related).description: A severe syndromic long QT syndrome caused by CACNA1C variants. It can produce marked QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, syndactyly, characteristic facial features, developmental abnormalities, and cardiac arrest in infancy or childhood.

Strongyloidiasis.description: Infection with Strongyloides stercoralis, a soil-transmitted intestinal nematode acquired in tropical and subtropical regions. It can cause chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, skin manifestations, and eosinophilia.

Hookworm infection.description: Intestinal infection with Ancylostoma or Necator species, usually acquired through skin exposure to contaminated soil. It may cause transient rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, eosinophilia, and chronic blood-loss anemia.

Toxocariasis (visceral larva migrans).description: A helminthic infection caused by Toxocara larvae, often acquired from contaminated soil or food. Larval migration can produce marked eosinophilia, rash, constitutional symptoms, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A disorder characterized by persistent, marked eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ involvement after secondary causes such as parasites, medications, and malignancy are excluded. It can affect the gastrointestinal tract, skin, spleen, and bone marrow.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm with sustained eosinophilia, often associated with constitutional symptoms, splenomegaly, marrow eosinophilic proliferation, and possible skin or gastrointestinal organ infiltration.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic.description: A highly malignant diffuse astrocytic brain tumor that can show necrosis, ring enhancement, extensive edema, and intratumoral hemorrhage. The imaging and immunohistochemical profile shown, including GFAP and Olig2 positivity with absent IDH1 staining and retained ATRX, are most consistent with glioblastoma.

High-grade astrocytoma with intratumoral.description: A malignant astrocytic glioma that may cause seizures, cerebral edema, necrosis, contrast enhancement, and bleeding within the tumor. Glioblastoma is the highest-grade and most likely form in this setting.

Oligodendroglioma, high grade.description: A diffuse glioma that commonly affects younger adults and often presents with seizures. Higher-grade tumors can enhance, become necrotic, and occasionally bleed, although molecular testing for IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion would be required for diagnosis.

Cerebral abscess.description: A focal collection of infection within brain tissue that may appear as a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema and can cause seizures or impaired consciousness.

Hemorrhagic brain metastasis.description: Metastatic tumors in the brain may bleed and present abruptly with seizures, coma, edema, and a contrast-enhancing mass. Melanoma, renal-cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid carcinoma are classic hemorrhagic metastases.

Histoplasma capsulatum vertebral osteomy.normalized_text: Histoplasma capsulatum vertebral osteomyelitis (disseminated histoplasmosis involving the lumbar spine)
Histoplasma capsulatum vertebral osteomy.description: A fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum that can disseminate from the lungs to bone, rarely causing destructive vertebral osteomyelitis and paravertebral inflammatory masses. Calcified thoracic lymph nodes/granulomas can reflect prior pulmonary histoplasmosis.

Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/disciti.description: Usually bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It can produce progressive pain, vertebral destruction, and paravertebral or epidural inflammatory collections.

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine causing slowly progressive vertebral destruction, disc involvement, paraspinal abscesses, chronic pain, and constitutional symptoms. It may occur without prominent pulmonary symptoms.

Spinal malignancy or metastatic vertebra.normalized_text: Spinal malignancy or metastatic vertebral disease
Spinal malignancy or metastatic vertebra.description: Cancer metastatic to the spine, or less commonly a primary spinal tumor, can cause progressive mechanical and nocturnal back pain, weight loss, vertebral destruction, and soft-tissue mass effect.

Disseminated talaromycosis (Talaromyces.description: A systemic fungal infection that can involve the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, soft tissues, and other organs, particularly in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: An invasive infection caused by Cryptococcus species that commonly affects the lungs and central nervous system but may disseminate to lymph nodes, skin, soft tissue, and the orbit.

Disseminated invasive aspergillosis.description: A severe mold infection, usually occurring in immunocompromised patients, that begins in the lungs and can spread hematogenously to the skin, orbit, lymph nodes, and other tissues.

Disseminated mucormycosis.description: A rapidly progressive invasive fungal infection caused by Mucorales molds that may involve the lungs, orbit, skin, and soft tissue, often producing tissue necrosis.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, lymph nodes, and extrapulmonary tissues, causing constitutional symptoms and diffuse pulmonary abnormalities.

Congenital Zika virus syndrome.description: Fetal neurologic injury caused by maternal Zika virus infection during pregnancy, which may include microcephaly, ventriculomegaly, cortical malformations, intracranial calcifications, and other brain abnormalities. Fetal infection can occur despite a negative amniotic-fluid NAT result.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A transplacentally acquired CMV infection that can cause fetal ventriculomegaly, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, growth restriction, hearing loss, and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Fetal cerebral aqueductal stenosis causi.normalized_text: Fetal cerebral aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Fetal cerebral aqueductal stenosis causi.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct impairs cerebrospinal-fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, typically causing enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11, spata.normalized_text: Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11, spatacsin-related hereditary spastic paraplegia)
Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11, spata.description: An autosomal-recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG11 mutations. It commonly causes progressive lower-limb spasticity, gait impairment, cognitive decline, dysphagia, white-matter abnormalities, and thinning of the corpus callosum.

Spastic paraplegia type 15 (SPG15, ZFYVE.normalized_text: Spastic paraplegia type 15 (SPG15, ZFYVE26-related hereditary spastic paraplegia)
Spastic paraplegia type 15 (SPG15, ZFYVE.description: A rare autosomal-recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia that resembles SPG11 and may produce progressive spastic paraparesis, intellectual/cognitive decline, dysphagia, white-matter disease, and a thin corpus callosum.

Spastic paraplegia type 21 (SPG21, Maspa.normalized_text: Spastic paraplegia type 21 (SPG21, Maspardin-related hereditary spastic paraplegia)
Spastic paraplegia type 21 (SPG21, Maspa.description: An autosomal-recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia characterized by slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, gait dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and sometimes dysarthria or swallowing difficulty.

Adult-onset leukodystrophy with heredita.normalized_text: Adult-onset leukodystrophy with hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotype
Adult-onset leukodystrophy with heredita.description: A group of inherited white-matter disorders that can present in adulthood with progressive pyramidal tract dysfunction, spastic gait, cognitive decline, and dysphagia. SPG11 itself may be considered within the broader complicated-HSP/leukodystrophy spectrum.

Functional mediastinal paraganglioma (ca.description: A catecholamine-secreting extra-adrenal neuroendocrine tumor arising from paraganglionic tissue in the mediastinum, often adjacent to the heart or great vessels. It commonly produces norepinephrine and can cause severe episodic hypertension.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal medulla that causes episodic or sustained hypertension, headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis. It is an important consideration during pregnancy because of major maternal and fetal risk.

Preeclampsia.description: A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation, usually associated with proteinuria and/or maternal organ dysfunction. Severe disease can cause headache and marked hypertension.

Hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis.description: Excess thyroid hormone production can produce sympathetic-like symptoms, including palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and systolic hypertension, but it does not usually cause marked catecholamine metabolite elevation.

Nocardia brain abscess (cerebral nocardi.description: A focal bacterial brain infection caused by Nocardia species, an opportunistic branching filamentous bacterium that commonly affects patients receiving chronic immunosuppression and can form ring-enhancing cerebral abscesses.

Pyogenic bacterial brain abscess.description: A localized collection of pus within the brain caused by bacteria, typically producing headache, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits, edema, and a ring-enhancing lesion on MRI.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: An opportunistic infection caused by Toxoplasma gondii that produces focal encephalitis and often multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in severely immunocompromised patients.

Cerebral aspergillosis.description: A fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by Aspergillus species, usually occurring in markedly immunocompromised patients and causing hemorrhagic infarcts, abscesses, or ring-enhancing lesions.

Glioblastoma.description: An aggressive primary glial brain tumor in older adults that can present with rapidly progressive focal neurologic deficits, cognitive changes, headache, edema, necrosis, and irregular ring enhancement.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A severe atypical bacterial pneumonia acquired by inhalation of aerosolized freshwater, often from lakes, plumbing, hot tubs, or air-conditioning systems. It can progress from focal to multilobar or bilateral infiltrates.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia d.normalized_text: Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia d.description: Pneumococcal pneumonia is a common cause of acute community-acquired lobar pneumonia, producing fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and focal bronchial breathing.

Community-acquired pneumonia due to Kleb.normalized_text: Community-acquired pneumonia due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Community-acquired pneumonia due to Kleb.description: Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause severe necrotizing or multilobar bacterial pneumonia, particularly in people with diabetes, chronic alcohol use, or impaired host defenses.

Melioidosis pneumonia (Burkholderia pseu.description: Melioidosis is an environmental infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired through contact with contaminated soil or surface water. Pneumonia may be acute, severe, multifocal, and more likely in patients with diabetes.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis is a chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A positive Mantoux test indicates prior sensitization but does not by itself establish active disease.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RA.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RAPSN deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to RA.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by impaired clustering of acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. It commonly presents in infancy with severe generalized and respiratory weakness.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to CH.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to CHRNE or other acetylcholine-receptor subunit deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to CH.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by reduced expression or abnormal function of the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Severe forms can cause neonatal respiratory insufficiency and persistent ocular-bulbar weakness.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MU.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MUSK deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to MU.description: A congenital neuromuscular-junction disorder caused by biallelic MUSK variants, disrupting formation and maintenance of the postsynaptic motor endplate. It may cause severe neonatal respiratory weakness, ptosis, and bulbar dysfunction despite negative serum MuSK antibodies.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LR.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LRP4 deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to LR.description: A rare postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by impaired agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling, leading to defective neuromuscular-junction development. Clinical severity ranges from neonatal respiratory failure to ocular, bulbar, and limb weakness.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to DO.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to DOK7 deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome due to DO.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by abnormal Dok-7 signaling at the neuromuscular junction. It usually produces limb-girdle, neck, and respiratory weakness, often with preserved reflexes and negative autoimmune antibodies.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, acute kidney injury, and calcium oxalate crystal deposition in urine.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion metabolized to formic acid, producing a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and often an elevated osmolal gap; it classically causes visual toxicity.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.description: A diabetic metabolic emergency caused by insulin deficiency, leading to hyperglycaemia, ketone production, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and Kussmaul respirations.

Salicylate poisoning.description: Aspirin or salicylate toxicity can cause agitation, tachypnoea, respiratory alkalosis followed by high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate in severe poisoning.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.description: A self-limited inflammatory thyroid disorder, often occurring after a viral upper-respiratory illness. It causes thyroid enlargement, neck discomfort, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and sometimes transient thyrotoxicosis.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis.description: A rare bacterial infection of the thyroid gland that can cause fever, neck swelling, thyroid pain, cellulitis, and sometimes formation of a thyroid abscess.

Viral thyroiditis associated with an acu.normalized_text: Viral thyroiditis associated with an acute viral upper-respiratory infection
Viral thyroiditis associated with an acu.description: Inflammation of the thyroid occurring during or shortly after a viral illness; common triggers include enteroviruses, influenza-like viruses, adenovirus, and other respiratory viruses.

Coccidioidomycosis (primary pulmonary or.normalized_text: Coccidioidomycosis (primary pulmonary or disseminated Valley fever)
Coccidioidomycosis (primary pulmonary or.description: A fungal infection caused by Coccidioides species, acquired through inhalation of spores in the southwestern United States. It commonly causes fever, fatigue, headache, and respiratory symptoms; extrapulmonary dissemination is uncommon but can involve many organs.

Lemierre syndrome (internal jugular sept.normalized_text: Lemierre syndrome (internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis after pharyngitis)
Lemierre syndrome (internal jugular sept.description: A potentially severe complication of pharyngitis, usually due to Fusobacterium necrophorum, characterized by persistent fever, unilateral neck pain or swelling, internal jugular vein thrombosis, and possible septic emboli.

Whipple disease.description: A rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, classically producing malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, and mesenteric lymph-node involvement. It can also involve the heart, nervous system, joints, and pancreas.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, usually causing abrupt upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Causes include gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia, medications, ischemia, and systemic disease.

Medication-induced pancreatitis or enter.description: Some medications, including certain lipid-lowering agents and other cardiovascular drugs, can cause diarrhea, liver-enzyme abnormalities, pancreatitis, or pancreatic enzyme elevation. Drug-related gastrointestinal toxicity may worsen after a dose increase.

Intestinal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma involving the small bowel or mesenteric lymph nodes can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, early satiety, weight loss, constitutional symptoms, and abdominal lymphadenopathy.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.normalized_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possible acute exacerbation
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of mesenteric arteries can cause intestinal ischemia, typically with postprandial abdominal pain, food avoidance, diarrhea, and weight loss. Severe acute ischemia can cause abrupt abdominal pain.

Disseminated gonococcal infection (gonoc.description: Systemic spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can cause migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and/or septic arthritis, often after asymptomatic genital infection.

Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis w.normalized_text: Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis with polyarticular involvement
Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis w.description: Bacterial infection of one or more joints, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing acute painful warmth, effusion, and restricted motion; polyarticular disease can occur with bacteremia.

Reactive arthritis following sexually tr.normalized_text: Reactive arthritis following sexually transmitted infection
Reactive arthritis following sexually tr.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis that develops after genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, commonly associated with Chlamydia trachomatis and sometimes gonococcal infection.

Lyme arthritis.description: A late manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection causing intermittent or persistent inflammatory arthritis, usually affecting large joints such as the knee.

Rheumatoid arthritis.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that typically causes symmetric small-joint synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness, and progressive joint damage if untreated.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Primary bilateral adrenal diffuse large.normalized_text: Primary bilateral adrenal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary bilateral adrenal diffuse large.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving one or both adrenal glands, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It commonly presents with fever, adrenal-region or back pain, elevated LDH, cytopenias, and bilateral adrenal masses without prominent peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive lymphoma in which malignant B cells proliferate mainly within small blood vessels rather than forming obvious lymph nodes or masses. It can cause persistent fever, high LDH, cytopenias, liver abnormalities, pulmonary findings, and adrenal involvement.

Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral adrenal tuberculosis
Disseminated tuberculosis with bilateral.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can disseminate and involve the adrenal glands, causing bilateral adrenal enlargement, fever, constitutional symptoms, anemia, abnormal liver tests, and eventually adrenal insufficiency.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with adrenal.description: Disseminated infection with Histoplasma can involve the reticuloendothelial system and adrenal glands, producing fever, cytopenias, liver enzyme elevation, bilateral adrenal masses, and adrenal insufficiency, especially in immunocompromised patients.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.normalized_text: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secondary to occult lymphoma or infection
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.description: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is a severe hyperinflammatory syndrome, often triggered by lymphoma or infection, causing persistent fever, rapidly progressive cytopenias, liver dysfunction, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers including LDH.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (PA.description: A congenital or acquired abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, creating a right-to-left shunt. Large lesions may produce a pulmonary bruit and exertional breathlessness.

Complex pulmonary arteriovenous fistula.description: A large or complex subtype of pulmonary arteriovenous malformation involving multiple feeding pulmonary arteries and/or draining pulmonary veins, often appearing as prominent tortuous vascular structures on contrast CT.

Pulmonary artery aneurysm with arteriove.normalized_text: Pulmonary artery aneurysm with arteriovenous communication
Pulmonary artery aneurysm with arteriove.description: An abnormal focal enlargement of a pulmonary arterial segment, sometimes associated with a congenital arteriovenous fistulous connection and turbulent blood flow.

Pulmonary venous varix.description: A localized dilatation of a pulmonary vein that can mimic a pulmonary vascular malformation on imaging; it is often congenital and may occasionally cause chest symptoms or a vascular murmur when associated with abnormal vascular flow.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: A fibroinflammatory manifestation of IgG4-related disease in which inflammatory tissue develops in the retroperitoneum, often around the aorta, ureters, and iliac vessels. Venous or lymphatic compression can cause severe bilateral leg edema.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A rare inflammatory condition causing fibrotic tissue to form around retroperitoneal structures, particularly the abdominal aorta, iliac vessels, and ureters. Compression of pelvic veins or lymphatic vessels may produce bilateral lower-limb edema.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can present as retroperitoneal soft-tissue masses or lymph node enlargement that compress the inferior vena cava, iliac veins, or lymphatic drainage, causing bilateral leg swelling.

Inferior vena cava or bilateral iliac ve.normalized_text: Inferior vena cava or bilateral iliac venous obstruction due to retroperitoneal mass effect
Inferior vena cava or bilateral iliac ve.description: Obstruction or compression of the inferior vena cava or common iliac veins can cause marked, symmetrical lower-limb edema. In this case, retroperitoneal fibrosis or another retroperitoneal process could be the underlying cause.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete collapse of a lung, occurring without known underlying lung disease; common in young otherwise healthy men.

Large left pneumothorax without tension.normalized_text: Large left pneumothorax without tension physiology
Large left pneumothorax without tension.description: A substantial collection of pleural air causing lung collapse but without clear clinical or radiographic evidence of hemodynamic compromise or major mediastinal shift.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening pneumothorax in which trapped pleural air increases intrathoracic pressure, potentially causing mediastinal displacement, impaired venous return, hypoxia, and shock.

Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis causing mitral regurgitation
Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.description: An autoimmune inflammatory complication of prior group A streptococcal streptococcal infection, characterized by migratory polyarthritis and carditis. Rheumatic valvulitis commonly affects the mitral valve and can cause acute mitral regurgitation and heart failure.

Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve regurgitation and inflammatory arthritis
Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, usually involving a valve, which can cause fever, a new or worsening regurgitant murmur, heart failure, and immune-mediated musculoskeletal manifestations.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory arthritis and cardiac involvement
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause constitutional symptoms, inflammatory joint pain, serositis, myocarditis, or valvular abnormalities. It occurs most often in young women.

Reactive arthritis.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis that develops after gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, usually affecting the lower extremities asymmetrically and sometimes accompanied by enthesitis, conjunctivitis, urethritis, or mucocutaneous lesions.

Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epi.normalized_text: Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epidural extension
Aggressive vertebral hemangioma with epi.description: A benign vascular lesion of a vertebral body that can enlarge into the epidural space or posterior elements, causing spinal canal narrowing and nerve-root compression.

Lumbar spinal epidural cavernous hemangi.description: A vascular malformation in the epidural space that may compress the thecal sac or lumbar nerve roots and mimic a disc herniation or nerve-sheath tumor.

Lumbar facet synovial cyst.description: A fluid-filled degenerative cyst arising from a lumbar facet joint, often causing lateral recess or foraminal nerve-root compression and sciatica.

Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopath.description: Displacement of lumbar disc material that compresses a nerve root, producing low-back pain and sciatica, commonly affecting one leg.

Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative disease
Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.description: Narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina from degenerative disc, facet, and ligament changes, leading to nerve-root compression.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML).description: A hematologic malignancy causing bone-marrow failure, often leading to fatigue from anemia and recurrent infections from neutropenia; persistent oral or perioral infections may occur.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infec.description: HIV progressively impairs immune function and can cause persistent or recurrent herpes simplex infection, recurrent throat infections, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).description: A chronic B-cell leukemia that may cause fatigue, painless lymphadenopathy, and increased susceptibility to recurrent bacterial or viral infections because of impaired immune function.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A group of lymphoid cancers that can present with cervical lymph node enlargement, constitutional symptoms, and immune dysfunction causing recurrent infections.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral cavity
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral.description: A malignant epithelial tumor that may present as a persistent nonhealing ulcer or crusted lesion of the lip and can spread to cervical lymph nodes.

Chronic enteropathy associated with SLCO.normalized_text: Chronic enteropathy associated with SLCO2A1 (CEAS), also called cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis
Chronic enteropathy associated with SLCO.description: A rare inherited small-intestinal disorder characterized by chronic superficial ulcers, multiple intestinal strictures, protein loss, gastrointestinal bleeding, and severe iron-deficiency anemia, often beginning in childhood.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and may cause diarrhea, intestinal ulceration, strictures, bleeding, malnutrition, anemia, and joint manifestations.

Intestinal Behcet disease.description: A systemic inflammatory vasculitic disorder that can produce deep intestinal ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal symptoms, anemia, and inflammatory arthritis; it is usually associated with recurrent oral or genital ulcers.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the ileocecal region, which can cause chronic diarrhea, ulceration, strictures, intestinal obstruction, bleeding, anemia, and low albumin.

NSAID-induced enteropathy with diaphragm.normalized_text: NSAID-induced enteropathy with diaphragm-like small-bowel strictures
NSAID-induced enteropathy with diaphragm.description: Chronic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can cause small-bowel erosions, ulcers, occult or overt bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, protein loss, and multiple short strictures known as diaphragm disease.

Dupuytren disease (Dupuytren contracture.description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia causing nodules and fibrous cords that progressively pull the fingers into flexion, most commonly affecting the ring and little fingers.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon and A1 pulley that can cause painful catching, locking, or inability to extend an affected finger.

Camptodactyly.description: A condition characterized by flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint, usually affecting the little finger and often beginning in childhood or adolescence.

Flexor tendon contracture due to prior t.normalized_text: Flexor tendon contracture due to prior trauma or scarring
Flexor tendon contracture due to prior t.description: Scarring of the flexor tendons, tendon sheath, or surrounding soft tissues can restrict tendon glide and result in finger flexion contractures.

Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to Treponem.normalized_text: Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to Treponema pallidum
Syphilitic lymphadenitis due to Treponem.description: Lymph-node involvement by syphilis, often producing prominent regional or generalized lymphadenopathy with follicular hyperplasia and plasmacytosis. Inguinal nodes are commonly involved, particularly with genital or anorectal infection; fever and other systemic symptoms may occur in secondary syphilis. The histologic appearance and spirochete staining are supportive.

HIV-associated lymphoma.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, is more common in people with advanced HIV and may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes and constitutional symptoms.

HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman.description: A lymphoproliferative disorder associated with HHV-8 and HIV that causes systemic inflammatory symptoms and generalized or regional lymphadenopathy. It can coexist with Kaposi sarcoma.

Bacterial inguinal lymphadenitis.description: Reactive or suppurative inflammation of inguinal lymph nodes caused by infection draining from the lower extremities, genital region, perineum, or anorectal area. In people with HIV, atypical and opportunistic bacterial infections are also possible.

Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal he.description: A complication of an inguinal hernia in which herniated bowel or tissue becomes trapped, potentially causing ischemia, obstruction, severe pain, and systemic illness.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor
Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor.description: A malignant small-round-cell tumor arising from bone or the chest wall, most often affecting children and adolescents. Rib involvement may cause pleural effusion, chest-wall pain, dyspnea, and referred shoulder pain.

Primary chest-wall Ewing sarcoma (periph.normalized_text: Primary chest-wall Ewing sarcoma (peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor)
Primary chest-wall Ewing sarcoma (periph.description: A subtype of the Ewing sarcoma family arising in the soft tissues of the thoracopulmonary region, historically called an Askin tumor. It commonly presents with chest-wall pain, a pleural mass or effusion, and respiratory symptoms.

Osteomyelitis of the rib with parapneumo.normalized_text: Osteomyelitis of the rib with parapneumonic pleural effusion or empyema
Osteomyelitis of the rib with parapneumo.description: Infection of a rib can cause focal bony pain and tenderness and may extend into adjacent pleura, producing pleural fluid and breathing difficulty.

Stress fracture or pathological fracture.normalized_text: Stress fracture or pathological fracture of the fifth rib
Stress fracture or pathological fracture.description: A rib stress fracture may occur after repetitive physical activity, including dancing, and causes focal pain and tenderness. A pathological fracture can occur when an underlying bone lesion weakens the rib.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib (eosinophilic granuloma)
Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib.description: A focal lytic bone lesion caused by proliferation of Langerhans cells, often affecting children and adolescents. It can involve ribs and produce persistent localized pain, tenderness, and occasionally a pathological fracture or pleural reaction.

Primary splenic Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A rare form of classical Hodgkin lymphoma initially confined to or predominantly involving the spleen, often producing constitutional symptoms and splenomegaly. The cytology images are suggestive of Reed-Sternberg-type cells with CD30-positive staining.

Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.normalized_text: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lym.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that may present as an isolated splenic mass or diffuse splenic enlargement with systemic inflammatory symptoms.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.description: A severe hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by excessive immune activation, often triggered by lymphoma or infection; it commonly causes fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, and very high ferritin levels.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection that can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, massive splenomegaly, anemia, and hyperferritinemia, particularly in endemic regions.

Splenic tuberculosis.description: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis involving the spleen can present with prolonged fever of unknown origin, weight loss, night sweats, anemia, splenomegaly, and splenic lesions.

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.normalized_text: Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) with cardiac involvement
Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) w.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the kidneys, heart, nervous system, skin, and eyes.
