Cardiac involvement commonly causes concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and myocardial injury.

Hypertensive heart disease with left-ven.normalized_text: Hypertensive heart disease with left-ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive heart disease with left-ven.description: Long-standing hypertension can cause pressure-overload left-ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, left-atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, and demand-related myocardial injury.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: A genetic myocardial disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, impaired diastolic filling, arrhythmias, chest discomfort, and possible elevated cardiac biomarkers.

Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.normalized_text: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory infarction)
Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.description: An acute focal cerebral infarction caused by interruption of arterial blood flow, often involving the middle cerebral artery in term newborns. It commonly presents in the first days of life with focal clonic seizures. The diffusion-restricted left cerebral lesion on MRI is consistent with acute ischemic infarction.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE).description: Brain injury caused by impaired oxygen delivery and/or cerebral perfusion around the time of birth. Neonatal seizures can occur during the first day of life, but HIE more often produces diffuse neurologic abnormalities and bilateral or widespread MRI injury rather than a single arterial-territory lesion.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage, includ.normalized_text: Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage, including hemorrhagic stroke
Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage, includ.description: Bleeding into brain tissue, ventricles, or surrounding spaces can cause neonatal seizures. In term infants, focal parenchymal hemorrhage or hemorrhagic transformation of an infarct may present with seizures, although MRI characteristics would need to demonstrate blood products to confirm this.

Native aortic valve infective endocardit.normalized_text: Native aortic valve infective endocarditis with severe aortic regurgitation and acute heart failure
Native aortic valve infective endocardit.description: Infection of the aortic valve, often bacterial, causing valve destruction or vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation, systemic inflammation, and decompensated heart failure. Dental manipulation can precede bacteremia and endocarditis.

Culture-negative infective endocarditis.description: Endocarditis in which routine blood cultures may be negative, often due to prior antibiotics or difficult-to-culture organisms such as Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, fungi, or HACEK organisms. It can still cause severe valvular regurgitation, emboli, and heart failure.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to severe aortic regurgitation
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Failure of the heart to maintain adequate circulation because of major leakage through the aortic valve. Severe acute or subacute aortic regurgitation can produce pulmonary congestion, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and rapidly progressive exercise intolerance.

Septic systemic embolization from infect.normalized_text: Septic systemic embolization from infective endocarditis
Septic systemic embolization from infect.description: Fragments of infected valve vegetation can embolize to systemic organs, causing painful infarcts or abscesses in the kidneys, spleen, spine, brain, or peripheral arteries. This is a complication of left-sided infective endocarditis.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, usually from venous thrombosis, causing acute or subacute dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and respiratory alkalosis. It is an important alternative cause of severe dyspnea in a young traveler, although it does not fully explain the murmur and inflammatory syndrome.

Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis with.normalized_text: Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis with portal venous thrombosis
Superior mesenteric vein thrombosis with.description: Occlusion of the superior mesenteric and/or portal venous system can cause mesenteric venous congestion, bowel-wall edema, abdominal pain, and inflammatory-marker elevation; it may progress to intestinal ischemia if untreated.

Mesenteric panniculitis.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is an inflammatory disorder of mesenteric fat that causes abdominal pain and CT findings of increased mesenteric fat density, sometimes with a pseudocapsule or small mesenteric nodes.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation usually presents with acute epigastric pain, nausea, and elevated serum lipase or amylase; severe cases can produce systemic inflammation.

Hematometrocolpos due to imperforate hym.description: Accumulation of retained menstrual blood in the vagina and uterus caused by congenital obstruction at the hymen. It commonly presents around puberty with pelvic pain and a midline pelvic fluid-filled mass containing internal echoes.

Hematometrocolpos due to a transverse va.normalized_text: Hematometrocolpos due to a transverse vaginal septum
Hematometrocolpos due to a transverse va.description: A congenital transverse vaginal septum can obstruct menstrual outflow, producing retained blood within the vagina and uterus (hematometrocolpos) and causing recurrent pelvic pain after menarche.

Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.normalized_text: Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly (OHVIRA syndrome)
Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.description: A Müllerian anomaly, typically uterus didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal agenesis, that may cause hematocolpos or hematometrocolpos and recurrent pelvic pain after menarche.

Acute appendicitis.description: Inflammation of the appendix, usually causing progressive abdominal pain that often migrates to the right lower quadrant and may be associated with fever, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia.

Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion associated with an ovarian cyst
Ovarian torsion associated with an ovari.description: Twisting of the ovary around its vascular pedicle, often in the presence of an ovarian cyst or enlarged ovary. It produces acute pelvic pain and requires urgent evaluation.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome caused by deletions of chromosome 11p11.2, commonly involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple osteochondromas/exostoses, enlarged parietal foramina, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, craniofacial differences, and growth impairment.

Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple.normalized_text: Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple osteochondromas), especially EXT2-related
Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder caused mainly by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, producing multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the metaphyses of long bones. EXT2 loss is also a major feature of Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.

11p11.2 deletion syndrome involving PHF2.description: A chromosomal microdeletion disorder of 11p11.2. Deletion of PHF21A contributes to neurodevelopmental impairment and craniofacial features, ALX4 deletion is associated with enlarged parietal foramina, and EXT2 deletion causes multiple exostoses; this combination is generally termed Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.

Crusted scabies (Norwegian scabies).description: A severe, highly contagious Sarcoptes scabiei infestation with a large mite burden, typically occurring in immunocompromised patients. It may present atypically with little or no itching and can cause widespread crusted, erosive, or ulcerated lesions.

Classic scabies.description: A superficial infestation of the skin by Sarcoptes scabiei mites, usually causing intensely pruritic papules, burrows, and excoriations, often involving the hands, wrists, axillae, waist, and genital region.

Ecthyma gangrenosum.description: A necrotic ulcerative skin infection classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia in neutropenic or otherwise immunocompromised patients. Lesions may evolve into painful necrotic ulcers with dark eschars.

ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic gl.description: A rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis caused by necrotizing and crescent-forming inflammation of glomeruli, often with little or no immune-complex deposition. It may occur despite negative ANCA testing and can be limited to the kidneys.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.normalized_text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (anti-GBM disease, renal-limited form)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target the glomerular basement membrane, producing severe crescentic glomerulonephritis. Some patients have kidney-only disease without pulmonary hemorrhage.

Immune-complex crescentic glomerulonephr.description: A severe form of glomerulonephritis in which immune-complex deposition causes glomerular inflammation and crescents, leading to rapidly progressive kidney failure. It may occur with lupus, infection-related glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, or other immune disorders.

IgA nephropathy with rapidly progressive.normalized_text: IgA nephropathy with rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis
IgA nephropathy with rapidly progressive.description: IgA nephropathy is an immune-complex glomerular disease that commonly causes hematuria; rarely, extensive crescent formation causes rapidly progressive renal failure.

Postinfectious glomerulonephritis with c.description: Glomerular inflammation following a bacterial infection, often streptococcal, that can produce hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and occasionally rapidly progressive renal failure due to crescents.

Myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma/ch.normalized_text: Myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma/chloroma) involving the extrahepatic bile duct
Myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma/ch.description: A localized tumor of immature myeloid cells that can occur outside the bone marrow, sometimes preceding or occurring without detectable acute myeloid leukemia. Rare involvement of the bile ducts can cause obstructive jaundice.

Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the bile duct
Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoma arising in or infiltrating the extrahepatic biliary tract can form a mass and produce obstructive jaundice. Most biliary lymphomas are B-cell lymphomas, although other hematolymphoid subtypes are possible.

Cholangiocarcinoma (hilar or extrahepati.normalized_text: Cholangiocarcinoma (hilar or extrahepatic bile duct carcinoma)
Cholangiocarcinoma (hilar or extrahepati.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts that commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice, cholestatic liver test abnormalities, and biliary ductal dilatation.

Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliar.normalized_text: Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliary tract
Histiocytic sarcoma involving the biliar.description: A rare aggressive hematolymphoid malignancy composed of histiocytic cells. It is generally CD45 positive and often lacks B-cell, T-cell, and NK-cell markers; extranodal involvement can produce mass-related obstruction.
